The original version of this article unfortunately contained a few errors.

In the Abstract Results, the percentage of male patients included in this study should be 60.6% and the sentence "From baseline (54.3%), TIR changed at week 12 (mean change 0.3% [+- 14.3]; p = 0.8383) and at week 24 (+ 4.5% [+- 14.9], p = 0.078)" should have read "From baseline (54.3%), TIR changed at week 12 (mean change 0.3% [+- 14.3]; p = 0.8383) and at week 24 (+ 3.0% [+- 14.9], p = 0.078)." The sentence "At week 24, there was a significant reduction in the HbA1c value (8.1 +- 0.6% vs. 7.7 +- 0.9%; p < 0.001)..." should have read "At week 24, there was a significant reduction in the HbA1c value (8.1 +- 0.7% vs. 7.7 +- 0.9%; p < 0.001)...".

In the Abstract Conclusions, the sentence "Although switching to Gla-300 in poorly controlled PwT1D did not significantly reduce TIR, it significantly decreased HbA1c values and glycemic variability without changes in BW and basal insulin dose" should have read "Switching to Gla-300 in poorly controlled PwT1D significantly decreased in HbA1c, improved time in range (TIR), reduced glycemic variability without change in body weight and basal insulin dose in 12 and 24 weeks."
In Table 1, the mean/SD value for male patients was given as 60.4 but should have been 60.6.

In the Results, Efficacy, Primary Endpoint section, the mean (SD) change at approximately week 24 was given as 4.5% but should have been 3.0%. The mean (SD) TBR (< 70 mg/dl) at baseline was given as 3.8% but should have been 3.9%. The sentence "However, TBR at 24 weeks was 0.1% +- 0.7 for BMI > 30 kg/m2 and 0.20% +- 0.8; n = 25 for prior insulin detemir treatment)" should have been "However, TBR at 24 weeks was 0.5%; +- 2.8 for BMI > 30 kg/m2 and - 1.0% +- 3.5; n = 25 for prior insulin detemir treatment)."

In the Results, Efficacy, Secondary Endpoints section, the sentences "At week 24 after switching to Gla-300, there was a significant reduction in the HbA1c value (8.1 +- 0.6% vs. 7.7 +- 0.9%; p < 0.001), a reduction in the CV% of plasma glucose (36.1 +- 12.4% vs. 32.8 +- 9.6%, p = 0.056), and increase in total insulin dose (51.4 +- 12.4% vs. 53.1 +- 27.53), increase in bolus insulin dose (26.5 +- 16.3 U/day vs. 27.9 +- 16.6 U/day; p = 0.042; Supplementary Fig. 1). FPG, BW and basal insulin dose were not significantly changed."

In the Results, Efficacy, Patient-Reported Outcome:Diabetes Treatment Satisfaction Questionnaire section, the sentence "Perceived frequency of hyperglycemia (item 2 of DTSQ) slightly decreased from 3.6 (+- 1.23, n = 93) at baseline to 2.94 (+- 1.39, n = 93) at approximately week 24 (change from baseline: - 0.62 +- 1.44)" should have read "Perceived frequency of hyperglycemia (item 2 of DTSQ) slightly decreased from 3.6 (+- 1.23, n = 93) at baseline to 2.94 (+- 1.39, n = 77) at approximately week 24 (change from baseline: - 0.62 +- 1.44)."

passages.text: Hereditary kidney disease with auditory abnormalities: analysis of mutations and clinical phenotypes

Clinical observations have indicated that multiple gene mutations can concurrently lead to both renal and auditory abnormalities. To explore the genetic basis of such conditions, this study first searched the PubMed database for relevant diseases and syndromes, followed by a literature review to identify representative diseases with high penetrance of both renal and auditory impairments. Building on this foundation, this review focuses on analyzing the genotype-phenotype correlations of eleven selected hereditary diseases and outlines their corresponding diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. Furthermore, to aid in clinical differential diagnosis, non-genetic factors that may cause renal and auditory dysfunction are also summarized. The findings of this study aim to deepen the understanding of these complex hereditary diseases and provide theoretical support for clinical diagnostic and treatment decisions.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12920-025-02178-5.
Introduction

The connection between the kidney and the ears was first introduced in the ancient Chinese medical text Huangdi Neijing - Suwen: Golden Coffer True Words. In modern medicine, Edith Porter first linked ear and kidney developmental abnormalities in 19461. With recent advancements in and widespread adoption of genetic testing technologies, an increasing number of related genetic disorders have been identified and reported, revealing that certain gene mutations can simultaneously cause both kidney and auditory abnormalities.

This paper primarily examines the correlation between genotype and clinical phenotype of the eleven hereditary diseases (Table 1), and outlines relevant diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. Furthermore, the study aims to comprehensively assess genetic and non-genetic factors associated with kidney and auditory abnormalities, summarizing shared features and individual characteristics, offering practical insights for clinical differential diagnosis.

passages.text: Methods
Clinical question

To guide this review, we formulated a clinical question based on the Population, Interest, and Outcome (PICO) framework: In patients presenting with concurrent kidney and auditory abnormalities (P), what are the responsible genetic mutations (I), and what are the correlations between genotype and clinical phenotype, as well as the associated diagnostic and therapeutic strategies (O)?
Search strategy

A multi-stage systematic literature search was performed. First, to understand the broader landscape of genetic links, a preliminary query was performed in the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) database for phenotypes "kidney abnormalities" (HP:0000077) and "auditory abnormalities" (HP:0000364). This initial step identified approximately 450 potentially associated genes (Supplementary Table S1) and served as a background exploration to illustrate the scope of genetic connections, rather than for primary study selection, as some associations may lack robust clinical validation.

Next, to identify clinically recognized genetic diseases for this review, a focused primary search was conducted in the PubMed database up to December 2024. The search strategy utilized the following Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and keywords: ("Kidney Diseases"[Mesh]) AND ("Mutation"[Mesh] OR "Genetic Diseases, Inborn"[Mesh]) AND ("Hearing Loss"[Mesh] OR "Deafness"[Mesh]).
Study selection: inclusion and exclusion criteria

The titles and abstracts of the retrieved articles were independently screened. For the diseases identified during this process, a more detailed literature review was conducted using the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) and Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) databases.
Inclusion criteria
Studies describing monogenic diseases or syndromes that present with both kidney and hearing abnormalities as recognized and recurrent clinical features.
Articles reporting specific gene mutations as the established cause for these concurrent phenotypes.
Original research articles, review articles, and case reports that provided clear genotype-phenotype correlations.
Exclusion criteria
Studies where the association between a gene and the phenotype was purely based on computational predictions without clinical validation.
Studies where kidney or hearing impairment was an incidental or non-recurrent finding.
Studies focused on acquired (non-genetic) causes of kidney and hearing disorders.
Data extraction and synthesis
The literature search and screening process is summarized in the PRISMA flowchart (Fig. 1).
Study flow diagram

Finally, we identified eleven hereditary diseases where the co-occurrence of kidney and hearing problems is most frequent and well-established. These diseases form the primary focus of this review (Table 1). The correlations between their respective genotypes and clinical phenotypes, along with diagnostic and therapeutic approaches, are discussed in detail. Diseases or syndromes where the association was less common were briefly summarized in the "1.12 Others" section.
Results
The association between genotype and clinical phenotype of eleven hereditary diseases and discussion of diagnostic and treatment strategies
Alport syndrome

Alport syndrome (AS) is caused by mutations in COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5, which encode the alpha3-alpha5 chains of type IV collagen. These mutations result in structural and functional abnormalities in the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), cochlea, and ocular basement membranes, causing impaired glomerular filtration, sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), and ocular abnormalities.
COL4A5 mutations are the most common, accounting for approximately 85% of cases.

As a result of the hemizygous X chromosome genotype in males, they exhibit more severe clinical manifestations, often progressing to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) by 20-30 years. Females, owing to skewed X-chromosome inactivation, show more variable clinical features and a lower incidence of ESRD. Among male X-linked Alport syndrome (XLAS) patients, 52.3-76% progress to ESRD, and 66.83-82.5% develop hearing loss, and this occurs irrespective of age.

Mutations in COL4A3 or COL4A4 are associated with autosomal inheritance. Approximately 14% of cases are autosomal recessive Alport syndrome (ARAS), and 1% are autosomal dominant Alport syndrome (ADAS). Compared to XLAS, these cases exhibit slower progression, with later onset of ESRD and fewer extrarenal manifestations. Rarely, biallelic mutations in COL4A3 and COL4A4 result in phenotypes that are intermediate between autosomal single-gene inheritance and XLAS.

For patients with persistent hematuria or hematuria with proteinuria, diagnosis may be based on the following: electron microscopy showing GBM abnormalities (e.g., lamina densa tears, stratification, irregular thickness, or a reticular appearance); immunofluorescence revealing abnormal type IV collagen alpha-chain staining; or genetic testing identifying pathogenic mutations in COL4A3, COL4A4, or COL4A5 per the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG). However, heterozygous pathogenic mutations in COL4A3 or COL4A4 alone are insufficient for diagnosing autosomal dominant ADAS. A definitive diagnosis requires clinical and pathological correlation, excluding conditions like thin basement membrane nephropathy.

At present, no curative treatment exists for AS. Early pharmacological interventions aim to slow disease progression, with renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) blockers as first-line therapy. Indications include males with XLAS, patients with ARAS, or biallelic mutations resembling ARAS/XLAS, as well as females with XLAS, ADAS, recurrent microalbuminuria or proteinuria unrelated to infection, or unclear genetic diagnoses with hematuria and proteinuria. For adult AS, sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors may be considered as an adjunct treatment option. In cases of aldosterone escape, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) may serve as an additional therapeutic option. Endothelin receptor antagonists (ERAs) emerge as a promising therapeutic strategy for AS. however, further research is required to establish their safety and efficacy.Once ESRD develops, renal replacement therapy is required. Patients with hearing loss are advised to avoid noisy environments and ototoxic medications. Hearing aids and cochlear implants may be recommended as appropriate.
MYH9-related diseases

MYH9-related diseases is an autosomal dominant disorder (ADD) caused by mutations in the MYH9 gene, which encodes non-muscle myosin IIA (NMMHC-IIA), a motor protein involved in cell migration, division, polarity, and morphology. Dysfunction of this protein results in multisystem impairments, including hematologic, renal, and auditory impairments. In the kidney, NMMHC-IIA maintains podocyte cytoskeleton integrity, and its dysfunction can cause proteinuria and hematuria. In the inner ear, it regulates hair cell function, and its dysfunction can result in SNHL.

Diagnosis of MYH9-related disorder relies on peripheral blood smear findings, family history, and specific laboratory tests. Key diagnostic features include giant platelets, elevated mean platelet volume, and abnormal platelet and leukocyte histograms. Family history of similar traits in first-degree relatives supports the diagnosis. Immunostaining of NMMHC-IIA inclusions in leukocytes is the diagnostic gold standard. Differential diagnosis must rule out conditions such as iron deficiency anemia, and screening for hearing, ophthalmologic, and renal function is recommended.

Treatment focuses on preventing bleeding risks, including avoiding platelet inhibitors (e.g., aspirin), maintaining oral hygiene, using nasal ointments for epistaxis, and addressing iron deficiency anemia to improve platelet-endothelial interactions. Hormonal regulation and antifibrinolytics can control heavy menstrual bleeding in women. RAAS blockers may slow kidney function decline. While no specific treatment exists for hearing loss, patients are advised to avoid exposure to loud noise. During surgery, desmopressin and tranexamic acid should be used,
alongside postoperative thrombosis prevention measures. Vaccinations (e.g., for pertussis and measles) are recommended to minimize the risk of bleeding and megakaryocyte injury.
Alstrom syndrome

Alstrom syndrome (ALMS) is an autosomal recessive disorder (ARD) recognized as both a multisystem metabolic disorder and a ciliopathy. The ALMS1 gene encodes the ALMS1 protein, which is essential for cell division, flagella and cilia formation, and is expressed across various tissues, contributing to multisystem involvement. It is critical for centrosome structure and function, maintaining epithelial cell polarity and primary cilia formation, which are essential for maintaining kidney function and supporting auditory hair cell activity critical to hearing.

Clinical symptoms of ALMS typically begin in infancy and worsen with age. Early signs include nystagmus and cardiomyopathy, and the most prevalent symptoms are vision and hearing impairments. Other manifestations include cardiovascular issues (e.g., myocarditis, fibrosis, congestive heart failure), endocrine abnormalities (e.g., childhood obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism), respiratory infections, chronic kidney disease, gastrointestinal issues (e.g., GERD, cecal volvulus), neurological symptoms (e.g., seizures, reflex impairment), and mental health problems (e.g., anxiety, depression).
Diagnosis primarily relies on genetic testing, with clinical features such as visual impairment, cardiomyopathy, and heart failure serving as key diagnostic indicators.

There is no curative treatment for ALMS. Management focuses on symptomatic interventions and slowing disease progression, including: 1.Monitoring BMI, body fat, and screening for and managing metabolic complications (e.g., obesity, type 2 diabetes) with appropriate interventions. 2. Regular kidney function assessments. 3. Ophthalmologic care and Braille training for vision loss, and hearing aids or cochlear implants for hearing impairment. 4. Routine cardiac evaluations and management of complications (e.g., heart failure, arrhythmias). 5. Preventing and treating respiratory infections. Given its multisystem nature, treatment should be individualized and multidisciplinary.
HDR syndrome

Hypoparathyroidism, deafness, and renal dysplasia syndrome (HDRS) is an ADD caused by mutations in the GATA3 gene. GATA3 encodes a key transcription factor widely expressed in various tissues, particularly in the kidneys, inner ear, and parathyroid glands. It regulates cell differentiation and function in these tissues, playing a crucial role in nephron formation, inner ear sensory epithelium function, and parathyroid cell differentiation.

annotations.text: Hypoparathyroidism, deafness, and renal dysplasia syndrome

passages.text: The main clinical features of HDRS are hypoparathyroidism, SNHL, and renal dysplasia. GATA3 mutations cause hypocalcemia and symptoms like tetany, with over 90% of patients experiencing hearing loss and 60-70% presenting with renal abnormalities, such as renal dysplasia, polyuria, or dysuria, or dysuria. Rare cases may also include skeletal anomalies or cognitive impairments.

There are no formal diagnostic guidelines for HDRS. However, a preliminary diagnosis can be made if a patient presents with the classic triad of hypoparathyroidism, sensorineural hearing loss, and renal dysplasia or two features alongside a family history. Genetic testing is required for confirmation.

Treatment is symptomatic and supportive, including: Calcium and vitamin D supplementation for hypocalcemia.Early use of hearing aids or cochlear implants for children with hearing loss. Monitoring asymptomatic renal cysts or small kidneys, with symptomatic renal or urinary tract conditions managed with appropriate medical or surgical interventions. Regular kidney function monitoring to prevent or delay progression to ESRD.Genetic counseling is recommended for affected individuals and their families.
Bartter syndrome type IV

Bartter syndrome (BS) is a heterogeneous hereditary tubulopathy resulting from defects in ion transport proteins in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle and/or distal tubules. Clinically, it is characterized by hypokalemia, hypochloremia, metabolic alkalosis, elevated plasma prostaglandin E2, high renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activity, and normal blood pressure. BS type IV by mutations in CLCNKA, CLCNKB, and BSND genes is linked to hearing impairment.

Type IV BS is an autosomal ARD divided into subtype IVa (caused by BSND mutations) and subtype IVb (caused by CLCNKA and CLCNKB mutations). BSND encodes Barttin, which maintains the activity of CLC-K channels, while CLCNKA and CLCNKB encode CLC-K channel subunits. CLC-K channels are primarily expressed in the distal tubules and inner ear, regulating sodium, potassium, and chloride balance. Mutations disrupt channel function, leading to impaired renal electrolyte transport, metabolic imbalances, and inner ear hair cell damage, causing kidney dysfunction and sensorineural or mixed hearing loss.

Family history, prenatal genetic testing, and amniotic fluid analysis can aid in early detection and diagnosis. Patients typically present with hypokalemia, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, and normal or low blood pressure, which differentiates BS from other potential causes of hypokalemia. Diagnosis is confirmed through genetic testing.

Treatment aims to correct electrolyte imbalances, prevent complications, and improve quality of life:1. For polyhydramnios in pregnant women, amniocentesis or cautious use of cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibitors may be considered.2. Encourage potassium- and magnesium-rich diets while discouraging foods that may worsen metabolic alkalosis or hypokalemia.3. If electrolyte replacement is inadequate, COX inhibitors can help. Potassium-sparing diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs may be used as adjunct therapy.4. Cochlear implants may enhance language development in patients with SNHL. Long-term follow-up is essential to assess treatment efficacy, monitor growth, and adjust therapy plans accordingly.
EAST/SeSAME syndrome

EAST/SeSAME syndrome ("epilepsy, sensorineural hearing loss, ataxia, salt-wasting, and intellectual disability") is an ARD caused by KCNJ10 gene mutations. This gene encodes the inward-rectifying potassium channel protein Kir4.1, a protein responsible for regulating potassium ion flow and maintaining cell membrane potential. Kir4.1 is predominantly expressed in the kidney, inner ear, and glial cells of the brain. Mutations impair Kir4.1 function, leading to significant electrolyte imbalances and neurological dysfunctions. Renal dysfunction leads to urinary loss of Na+, K+, and Mg2+, activation of RAAS, and hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Inner ear electrolyte imbalance damages hair cells in the cochlea, leading to SNHL.

Diagnosis is based on electrolyte disturbances and neurological abnormalities. KCNJ10 mutations cause hypomagnesemia, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, manifesting as epilepsy, ataxia, SNHL, and intellectual disability. Patients with these symptoms and/or a family history should undergo genetic testing.

Treatment focuses on individualized symptom management to improve quality of life, including:1. Antiepileptic drugs for seizure control.2. Electrolyte supplementation (Mg2+ and K+) to address deficiencies caused by renal dysfunction.3. Hearing aids for auditory support.4. Mobility aids and therapies to improve balance and coordination for ataxia.
Hereditary distal renal tubular acidosis

Hereditary distal renal tubular acidosis (dRTA) is caused by mutations in SLC4A1, ATP6V1B1, ATP6V0A4, FOXI1, and WDR72 genes, which impair acid secretion in distal tubules and collecting ducts, thereby impairing the kidney's ability to maintain acid-base homeostasis. ATP6V1B1 and ATP6V0A4 encode the B1 and A4 subunits of H+-ATPase and are typically inherited in an AR manner. H+-ATPase, located in distal tubular cells, regulates acid-base homeostasis and energy metabolism. SLC4A1 encodes anion exchanger 1. which is commonly associated with autosomal recessive inheritance in Asian populations, regulating HCO - reabsorption and urine acidification. Mutations in FOXI1 and WDR72 are linked to defective acid secretion in collecting ducts.

Renal symptoms of dRTA are characterized by acid-base imbalances, nephrolithiasis, and nephrocalcinosis. Extrarenal symptoms include hearing loss, rickets, growth retardation, and osteomalacia. H+-ATPase dysfunction in the inner ear disrupts electrolyte balance, resulting in SNHL. dRTA patients with ATP6V1B1 mutations often demonstrate a spectrum of hearing loss severity.

Diagnosis is based on clinical features and laboratory findings, including hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (normal anion gap), hypokalemia, persistently high urine pH (> 6.0), reduced titratable acid and NH4+ in urine, growth delay, or unexplained rickets. After excluding secondary causes (e.g., gastrointestinal disorders, diuretic use), genetic testing is recommended, especially in cases with hearing loss, to identify ATP6V1B1 mutations.

The primary treatment focuses on addressing metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia through alkali and potassium supplementation, preventing acute complications, and mitigating chronic complications such as growth retardation, nephrocalcinosis, and rickets. A new therapeutic drug, ADV7103, is a buffered combination preparation comprising potassium citrate and potassium bicarbonate, which has been approved by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for the treatment of dRTA.
Pendred syndrome

Pendred syndrome (PDS) is an ARD caused by mutations in the SLC26A4 gene, which encodes pendrin, a key ion transport membrane protein. Pendrin is responsible for chloride and iodide transport and is expressed in the apical membrane of thyroid follicular cells inner ear sensory cells, and renal intercalated cells. In the thyroid, pendrin supports iodide organification for thyroid hormone synthesis. Mutations impair this process, leading to goiter and hypothyroidism. In the inner ear, pendrin is essential for maintaining ionic balance and cochlear development. Mutations cause ionic imbalance, resulting in SNHL, which is a common cause of hereditary deafness and accounts for approximately 10% of such cases. In the kidney, pendrin regulates bicarbonate secretion during metabolic alkalosis, and its dysfunction increases the risk of metabolic alkalosis.

PDS diagnosis is primarily based on the presence of familial goiter and congenital SNHL. Hearing loss typically involves high frequencies, and is associated with reduced cochlear nerve responses, as observed in audiometry and auditory brainstem response testing. Inner ear imaging (CT/MRI) often shows structural abnormalities like enlarged vestibular aqueducts or dilated endolymphatic sacs and ducts. Thyroid ultrasound may reveal diffuse or nodular enlargement with elevated thyroglobulin levels. A positive hydrogen peroxide organification test may support the diagnosis, which is ultimately confirmed through genetic testing.

Treatment focuses on the management SNHL and goiter. Early hearing loss can sometimes be treated with corticosteroids and neurotrophic agents. Hearing aids or cochlear implants are recommended to address SNHL. Goiter is managed with thyroid hormone replacement, with surgery reserved for severe compression symptoms or suspected malignancy.
Fabry disease

Fabry disease (FD) is a rare X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in the GLA gene. These mutations reduce or eliminate alpha-Gal A enzyme activity leading to the accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) and its derivatives in various tissues, particularly affecting the kidneys, heart, central nervous system, and inner ear. Male patients, with only one X chromosome, typically exhibit more severe symptoms, while female carriers show variable severity due to X-chromosome inactivation.
FD is classified into two types based on GLA mutations and alpha-Gal A activity levels:

Classical FD is more common in males, with early symptoms in childhood or adolescence, including pain in extremities, angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis, gastrointestinal issues, and ocular/ear abnormalities. It progresses to severe kidney, heart, and cerebrovascular complications, often causing early mortality. Late-onset FD patients usually retain some alpha-Gal A activity, with symptoms typically appearing in adulthood. Organ involvement is milder and usually limited to the kidneys or heart.

Hearing loss is a frequent manifestation in FD, predominantly sensorineural but occasionally conductive or mixed. It resembles age-related hearing decline but starts earlier, progresses faster and is more severe. Tinnitus and sudden hearing loss are also frequent, especially in younger patients.

Diagnosis relies on clinical features, alpha-Gal A activity measurement, and genetic testing. In male patients, alpha-Gal A activity is typically reduced to less than 25-30% of normal levels. In females patients, alpha-Gal A activity demonstrates wide variability due to X-chromosome inactivation. Biomarkers like Gb3 and lyso-Gb3 are also useful.

The treatment includes: (1) enzyme replacement therapy (ERT): Recombinant alpha-Gal A (e.g., agalsidase alpha or beta) and the new ERT drug Pegunigalsidase-alpha (PRX-102) supplements the deficient alpha-Gal A enzyme, reduce Gb3 accumulation, delay organ damage, and improve mild to moderate hearing loss. (2) Enzyme Enhancement Therapy: Migalastat is suitable for patients with amenable mutations. (3) Substrate Reduction Therapy (SRT): Medications such as Lucerastat work by inhibiting the glycosphingolipid biosynthesis pathway to reduce Gb3 accumulation, representing a novel approach for treating FD. (4) Addresses specific symptoms such as pain, hearing loss, or organ complications.
Branchio-oto-renal syndrome

Branchio-oto-renal Syndrome (BORS) is an autosomal dominant disorder ADD caused by mutations in EYA1, SIX1, and SIX5. These genes are critical for the development of the ears, kidneys, and neck tissues during embryogenesis.

EYA1 is the most common causative gene, encoding the EYA1 protein, a transcriptional coactivator that regulates signaling pathways like Wnt/beta-catenin and Hedgehog, influencing cell proliferation and differentiation. In the kidney, EYA1 regulates genes related to the urea cycle and nephron development (e.g., WT1, WNT4), contributing to nephron formation. In the ear, it regulates the development of sensory hair cells and the cochlea. Mutations in SIX1 and SIX5 are less common. SIX1 encodes a transcription factor that activates genes like WNT4 and GDNF, essential for nephron, cochlear, and vestibular development. SIX5 mutations likely act synergistically with SIX1.

Clinical features of BORS include abnormalities in the ears, neck, and kidneys. Hearing loss, present in 64-100% of cases, is the most common feature, often as mixed hearing loss (MHL). Kidney anomalies, seen in 38-70% of patients, range from structural defects and agenesis to functional decline, significantly impacting long-term health.

annotations.text: abnormalities in the ears, neck, and kidneys

passages.text: Chang et al. proposed diagnostic criteria for BORS, combining major and minor features. Major features: (1) Branchial anomalies (e.g., cysts, fistulas); (2) Hearing loss (sensorineural, conductive, or mixed); (3) Preauricular pits; (4) Kidney abnormalities. Minor features: (1) Outer ear malformations; (2) Middle ear anomalies; (3) Inner ear anomalies; (4) Facial deformities; (5) Auricular tags; (6) Palatal abnormalities.Diagnosis requires meeting one of the following: three major criteria; two major and two minor criteria; or one major feature with a first-degree relative diagnosed with BORS. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.

infons.name: Renal Genital and Middle Ear Anomalies

passages.text: The treatment of BORS is primarily supportive. Uninfected preauricular and branchial cleft fistulas typically do not require intervention, but surgical excision is indicated when infection occurs. Hearing loss can be managed with hearing aids, cochlear implants, or middle ear surgery to improve auditory function. In cases with complex ear structural abnormalities, bone conduction implants and individualized hearing rehabilitation should be considered. Patients with renal malformations should undergo regular monitoring of kidney function and imaging, avoid nephrotoxic agents, while mild cases can often be managed pharmacologically. Severe cases may require dialysis or kidney transplantation.

Genetic counseling and prenatal diagnosis are crucial for families with known mutations. Emerging therapies such as gene and stem cell treatments offer potential cures. Gene therapy has partially restored hearing in animal models by introducing normal genes into the cochlea. Regulating Notch signaling in the cochlea may also promote hair cell regeneration, providing new approaches for genetic hearing loss.
Townes-brocks syndrome

Townes-Brocks Syndrome (TBS) is a rare ADD, also known as the anus-hand-ear syndrome. It is caused by mutations in the SALL1 gene, which encodes the SALL1 protein, a zinc-finger transcriptional repressor. SALL1 suppresses specific gene expression by binding DNA or RNA and is thought to function as part of the NuRD histone deacetylase complex (HDAC), associated with chromatin condensation and transcriptional repression.

SALL1 is critical for the development of multiple organ systems during embryogenesis. In the kidney, it plays a critical role in ureteric bud formation and orientation, and mutations disrupt nephron development. In the ear, mutations impair inner ear formation, resulting in SNHL as well as outer and middle ear anomalies.

infons.name: Renal Genital and Middle Ear Anomalies

passages.text: The common clinical phenotypes of TBS include ear malformations (such as microtia, auricular deformities, external auditory canal atresia, and protruding ears), anorectal malformations (such as rectal malformations, anal stenosis, and atresia), hand and foot deformities (such as polydactyly, triphalangeal thumb deformity, and thumb clefts), and renal developmental abnormalities (such as renal hypoplasia, unilateral or bilateral renal agenesis, multicystic renal dysplasia, and horseshoe kidney). Some patients may progress to ESRD, which may require dialysis or kidney transplantation. Additionally, a small proportion of TBS patients may present with cardiovascular abnormalities (such as ventricular septal defects) or cognitive impairment.

infons.name: External Auditory Canal Bilateral Atresia Of With Congenital Vertical Talus

passages.text: Diagnosis is based on characteristic clinical features: anorectal malformations, ear anomalies, and thumb deformities. Secondary features include hearing loss, foot deformities, renal impairment, genitourinary anomalies, and congenital heart disease. Due to the phenotypic variability of TBS, genetic testing is critical for confirming the diagnosis.

Treatment of TBS involves a multidisciplinary and individualized approach: Early use of hearing aids for hearing loss. Immediate surgical repair for anal atresia. Corrective surgery for severe hand deformities. Regular monitoring of kidney function, with dialysis or transplant as needed. Surgical or medical intervention for congenital heart defects. Avoidance of nephrotoxic and ototoxic medications. Genetic counseling and risk assessment for family members are crucial for early identification and effective management of potential cases.
Other

In addition to the aforementioned diseases, several genetic disorders and associated mutations have a less prominent association with renal and auditory abnormalities or exhibit reduced phenotypic expression and are therefore not discussed in detail. These include Bardet-Biedl syndrome, Dent disease, Galloway-Mowat syndrome, Kallmann-De Morsier syndrome, Lowe syndrome, Lowe-like syndrome, Muckle-Wells syndrome, Nail-patella syndrome, NSDHF syndrome, Okihiro syndrome, Senior-Loken syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, Wolfram syndrome, as well as certain mitochondrial disorders, such as MELAS syndrome and RMND1-related diseases. The relevant mutated genes are listed in Appendix 1.

Non-genetic etiological factors can contribute to renal and auditory dysfunction, including: (1) Drug-induced renal and auditory damage, including aminoglycoside antibiotics (e.g., gentamicin, kanamycin, neomycin), other antibiotics and antimicrobial agents (e.g., besifloxacin, with reversible ototoxicity; erythromycin; isoniazid), immunosuppressive drugs (e.g., tacrolimus, ipilimumab), chemotherapy agents (e.g., cisplatin, methotrexate, doxorubicin, and their combination therapies, such as cisplatin combined with kanamycin), as well as specific treatments (e.g., inhaled tobramycin, intratympanic corticosteroid injections), and other drugs, including methadone, furosemide, and first-line anti-tuberculosis medications; (2) Bromate poisoning; (3) Parasitic infections, such as scrub typhus; (4) Chronic kidney disease (CKD): Studies indicate that patients with CKD have an increased risk of developing sudden-onset SNHL and Meniere's disease compared to the general population possibly due to delayed transmission between the auditory nerve and auditory pathways, which results in hearing impairment. (5) In patients with ESRD, anemia has also been identified as a significant factor contributing to hearing impairment.
Differential diagnosis

For patients with kidney and hearing impairments, differential diagnosis should be guided by medical history and clinical presentation.When a patient presents with hearing impairment and glomerular dysfunction, AS should be prioritized as a potential diagnosis. If accompanied by hematologic abnormalities, MYH9-related disease may warrant consideration. FD can often be identified through symptoms such as peripheral neuropathy and skin angiokeratomas, while multisystem involvement in infants suggests the possibility of ALMS.

When damage involves the renal tubules or interstitium, conditions such as HDRS, BS-IV, and EAST/SeSAME syndrome should be considered. These may be further differentiated based on the characteristics of metabolic acid-base imbalances and electrolyte disturbances.
Additionally, BORS and TBS are marked by distinctive developmental anomalies, which can be identified based on abnormalities in the ears, face, and kidneys.See Fig. 2 for the diagnostic flowchart.

Differential Diagnosis of Patients with Kidney Dysfunction and Hearing Impairment. For patients with renal and hearing impairment, non-genetic etiologies should be excluded first. When patients exhibit hearing impairment and glomerular dysfunction (such as hematuria and proteinuria), Alport syndrome should be considered as a priority. If there are accompanying hematologic abnormalities, such as platelet dysfunction leading to bleeding tendencies such as epistaxis, gingival bleeding, and skin ecchymosis, MYH9-related disease should be highly considered. Fabry disease should be considered based on the presence of symptoms such as distal sensory abnormalities, cutaneous vascular keratomas, hypohidrosis or anhidrosis, and corneal opacity. For patients who present with multi-systemic involvement, including vision impairment, obesity, heart disease, and diabetes during infancy or early childhood, Alstrom syndrome should be highly suspected. When patients exhibit hearing impairment and renal tubular or interstitial dysfunction, differential diagnoses should include hypoparathyroidism, deafness, and renal dysplasia syndrome, Bartter syndrome type IV (BS-IV type), EAST/SeSAME syndrome, hereditary distal renal tubular acidosis (dRTA), and Pendred syndrome (PDS). If metabolic alkalosis, hypokalemia, and hypochloremia are present, BS-IV type should be considered as a priority. If severe metabolic alkalosis is accompanied by hypothyroidism or goiter, PDS should be suspected. On the other hand, if metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia are observed, EAST/SeSAME syndrome or dRTA should be considered. EAST/SeSAME syndrome is particularly characterized by disturbances in multiple electrolytes and neurological manifestations such as hypomagnesemia, hyponatremia, hypochloremia, epilepsy, ataxia, and intellectual disability. In contrast, dRTA is primarily associated with renal tubular dysfunction and may present with hypokalemia and acidosis. Branchio-Oto-Renal Syndrome (BORS) and Townes-Brocks Syndrome (TBS) exhibit distinct clinical features when compared to the previously mentioned conditions, with multi-system developmental anomalies often evident in the neonatal period. When developmental abnormalities are observed in the external ear, kidneys, face, and oral cavity, BORS should be suspected. Conversely, if malformations are noted in the ears, anus, hands and feet, and kidneys, TBS should be considered as a possible diagnosis.

Following the clinical assessment and differential diagnosis, which considers the patient's history, symptoms, and the approach outlined (see Fig. 2), genetic testing becomes a critical next step. This testing aims to confirm suspected hereditary kidney and hearing diseases. It also helps establish a precise molecular diagnosis.

Doctors have several genetic testing tools. Each tool offers unique benefits for specific clinical situations. For example, if a distinct syndrome like AS is strongly suspected from the initial findings, doctors might choose targeted Sanger sequencing for known AS genes. A focused gene panel could also be appropriate. However, when symptoms are less typical, overlap between conditions, or suggest a broader multisystem disorder like ALMS, comprehensive tests are very valuable. These include Whole Exome Sequencing (WES) or Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS). These methods can examine many genes at once.

A thorough understanding of how genotypes relate to clinical phenotypes is essential. This knowledge guides both the choice of tests and the interpretation of their results. Ultimately, this understanding is key for an accurate diagnosis.
Limitations

This review has several potential limitations. Firstly, our focus on well-documented genetic diseases, guided by our specific PubMed search strategy, means that this review might not cover every possible syndrome. Some rare, newly discovered, or atypical syndromes involving both kidney and hearing issues could be excluded. Secondly, the disease selection process itself introduces a potential limitation. The interpretation of the significance of clinical symptoms, while based on published literature by our team, can inherently carry a degree of subjectivity.
Conclusion

In clinical practice, genetic diseases often present with multi-organ involvement, and synchronous damage to the kidneys and auditory system is relatively common in patients with hereditary kidney diseases. However, clinicians (especially nephrologists) may have limited awareness of the broader spectrum of genetic diseases that can cause both renal and hearing impairments, beyond well-known conditions like AS and FD. This knowledge gap can hinder early diagnosis and effective intervention.Our review addresses this by focusing on 11 hereditary diseases with high clinical phenotype expression rates in both the kidney and auditory systems. We have summarized their pathogenic genotypes, pathogenesis, clinical characteristics, diagnostic strategies, and treatment progress. We aim for this review to fill a gap in the existing literature regarding comprehensive reviews of "kidney-hearing" related genetic syndromes.

Our synthesis reveals several primary pathogenic mechanisms underpinning these "kidney-hearing" syndromes. A significant group of disorders, including AS, MYH9-related diseases, ALMS, and HDRS, primarily impact renal function and hearing by influencing the expression of structural proteins encoded by specific gene mutations in the kidneys and inner ears. Damage to these key proteins due to genetic mutations often leads to renal dysfunction and hearing loss. A separate group of disorders, such as BS-IV type, EAST/SeSAME syndrome, dRTA, and PDS, cause renal and auditory impairment by disrupting ion pump functions, which result in electrolyte imbalances affecting both the inner ear and kidneys. Additionally, FD, which results from an enzyme deficiency, causes lysosomal storage disorders that indirectly affect kidney and inner ear function. These conditions frequently present with sudden SNHL as a common manifestation.

The pathogenesis of diseases such as BORS and TBS involves gene mutations during embryonic development that affect organ formation, leading to structural abnormalities in the kidney and ear, which subsequently impair their function.
The above genetic mutations, except for BORS, which primarily causes MHL, are predominantly linked to SNHL.

Additionally, certain genetic disorders, such as Bardet-Biedl syndrome and Dent disease, and specific gene mutations, may present with renal impairment and hearing loss; however, phenotypic expressivity in these conditions is typically low. Further research is required to better understand the correlation between genotype and phenotype.

In clinical practice, when encountering patients with both renal dysfunction and hearing impairment, the most likely diagnoses should be prioritized based on distinct clinical presentations and supporting test results, and genetic testing should be utilized when necessary. During the differential diagnosis process, not only should the aforementioned genetic conditions be considered, but non-genetic factors contributing to renal dysfunction and hearing impairment should also be ruled out to ensure a thorough and accurate diagnosis.
Ultimately, this review aims to serve as a valuable and practical reference for clinical professionals : particularly in nephrology, otolaryngology, and genetic counseling.

passages.text: Effects of molecular interactions between the exposome and oxylipin metabolism on healthspan

While aging is typically synonymous with the lifespan of an individual, the healthspan, or the total number of years an individual remains healthy and disease-free, is not necessarily related. A current, critical need in society has arisen as current populations are living longer than previous generations, thus increasing the number of people with age-associated diseases. However, the extent of all age mechanisms is not entirely known. Still, studies examining how the exposome, or an individual's cumulative exposures throughout their life, can influence or modulate aging processes will strengthen our understanding of how to keep individuals healthy and disease-free longer, bridging the gap between lifespan and healthspan. In contrast, previous research has also demonstrated that the exposome impacts aging. One subcategory of the exposome, the specific external, encompasses daily exposures such as diet, lifestyle factors, and occupational and environmental exposures. In this review, we focus on the interactions between factors of the exposome, such as vitamins and minerals, and their effects on aging, cell death, cellular senescence, and unsaturated fatty acid metabolism. We also discuss the interaction between oxidative fatty acid metabolism and aging itself. Overall, understanding how various exposures impact both the oxylipin profile and healthy aging will inform future interventions aimed at improving the healthspan and quality of life for this large aging population.
Graphical Abstract
The goal of this review is to highlight the current understanding of the interactions between the exposome and oxylipin metabolism on healthy aging.
1 Introduction-aging

Aging is a natural, ubiquitous process that refers to the progressive deterioration of functions and regulatory processes, resulting in a reduced ability to maintain homeostasis when challenged by external stresses and increases the interindividual variability in physiological responses. While the extent of all aging mechanisms is not entirely known, the current understanding of these complex mechanisms involves a combination of genetic, molecular, and environmental factors. Largely, aging is induced by the accumulation of damage due to exposure and response to a variety of stresses. In the field of aging research, hallmarks of aging have been established including genomic instability, telomere attrition, epigenetic alterations, loss of proteostasis, deregulated nutrient-sensing, mitochondrial dysfunction, cellular senescence, stem cell exhaustion, and altered intracellular communication. As more insights on aging mechanisms have been uncovered, these hallmarks have been expanded upon to include disabled macroautophagy/compromised autophagy, chronic inflammation, and dysbiosis.
1.1 Increased lifespans in current populations

In the past 70 years alone, the human population has almost tripled, from 2.9 billion (1950) to 7.8 billion (2020). With continued societal and medical progress, the world population is expected to continue this steep increase in the coming decades. This increase in population is partially due to current generations living longer than previous generations with the average life expectancy increasing from 47 to 73 years of age in this same time span. However, lifespan and healthspan, which is defined as the total number of years an individual remains healthy and disease-free, are not directly correlated. Decline in the healthspan and quality of life of elderly populations is largely due to age-associated diseases, leading to disability, frailty, and morbidity in these populations. Aging is a major risk factor and driver of a variety of health diseases and conditions affecting elderly populations. Specifically, aging has been shown to be a major risk in chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease (CVD), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, Alzheimer's disease (AD), and Parkinson's disease (PD). Thus, understanding the aging mechanism and how aging impacts healthspan will lead to novel interventions to improve the healthspan and the quality of life of this large aging population. Understanding the implications of perturbations to aging processes by the exposome, defined as an individual's cumulative exposure throughout their life-can inform intervention methods to keep individuals healthy and disease-free longer, bridging the gap between lifespan and healthspan.
1.2 Current understanding of aging mechanisms, and the influence of the exposome and oxylipin profile on aging

Aging is a complex, multifaceted process that involves the interplay of various mechanisms. Multiple theories explaining the molecular mechanisms of aging have been postulated. Most of these theories can be separated into two main categories: programmed and damage or error theories. Programmed theories suggest that aging is driven by genetically programmed pathways that limit the lifespan based on changes in gene expression for maintenance, repair, and defense response systems. Underneath the overarching branch of programmed theories are the programmed longevity, endocrine, and immunological theories. However, damage or error theories suggest that aging is the result of damage accumulation (i.e., ROS, DNA mutations, protein misfolding) in cells and tissues from cumulative environmental exposures over time. Aging effects result from the decline in the body's ability to repair this damage with age, leading to cellular dysfunction. However, one of the main characteristics of aging overall is the accumulation of cellular damage. Thus, many of the interactions of the aging hallmarks, cellular damage, and oxidative stress are summarized in Table 1.

Decades of research have demonstrated that aging is impacted by the exposome. Exposome is broadly defined by environmental exposures which people face in everyday life. For example, a recent epidemiological study by Argentieri et al. conducted an exposome-wide analysis of all-cause mortality using the UK Biobank data and identified that 25 specific exposures are associated with proteomic aging. While specific mechanisms on how the exposome impacts aging remain understudied, research has shown that the exposome, including diet, modulates endogenous unsaturated fatty acid metabolism, which generates hundreds, if not thousands, of lipid metabolites. These unsaturated fatty acid metabolites are key signaling molecules in many aspects of human physiology. For example, prostaglandins play an important role in inflammation, vascular tone, and pain perception. Recent studies also demonstrated that prostaglandins and the associated metabolic enzymes impact aging. However, the effects and associated mechanism of the exposome and unsaturated fatty acids metabolism on aging are underexplored. This review will discuss how senescence and aging pathways can be influenced by specific dietary and environmental exposures of the exposome (vitamins, metals, PUFAs, and oxylipins) and how the exposome can influence oxylipin (oxygenated polyunsaturated fatty acid derivative) metabolism. Overall, the review will examine how these exposures can impact healthy aging.
2 Exposome

The exposome (Figure 1) encapsulates all of the environmental (non-genetic) exposures experienced by an individual from an array of dietary, lifestyle, and demographic factors throughout the lifespan that impact health outcomes. Some researchers have broadened the definition of the exposome to include additional factors examining how the body reacts to environmental factors such as biological responses, behavior, and endogenous processes. The exposome includes a network of unique characteristics and exposures of an individual that may result in them being more or less susceptible to particular stressors in their environment. Overall, the exposome can be broken into three subcategories: internal, specific external, and general external. Despite the distinct exposure classifications, these subcategories are considered to be both overlapping and intertwining, and differentiating factors between these categories can be difficult. While all three subcategories are vitally important in understanding how the exposome impacts human health and disease, this review will focus on the molecular interactions of specific external factors on aging and oxidative lipid metabolism. Thus, the internal and general external factors are out of scope for this review and have been extensively reviewed elsewhere. Here, we will discuss these briefly below and the corresponding reviews for specific exposomal effects on health have been included.

The complete exposome. The exposome can be divided into three subcategories-internal, general external, and specific external, with these subcategories overlapping and intertwining with each other. Overall, the exposome consists of total exposures an individual is exposed to in their lifetime. Created with BioRender.
2.1 Internal

The internal or endogenous factors of the exposome encompass those that are specific to an individual. Specifically, these encompass the internal factors relating to host factors or the impact on cellular environments and processes. Internal factors can include physiology, aging, body morphology/somatotype, physical activity, and genome. These internal exposures can typically be measured using biomarkers of these endogenous processes.
2.2 General external

Despite overall exposures to the same environmental nuisances, individuals and groups can be impacted differently, and these differences can be partly attributed to the general external exposome. The general external factors are considered the social determinants of health as well as the wider effects of social, economic, and physiological status on health and disease. General external factors specifically consist of influences from location, education level, socioeconomic status - including food insecurity -, and physiological and mental stress.
2.3 Specific external

Specific external factors include those that have been most extensively studied in epidemiological studies examining exposure and environmental risk factors in disease. These factors include daily exposures attributed to diet, lifestyle factors, medical interventions, occupational and environmental exposures. Overall, external factors can be measured using survey instruments and personal sampling (recording). The effect of exposures classified under specific external exposome will be discussed in detail below.
3 Specific external exposome and aging healthspan

The most expansive exposure pathway includes ingestion of exogeneous materials ranging from dietary choices, lifestyle factors (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, caffeine), and medical interventions, namely, pharmaceuticals. Many of these exposures are chronic exposures, potentially leading to serious long-term health effects. Another common source of chronic exposures is external exposure to a host of occupational and environmental agents, including radiation, noise, infectious agents (i.e., pathogens), chemical contaminants, environmental pollutants, and additional occupational exposures (i.e., crystalline silica, diesel exhaust, radon, wood dust). While precautions for environmental and occupational exposure limits are in place, these direct or indirect potential occupational and environmental exposures can result in both short- and long-term health effects, leading to health disparities.

Apart from the abovementioned environmental toxicants, some of the other specific external exposures, specifically dietary choices, can have beneficial effects on health and healthy aging. The association between diet and oxidative stress and inflammatory processes has been widely examined. Plant-based diets consisting of anti-inflammatory and antioxidant-rich foods are associated with decreased levels of oxidative stress and inflammatory biomarkers, which have been extensively reviewed elsewhere. However, individual components of these diets (vitamins, polyunsaturated fatty acids) and specific metal exposures on healthy aging have not been extensively reviewed and will be discussed below.
3.1 Micronutrients

There are many crucial nutrients that are required for endogenous functions that must be obtained throughout the diet. Many of these play crucial roles in supporting various bodily functions, reducing oxidative stress, and maintaining cellular integrity. However, the absorption, metabolism, and utilization of these nutrients can decline with aging, resulting in a loss of protection against cellular processes. Aging-related changes may also affect dietary intake in older adults due to increased difficulty chewing and swallowing, changes in taste and smell, poor appetite, and self-restriction, all of which may result in deficiencies in obtaining the recommended dietary allowance of nutrients necessary for physiological functions. Conversely, some of these nutrients can trigger aging-related mechanisms such as cell death, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction.
3.1.1 Vitamins

Vitamins can be classified as either fat- or water-soluble. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored and accumulated in the liver and lipid tissues. Thus, some fat-soluble vitamins can be toxic if taken in excess. Meanwhile water-soluble vitamins (B and C) are not stored in the body as any excess is excreted and these vitamins need to be consumed regularly to prevent deficiencies. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2020-2025 details the daily nutritional goals for the essential vitamins needed at each age range. However, these guidelines have an upper age of 51+ years and thus do not consider the variability in absorption and utilization that may occur for later aging stages in life. Due to the antioxidant and oxidative stress reducing roles that vitamins play in vivo, more comprehensively understanding their effects in aging is of great interest in current geroscience research.

Several vitamins regulate programmed cell death mechanisms, with consequent implications in aging. While the role of vitamins in cell death, cellular senescence, and aging is not the focus of this review, we summarize the findings of vitamins in cell death/cellular senescence and aging in Tables 2, 3, respectively. The main mechanism of vitamin involvement in these processes is throughout their modulation of oxidative stress and interactions with antioxidant enzymes and vitagenes (i.e., genes that maintain cellular homeostasis during stressful conditions). This may potentially impact lipid oxidation, modulating oxylipin synthesis as vitamins A, B, E, and K have been shown to decrease or prevent lipid peroxidation, thereby inhibiting ferroptosis. Interactions with vitamins A and D also result in the upregulation of antioxidant enzymes to prevent cellular senescence, while a vitamin K-dependent protein (VKORC1) limits ROS production, also inhibiting cellular senescence. Likewise, vitamins A, B, E, and K have been shown to directly protect against cognitive decline and age-associated neurodegenerative diseases. In summary, vitamins play a critical role in aging and cell senescence, and various levels of exposure could significantly impact human healthspan.

The antioxidant capabilities of vitamins have been investigated for their ability to also modulate the lipid profile; thus, influencing aging and age-associated disease risk through this mechanism as well. One study examining variations to lipid classes after multi-micronutrient supplementation (Vitamin A, B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, B7, B9, B12, C, D3, E, calcium, phosphorous, iron, magnesium, and zinc) in children and adolescents found significant reductions in sterol esters (SEs), phosphatidylinositols (PIs), phosphatidylcholines (PCs), and lysophosphatidylcholines (LPCs), and that linoleic, oleic, palmitic, arachidonic, and stearic acid in various lipid classes (SE, PI, PC, LPC, and triacylglycerols) were reduced with supplementation. Another study examining long-term antioxidant micronutrient supplementation (Vitamin A, C, E, selenium, and zinc) after 7.5 years identified lower total cancer incidence and all-cause mortality in men but not in women. The authors hypothesize that this sex-based difference may be due to lower baseline antioxidant levels in men. While the interaction between dietary vitamin supplementation and disease prevention has been thoroughly reviewed elsewhere, current debates state that the benefits of micronutrient supplementation may be lacking among already well-nourished individuals. Two studies, one examining type 2 diabetes and the other examining cognition, also found insignificant benefits with vitamin supplementation. Although numerous studies have examined vitamins and aging, the complete involvement of vitamins in maintaining or perturbing healthy aging mechanisms is not entirely understood.
3.2 Metals

Humans also require various minerals and trace elements to sustain vital life processes. The "metallome" describes the entirety of metal and metalloid species (elemental distribution, equilibrium concentrations of free metal ions, and free metal content) in a biological system (cellular compartment, cell, tissue type, or organism). Metals ions such as calcium, chloride, chromium, cobalt, copper, fluorine, iodine, iron, magnesium, manganese, molybdenum, phosphorus, potassium, selenium, sodium, zinc, and more are necessary for physiological processes. It is estimated that one-third of all proteins require a metal cofactor, and therefore the body also contains mechanisms for regulating these metals from catalyzing cytotoxic reactions. Many analytical techniques are used to examine the metallome due to both their vital roles (regulatory cofactors, electrolytes, structural function, hormone synthesis, antioxidant activity, cell signaling, energy production, and implication in the prevention of several diseases) and negative consequences (highly toxic, involved in pathophysiology of disease and disease risk). Apart from essential metals needed to sustain physiological processes, humans are exposed to a wide variety of other metals in either environmental or occupational settings, which can have serious health outcomes.

passages.text: 3.2.1 Copper (Cu)

Copper is required by the body for a variety of functions and is required for structural and catalytic properties in many enzymes involved in growth, development, and maintenance. Copper is also important for the utilization of iron, synthesis of connective tissue, formation of red blood cells, energy production, and antioxidation. The majority (85%-95%) of copper in the body is bound to the multi-copper binding protein ceruloplasmin, but the remaining free copper can react generating ROS. Homeostatic regulation of copper absorption and excretion helps prevent toxicity and deficiency. Despite this regulation, copper deficiency and toxicity can occur in the liver, kidneys, brain, and endocrine system. Copper deficiency can cause a range of symptoms likely due to a decrease in the activity of ceruloplasmin and subsequent iron accumulation and oxidative stress. Copper deficiency can also affect the activity of other copper-containing enzymes, non-copper-containing enzymes within the oxidant defense system, and other ROS scavengers. The effect of copper deficiency in decreasing the ability to deal with oxidative stress was demonstrated by increased oxidative damage in a copper-deficient rat model. Copper toxicity also results in oxidative damage, but this effect is suggested to be more of a direct effect of copper itself interacting to cause oxidative stress throughout the body and perturbing the endocrine system. Copper toxicity in the pathogenesis of age-related diseases such as neurodegenerative diseases, diabetes, and atherosclerosis has been examined and reviewed extensively elsewhere. However, the effect of copper in age-associated diseases is thought to be due to free copper accelerating the production of toxic radicals. For neurodegenerative diseases, one study showed that low amounts of copper in distilled drinking water (0.12 parts per million) dramatically increased Abeta plaques and decreased cognitive performance in a cholesterol-fed rabbit AD model. Further, the amyloid precursor protein has copper-binding domains allowing it to function as a copper chaperone in the brain. Copper can also interact with Abeta peptides to produce H2O2, causing oxidation of Abeta, consequently generating protease-resistant soluble and cross-linked Abeta. In humans, those in the highest quintile of total copper intake, combined with a high fat diet, showed an markedly accelerated decline in cognition of at a rate of 19 years over a 6-year period. A copper-induced cell death (cuproptosis) in which copper exposure results in excessive cellular respiration leading to cell death has recently been described.

passages.text: 3.2.2 Iron (Fe)

Iron is a vital element for many biological processes including the formation and transport of oxygen in hemoglobin and myoglobin, cellular respiration in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, and DNA synthesis by ribonucleotide reductase. While excess iron is stored within ferritin in cells, excessive systemic iron can induce hepcidin to sequester iron. Meanwhile, iron deficiency can repress hepcidin expression to regulate the physiological concentrations of iron. Iron is tightly controlled at the systemic and cellular levels to prevent iron overload and toxicity, which is associated with liver disease, diabetes, osteoporosis, heart disease, atherosclerosis, and neurodegenerative diseases. Excess labile iron can result in oxidative stress as iron is a major catalyst in the generation of highly reactive free radicals through the Fenton reactions. Increased labile iron and subsequent lipid peroxidation due to ROS production are key features of ferroptosis, an iron-dependent cell death mechanism. Age-induced increases in iron due to loss of cellular iron homeostasis mechanisms subsequently increase oxidative stress, contributing to aging-related diseases. An iron deficiency can also result in systemic effects, driven by an increase in oxidative stress.

passages.text: 3.2.3 Arsenic (As)

Arsenic is a toxic metal and is included in multiple toxic substance and carcinogen lists. Arsenic has no known beneficial effects in vivo. Humans can be exposed to arsenic from contaminated water, plants (especially in rice), animal sources, and air and soil sources. Prolonged exposure to arsenic causes irreversible damage to the body in a range of organs and systems, including the skin and nervous, respiratory, cardiovascular, immune, hepatic, renal, urinary, and endocrine systems. Arsenic has been linked with skin, lung, bladder, liver, and kidney cancer. While the mechanism of arsenic toxicity is not entirely defined, lipid peroxidation induced by oxidative stress may be responsible. One study found that arsenic exposure can lead to a decrease in plasma HDL and an increase in plasma LDL, especially at high arsenic concentrations. Another meta-analysis found that arsenic can cause oxidative injury by reducing the anti-oxidative capacity, resulting in increased levels of oxidants and decreased levels of anti-oxidants. Arsenic may also contribute to multisystem decline through an induced acceleration of physiological aging processes. In an evaluation of epidemiological data, arsenic exposure was found to accelerate DNA methylation (a measure of biological aging), consequently affecting the risk of age-related morbidity. Specifically, arsenic exposure increased the risk of CVD incidence, CVD mortality, and all-cause mortality. Arsenic also triggers nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) by inducing ferroptosis via the Mfn2/IRE1alpha-ACSL4 pathway, contributing to the lipid metabolism disturbances associated with NASH.

passages.text: 3.2.4 Cobalt (Co)

Cobalt exposure is typically through food intake, mainly through fish and vegetables, or from inhalation of airborne particles from industrial emissions. Cobalt-contaminated water is very rare. Chronic exposure to cobalt is associated with cardiac abnormalities, gastrointestinal disturbances, lung disease, and cancer. A study of data from the NHANES found that cobalt exposure, even within normal range, may be a risk factor for age-related mobility effects. Cobalt exposure is associated with oxidative stress, as in vivo and in vitro lung samples exposed to cobalt showed an increase in the oxidized form of glutathione (GSSG), decreased reduced form of glutathione (GSH), and increased activity of the pentose phosphate pathway. Oxidative stress due to cobalt may also be a mechanism underlying the pathogenesis of PD. Cobalt, in the presence of calcium, can also trigger mitochondrial oxidative stress inducing apoptosis.
3.2.5 Cadmium (Cd)

Exposure to the toxic heavy metal cadmium is largely through tobacco smoke, diet, or occupational exposure. Cadmium accumulates in the body and has a biological half-life of 10 years, resulting in chronic endogenous exposure. Therefore, urine cadmium functions as a biomarker of long-term cadmium exposure. Cadmium contributes to several age-related diseases such as diabetes, CVD, kidney disease, and bone disease (osteoarthritis, osteoporosis). It also contributes to oxidative stress by stimulating cytokine production, elevating levels of inflammation, and increasing mitochondrial damage. An epidemiological study examining NHANES data found that cadmium exposure is associated with increased whole-body phenotypic aging, and smoking (one of the main sources of cadmium exposure) was positively associated with aging. Another study using NHANES data demonstrated that urinary cadmium levels were negatively correlated with telomere length. Telomere shortening is a biomarker of aging and is capable of triggering cellular senescence. Oxidative stress induced via cadmium may be involved in the mechanisms underlying the development of PD. In cancer models, acute cadmium exposure can cause toxic effects. However, chronic exposure can lead to an adaptive reduction in ROS production, at the expense of aberrant gene expression, leading to cadmium-induced carcinogenesis. Cadmium has also been shown to induce multiple forms of cell death, including apoptosis, necroptosis, autophagy, and pyroptosis.
3.2.6 Selenium (Se)

The trace element selenium is required by the body as it is an element in amino acids and enzymes (selenoproteins) where it contributes to antioxidant defense, immune functions, and metabolic homeostasis. Selenium is a crucial cofactor for glutathione- and iodine-containing enzymes and is involved in thyroid function. However, selenium has a narrow margin of beneficial effects in the body as selenium toxicity can result in pro-oxidant functions and liver, lung, and neurological damage. Selenium deficiency can cause oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, endocrine and immunity dysregulation, reduced life expectancy, acceleration of aging processes, and increased vulnerability to age-related disease. Selenium deficiency has also been reported to increase in proportion to age and age-related diseases. Multiple studies, extensively reviewed elsewhere, examining older adults (largely centenarians) found that those with longer lifespans had either higher serum levels of selenium or much lower percentages of selenium deficiencies, suggesting that inadequate selenium could adversely affect optimal health in aging populations. Another study found that elderly adults with low levels of selenium experienced significantly higher rates of all-cause mortality than elderly adults with high levels of selenium. It is suggested that the role of selenium in aging may be due to selenoprotein involvement in redox homeostasis and anti-inflammatory activities. Selenium has also been linked to cellular senescence, as a downregulation in the expression of selenoproteins during selenium deficiency can activate senescence and low levels of selenium can result in shortened telomere length (a hallmark of senescence), which can be rescued by selenium administration. The selenoprotein GPX4 is an essential regulator of ferroptosis and directly prevents uncontrolled phospholipid peroxidation.

passages.text: 3.2.7 Lead (Pb)

Lead is a well-known toxic element, and exposure to lead can come from a variety of sources such as food, water, paint, air, and occupational settings. Previous lead exposures may alter the aging process as lead can be stored in reservoirs in bones which can protect the body from lead toxicity. However, age-related bone loss can release this stored lead into the bloodstream. A mix of epidemiological, clinical, and autopsy studies demonstrated a trend of increasing lead in the blood or bones with aging, although many results were not statistically significant. Low level lead exposure can result in hypertension, peripheral artery disease, kidney and neurodegenerative diseases, and cognitive impairment. Lead may induce oxidative stress in the pathophysiology of these diseases, leading to oxidative damage in the heart, liver, kidney, reproductive organs, and brain. A study examining oxidative stress and lead toxicity in lead-exposed workers found that there is a disruption to the oxidant/antioxidant balance in the workers compared to controls. Additionally, an accumulation of delta-aminolevulinic acid could potentially be a source of ROS in the pathophysiology of lead toxicity. Lead binds to the membrane of cells, acting as a stimulant for lipid oxidation which can lead to alterations in the lipid membrane composition. These alterations can affect membrane integrity, permeability, function, and susceptibility to lipid peroxidation, suggesting that lipids are highly involved in lead-induced toxicity.

passages.text: 3.2.8 Mercury (Hg)

Mercury is a toxic element that has been used for centuries. Mercury exposure can be due to contact with a variety of sources such as soil, air, water, plants and animals, and can still be found in some older fluorescent lightbulbs, thermometers, and batteries. A major issue of mercury is its bioaccumulation and biomagnification properties, as the most hazardous form (methylmercury) is found most frequently due to its quick absorption and slow excretion. Mercury poisoning has been associated with many health effects in both male and female reproductive systems, in utero development, and deleterious effects on the central nervous, renal, pulmonary, immune, gastrointestinal, and cardiovascular systems. Mercury can cross the blood brain barrier, causing oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuroinflammation, resulting in a wide range of neurological effects. Oxidative stress due to mercury exposure can also induce cell death by cytotoxicity and apoptosis. Mercury can also predispose tissues to aging and one study found that the percentage of people with inorganic mercury in the organs that commonly contain mercury (brain, kidney, thyroid, anterior pituitary, adrenal medulla and pancreas) increased with aging, with the highest levels of mercury in all six organs peaking in the 61-80 years group. Mercury levels slightly decreased in these organs, apart from adrenal medulla, suggesting that those who "aged successfully" likely had lower lifetime mercury exposure giving them an advantage in aging. However, these six organs have also been implicated in the process of accelerated aging; thus, mercury may accelerate aging processes in these organs via a variety of mechanisms. The presence of mercury in multiple organs may also offer an explanation to why certain disorders often occur together.

passages.text: Overall, exposure to metals over the lifespan and accumulation of heavy metals in vivo can result in toxic effects on many of the body's physiological processes. However, metal exposure, as discussed above, can catalyze cytotoxic reactions and affect oxidative stress, with more severe influential effects on oxidative stress when in combination with aging-related dysregulation of these physiological processes. The consequent oxidative stress resulting from metal exposure can also influence the lipid profile, with previous findings demonstrating that lead, mercury, iron, zinc, and arsenic affect dyslipidemia (measured via cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol). Meanwhile, other studies have examined changes in the metallome over aging in a variety of tissues, with Zhang et al. observing that mice on calorie restriction had shifted but similar trends to aging mice not on calorie restriction, demonstrating that changes in metabolism may slow aging. Despite numerous studies examining metals on aging processes, as well as effects of metal deficiency and toxicity on age-related diseases, reviewed elsewhere, the extent of metal involvement in oxidative stress, lipid profile modulation, and cell death influencing healthy aging mechanisms are still not entirely understood.
