A fourth COMBINE study is ongoing (COMBINE 4) and is expected to terminate by the end of 2025 (NCT06269107 ClinicalTrials.gov). COMBINE 4 compares treatment with IcoSema or IGla-100 for 40 weeks (followed by 5 weeks of follow-up) of 474 people with T2DM naive to insulin and GLP-1RA. and inadequately controlled on OGLA (HbA1c >=8.0%). The primary aim is difference in the end of study HbA1c. Seconday aims are differences in body weight and risk for hypoglycaemia.

At present there is no information relating to the possible development of an additional FRC of the weekly BI efsitora alfa plus the dual GLP-1- Glucose-dependent Insulinotropic Peptide (GIP) RA tirzepatide.
Comments to the IcoSema studies

The COMBINE studies have tested the FRC IcoSema versus each one of its two components icodec (COMBINE 1), and the GLP-1RA semaglutide (COMBINE 2), respectively. COMBINE 1 and COMBINE 2 confirm with the weekly FRC IcoSema the well expected advantages of treatment with two drugs (BI and GLP-1RA) as compared with one drug only, as already shown with daily FRCs IDegLira and iGlarLixi.

The COMBINE studies offer a clear example of the insulin dose-sparing effect of GLP-1RA given the observation of the ~50% lower insulin dose with IcoSema versus icodec, notably with better glycaemic control in COMBINE 1, and 57% lower insulin dose with similar glycaemic control versus BBT in COMBINE 3. Importantly, COMBINE 3 suggests the possibility for people with T2DM already on BBT of deintensification of their complex insulin regimens with daily basal and prandial insulins switching to a simple weekly dosing of FRC.

Similar to the observation with the daily FRC IDegLira, also with the weekly FRC in the COMBINE studies the dose of the GLP-1RA component semaglutide delivered weekly was low (0.48 and 0.54 mg/week, respectively), well below the doses approved and used for treatment of T2DM, and considerably lower than those proven efficacious in obese people.

Of note, when initiation of IcoSema is compared with icodec (COMBINE 1) or BBT (COMBINE 3), it takes a considerably longer time for IcoSema to control FPG versus the comparators. In COMBINE 1, there was a transient elevation of FPG which then decreased to values not different from icodec only at 18 weeks. This is similar to COMBINE 3 in which IcoSema resulted in a decrease of HbA1c and self-monitored pre-breakfast PG to values no different from those of BBT only at 18 and 24 weeks, respectively. This lag in glycaemic control of the weekly FRC IcoSema does not occur when the weekly BI icodec is given alone. This different outcome in COMBINE and ONWARDS studies is likely explained by the lower starting dose of the BI component icodec of the FRC IcoSema in the COMBINE studies (only 40 units/week) as compared with the dose of icodec in ONWARDS studies (70 units/weeks).
DISCUSSION

All the RCTs of the daily and weekly dosing of fFRCs of BI plus GLP-1RA have proven efficacy as compared with only one or only the other one, of its two components. No prospective, randomized trial, however, hitherto has compared the FRCs with the free, separate dosing of both its components independently titrated. The PK of IDegLira and iGlaLixi suggest lower s.c. absorption of liraglutide when combined with IDeg and lixisenatide when combined with IGla-100, respectively. This might result in lower plasma availability of the GLP-1RA after the injection of FRCs as compared with separate dosing of its components. Also, the PK of semaglutide is different when given with IcoSema as compared with semaglutide alone; however, in the opposite direction to liraglutide and lixisenatide.

At present, there are only indirect comparisons and retrospective observations in which either no difference, or greater efficacy on FPG with a trend for lower HbA1c has been reported with free versus FRCs. Despite the absence of ad hoc RCTs comparing FRCs with free combinations of its components titrated independently in the largely heterogeneous population with T2DM with quite different needs of BI and GLP-1RA, one can, however, imagine that FRCs have some beneficial effects in some people. As indicated by the available studies, people on OGLA who need to advance therapy with injectables, or people already on BI only, or on GLP-1RA only not at target HbA1c will experience a reduction in HbA1c with the FRCs, and will also benefit from a lower body weight and reduced risk of hypoglycaemia (vs. BI only). However, at the same time, it is expected that the daily FRCs will be less successful in people who need higher doses of BI (>60 U/day) and/or in those people who need higher doses of GLP-1RA for a given dose of BI. The latter is of particular relevance to people with obesity who may benefit from the weekly semaglutide at doses >0.5 mg/week or the dual agonist tirzepatide.
Differences between the FRCs IDegLira and iGlaLixi

At present there are no prospective RCTs comparing the FRCs IDegLira and iGlarLixi, only indirect comparisons and retrospective observations. There appears to be no difference in lowering HbA1c or a marginally greater efficacy of IDegLira along with a greater effect on body weight. However, the properties of the different components of the two FRCs may explain the different effects observed in people with T2DM.

Regarding the BI components, insulin degludec has a longer duration of action and a flatter pharmacodynamic profile over the 24 h as compared with IGla-100 and is associated with a lower risk for nocturnal hypoglycaemia. Regarding the GLP-1RA components, liraglutide is an acylated long-acting GLP-1RA analogue with a half-life of approximately 13 h and, therefore, has a prolonged effect over 24 h. In contrast, lixisenatide is a short-acting GLP-1RA analogue with a half-life of 2.8 h and will exert its effect primarily on the meal taken after dosing or meals taken within 4-6 h after dosing, as shown in the GetGoal-L clinical trial. Being a short-acting GLP-1RA analogue, lixisenatide lowers the PPG primarily by delaying gastric emptying markedly, although to a highly variable extent, depending on the baseline rate of gastric emptying. Because of such a mechanism, lixisenatide paradoxically reduces endogenous insulin secretion in response to meal ingestion (Figure 1). These effects of lixisenatide occur at doses below the usual therapeutic dose of 20 mug. In contrast, the long-acting liraglutide primarily stimulates endogenous insulin secretion in response to meal ingestion while still delaying gastric emptying, although to a lesser extent (Figure 1) because of tachyphylaxis which may occur with long-acting GLP-1RAs. Although the PK/PD of lixisenatide suggests twice daily dosing like exenatide, lixisenatide has been approved for once-a-day dosing based unfortunately on only one study in people with T2DM on metformin-only treatment. Surprisingly, no studies with twice- versus once-daily lixisenatide have been performed in people with more advanced progression of T2DM requiring injectables. As expected with a short-acting GLP-1RA given onceaday, the robust effects of morning dosing of lixisenatide observed at breakfast are to some extent reduced at lunch and nearly wane at the time of the evening meal. This is quite different from the effects of liraglutide which is less powerful in lowering PPG at breakfast as compared with lixisenatide, but more consistent in controlling PPG at lunch and dinner (Figure 2). These differences between lixisenatide and liraglutide observed in free combinations with BI are understandably carried over in the respective FRCs with BI.

There are no head-to-head studies comparing the adverse GI effects and tolerability of IDegLira and iGlarLixi. In a network meta-analysis for the first 12 weeks iGlarLixi was associated with less nausea and vomiting as compared with liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide and exenatide QW. However, as in the case of most research related to GLP-1RAs symptoms were assessed using the suboptimal participant 'self-report', rather than a validated measure, and the important distinction between loss of appetite (not bothersome) and nausea (which is) was not made. In future such studies, appropriate assessment of GI symptoms should be planned.

It should also be appreciated that there is no information about differences in the timing of the risk of hypoglycaemia with IDegLira and iGlarLixi. However, considering the different effects on breakfast PPG of lixisenatide as compared with Liraglutide (both given in the morning and associated with BI), with iGlarLixi one should monitor the risk of hypoglycaemia especially in the second half of the morning, whereas with IDegLira the risk might be greater later in the afternoon when insulin resistance is reduced as compared with the morning.
Who would benefit more from the FRC IDegLira, iGlaLixi, or IcoSema?

Based on the RCTs, IDegLira exhibits a similar PPG-lowering effect at each meal during the day, albeit slightly more at lunch and at the evening meal as compared with breakfast (Figure 1). In contrast, the morning dose of iGlarLixi exerts the greatest effect at breakfast, and less effect at lunch and especially at dinner (Figure 2). iGlaLixi improves post-breakfast PG more than IDegLira confirming the importance of delaying gastric emptying more than enhancing insulin secretion in lowering PPG. Therefore, iGlarLixi appears more suitable for people who usually take their largest CHO-rich meal at breakfast and have only light, low CHO meals later in the day. Alternatively, the iGlaLixi might be given prior to the largest CHO meal of the day, provided that the other meals are poor in CHO. As already mentioned, the short half-life of lixisenatide strongly suggests a twice-a-day use, but studies are needed to test this hypothesis and establish the degree of potential tachyphylaxis.

The more recent weekly FRC IcoSema may prove useful in those people who are on the weekly BI icodec already, or are candidates for it, and need to improve PPG. However, given the longer time required with IcoSema to control hyperglycaemia versus daily BI and BBT, care should be taken in people with remarkably poor control to improve hyperglycaemia initially with either daily BI or BBT prior to the switch to IcoSema. Alternatively, more aggressive titration algorithms than those used in COMBINE 1 and COMBINE 3 should be adopted, although this might translate into a too rapid an increase in the weekly semaglutide dose and side GI effects.
Lessons of the FRC studies

The FRCs make it practically easier and more convenient to administer BI and GLP-1RA as one dosing with higher chances of better compliance and adherence versus free combinations of the individual components. However, while the replacement of the BI component appears appropriate with the daily FRCs IdegLira and iGlarLixi, that of the GLP-1RA component may be less optimal. This limitation may apply especially to iGlarLixi in which the GLP-1RA component has a much shorter half-life as compared with that of IDegLira. However, even with IDegLira, the dose of liraglutide may be suboptimal, and the bioavailability reduced with the FRC. Also, with the most recent weekly FRC IcoSema, the dose of the GLP-1RA component semaglutide may be underestimated for the needs of some individuals, especially when obese.

One interesting application of IDegLira has recently been reported in a retrospective study demonstrating that this FRC can be used in the deintensification of the complex basal-bolus insulin regimen in older people with T2DM. The potential for maintaining or even improving glycaemic control with lower risk of hypoglycaemia, and only one injection as compared with multiple injections a day would be an important advantage of simplification for the old, frail population. These results are similar to those of previous studies based on free combinations of BIs and GLP-1RAs in people previously on a basal-bolus insulin regimen, which have established the feasibility of reducing the use of mealtime insulin. The recent COMBINE 3 study suggesting that deintensification of BBT might be possible also with the weekly FRC IcoSema calls for an ad hoc trial in this regard.
CONCLUSIONS

The availability of FRCs of basal insulin (BI) and GLP-1RAs offers a simplified option to advance therapy in T2DM to further improve glycaemic control, lower body weight without increasing, even lowering, the risk of hypoglycaemia. The combination of BI and GLP-1RA also reduces, or may avoid, the need for rapid-acting insulin at meal-time, even in people already on a basal-bolus insulin regimen, and is non-inferior to BBT.

Interestingly, when the FRCs became available some 10 years ago, the predominant recommendation to advance therapy beyond oral hypoglycaemic agents (OGLA) was to begin with the introduction of BI. Therefore, the introduction of FRCs was a significant innovation, offering the advantages of combining BI and GLP-1RA in a convenient and simplified manner. However, the more recent introduction of long-acting GLP-1RAs and the once-weekly dual agonist tirzepatide (GLP plus GLP-1) has changed the therapeutic options, making it now possible to intensify treatment of the GLP-1RA component relative to BI, as compared with the FRCs.

Given the considerable heterogeneity among people with T2DM and their varying therapeutic needs, the FRCs remain to have an important role today, for example, as the first injectable when advancing therapy is required after failure of OGLA. However, frequent longitudinal monitoring of glycaemic control remains essential to determine whether the person with T2DM should continue on FRC therapy or switch to separate dosing and titration of BI and GLP-1RA to enrich treatment with BI and/or GLP-1RA as needed.

passages.text: Incidental Identification of Potentially Affected Individuals Through Expanded Carrier Screening During Preconception or Early Pregnancy "Incidental Identification of Potentially Affected Individuals Through Expanded Carrier Screening During Preconception or Early Pregnancy."
ABSTRACT
Objective

Expanded carrier screening (ECS) is used to assess the reproductive probability of having an offspring affected by an autosomal recessive or X-linked recessive genetic disorder. Rarely, a presumably healthy individual may be identified to carry variants that could influence their health. This study aimed to investigate the incidence of potentially affected individuals, with the objective of improving counseling for ECS.

annotations.text: autosomal recessive or X-linked recessive genetic disorder

passages.text: Methods

A retrospective study of a cohort of 3001 individuals who sought ECS during early pregnancy or preconception was conducted. Potentially affected individuals carrying biallelic pathogenic variants for autosomal recessive diseases, as well as females carrying a heterozygous pathogenic variant for X-linked disease, were identified.
Results

A total of 13 potentially affected individuals (0.43%) were identified; 5 patients were homozygous or compound heterozygous for autosomal recessive diseases, and 8 were heterozygous for X-linked diseases. The majority of the potentially affected individuals were asymptomatic (85%, 11/13) at the time of assessment. Only two patients exhibited mild clinical manifestations.
Conclusion
People who intend to undergo ECS should be informed that they themselves may be identified as potentially affected individuals for whom clinical evaluation and surveillance are recommended.
Summary
What's already known about this topic?

ECS is performed during early pregnancy and preconception to inform participants about the risk of having an offspring affected by potential genetic disorders and to present available reproductive options.
ECS is generally conducted in healthy populations.
What does this study add?
People who intend to undergo ECS should be informed that they themselves may be identified as potentially affected individuals.
Although most potentially affected individuals exhibit mild manifestations or are even asymptomatic, clinical evaluation and surveillance are recommended.
Introduction

Initially, carrier screening was conducted in specific ethnic populations with a relatively high prevalence of certain diseases, such as screening Ashkenazi Jewish populations for Tay-Sachs disease. Owing to advancements in technology, especially next-generation sequencing (NGS), expanded carrier screening (ECS) has been clinically applied in screening for multiple diseases in pan-ethnic populations.

ECS is performed during early pregnancy and preconception to inform participants about the risk of having an offspring affected by potential genetic disorders and to present available reproductive options. The ECS panel used in our study was validated across 12 clinical centers in China, where 287 out of 16,669 screened couples (1.72%) were identified as at-risk couples (ARCs). Although ECS is generally conducted in healthy populations, there may be rare instances where individuals with a pathogenic genotype are identified. Disclosure of the findings to potentially affected individuals may either enable medical intervention for the treatment of existing diseases or initiate surveillance for dormant conditions to facilitate prompt treatment. However, disclosure may cause anxiety, especially for patients who are still asymptomatic. Whether to report these unanticipated findings, which are unrelated to the primary purpose of ECS, has not yet been well addressed.

Our study aimed to investigate the incidence of potentially affected individuals identified by ECS during pregnancy and preconception in a presumed healthy cohort, with the objective of providing improved counseling for ECS.
Materials and Methods
Study Design and Population

Our cohort included a total of 3001 individuals who sought ECS between August 2022 and August 2023 at the Obstetrics and Gynecology department of Peking Union Medical College Hospital. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) pregnant women at a gestational age < 14 weeks, (2) women planning a pregnancy, (3) male partners of these women, and (4) couples who willingly opted for invasive prenatal diagnosis upon being identified as ARCs, which were defined as couples in which both partners carried pathogenic (P) or likely pathogenic (LP) variants in the same autosomal recessive (AR) gene or the female carried an X-linked (XL) P or LP variant. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) conceived through artificial reproductive technology, (2) had a definitive diagnosis or phenotypes highly indicative of a single-gene disease within the scope of ECS, (3) had undergone allogeneic blood transfusions, organ transplants or immunotherapy within the past year, or (4) had a diagnosis of a malignant tumor in either the woman or her male partner. The term "potentially affected individuals" referred to individuals who carried genetic variants that might impact their health, and the criteria were as follows: (1) individuals who were homozygous or compound heterozygous for a P/LP variant in a gene for an autosomal recessive disease (ARD), (2) females who were heterozygous for a P/LP variant in a gene for an X-linked disease (XLD), and (3) females with premutation or full mutation in the FMR1 gene. The possibility of being identified as potentially affected individuals was explained during pre-test counseling. During post-test counseling, all participants received individual-based results. All potentially affected individuals were referred to clinical geneticists for comprehensive evaluation and counseling.
ECS Panel

The ECS panel covered genes related to 197 ARDs and 26 XLDs. In general, diseases included in the ECS panel exhibit either a profound to moderate phenotype or medical actionability. Profound diseases refer to those that result in a shortened lifespan during infancy or childhood, or those that cause intellectual disability; severe diseases refer to those that lead to death in early adulthood, impaired mobility, or a disabling malformation involving an internal organ; and moderate diseases refer to those that involve neurosensory impairment, immune deficiency, mental illness, or dysmorphic features. Medical actionability refers to clinical interventions, such as surgery, medication, or surveillance, that can improve patient health or prevent adverse outcomes. In addition, all included diseases present a relatively high carrier frequency ( 1/200 for ARDs and  1/40,000 for XLDs) in the Chinese population. Screening for XLDs was performed exclusively in females.
Genomic Testing
Genomic DNA was extracted from the participants' test samples, and three methods were utilized to detect distinct variants.
Target Region Capture Combined With High-Coverage Sequencing

First, a library was prepared after DNA fragmentation, followed by target region capture and enrichment using a customized probe kit (Bioscan Tech, Hangzhou, China). High-throughput sequencing was performed on MGI DNBSEQ-T7 sequencers. The obtained DNA sequences were then mapped to the human genome reference assembly hg19. Sequencing quality and coverage of the target regions were evaluated for all samples (Figure S1 A-C). Bioinformatics analysis and pathogenicity interpretation were subsequently performed. The probe region covered P/LP variants in all exons and reported introns of target genes, including single-nucleotide variants, insertion/deletion variants within 10 bp, partial gene deletions/duplications (including exon-level deletions/duplications in the DMD gene for Duchenne muscular dystrophy/Bayes muscular dystrophy), deletion/duplication of exon 7 in the SMN1 gene for spinal muscular atrophy, and HBA1/HBA2 gene deletions (-SEA, -alpha3.7, and -alpha4.2) for alpha-thalassemia. The pathogenicity of the variants was classified according to the standards and guidelines of the ACMG.
F8 Gene Inversion Variant Detection
Inversion of intron 1 and intron 22 of the F8 gene, which causes hemophilia A, was detected using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with electrophoresis analysis.
FMR1 Gene Variant Detection
The number and range of CGG repeats in the 5'-terminal noncoding region of the FMR1 gene, which causes fragile X syndrome, were determined using PCR with capillary electrophoresis analysis.
Case Identification

The ECS results were reviewed for individuals with at least two P/LP variants reported in a single gene for ARDs and one P/LP variant in a gene for XLDs. All identified variants were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Cis/trans configuration of proximal variants (<= 150 bp) was assessed through sequencing read co-occurrence analysis, whereas compound heterozygosity in distal variants required resolution through parental Sanger genotyping.
Outcome Measurements

The demographic and genotypic characteristics of the potentially affected individuals identified in the ECS cohort were meticulously analyzed, followed by clinical evaluation and recommendations for further health management. Demographic characteristics included sex, ethnicity, age, and pregnancy status (early pregnancy or planning pregnancy). Genotypic characteristics included the gene name, variant information, variant classification and supporting evidence, type of allele pair (homozygous, compound heterozygous, or heterozygous), associated disease and its inheritance mode, allele frequency in the East Asian population according to the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD) (v.2.1.1), and the frequency of each genotype in the ECS cohort. Outcomes were ascertained by reviewing health records. The flowchart of the study process is shown in Figure 1.
Flowchart of the study process.
Results
General Information of the ECS Cohort

Among the 3001 participants in our ECS cohort, there were 1454 couples (comprising women and their male partners) and 93 individual women. The mean age of the participants was 32 years (ranging from 22 to 64), with males averaging 33 years (ranging from 23 to 64) and females averaging 32 years (ranging from 22 to 51). The majority of the participants (92.1%) reported their ethnicity as Chinese Han, 7.8% reported their ethnicity as one of the three Chinese ethnic groups (Man, Hui and Mongolian), and the other 0.1% did not report their ethnicity. Among the 1547 female participants, 342 were in the early pregnancy stage, and 1205 were planning pregnancy. Among all 3001 subjects enrolled for ECS, a total of 1612 individuals carried at least one pathogenic variant. Furthermore, 28 (1.9%) ARCs were identified in the ECS cohort.
Potentially Affected Individuals
Demographic and Genotype Characteristics

A total of 13 (0.43%) potentially affected individuals were identified through ECS, with 5 out of 3001 (0.17%) individuals being homozygous or compound heterozygous for ARDs and 8 out of 1547 (0.52%) females being heterozygous for XLDs. No women with premutations or full mutations in the FMR1 gene were identified. Among the patients with variants for ARDs, three patients harbored a homozygous GJB2 NM_004004.6:c.109 G > A (p.Val37Ile), one harbored a compound heterozygous GJB2 NM_004004.6:c.235del (p.Leu79 fs)/c.109 G > A (Val37Ile), which causes autosomal recessive deafness 1A; and one patient harbored a homozygous GALC NM_000153.4:c.1901T > C (p.Leu634Ser) which is responsible for Krabbe disease. Among the patients with variants for XLDs, five patients harbored variants responsible for G6PD deficiency, with one patient with a G6PD NM_001360016.2:c.871 G > A (p.Val291Met), two with a G6PD NM_001360016.2:c.1388 G > A (p.Arg463His), and two with a G6PD NM_001360016.2:c.1376 G > T (p.Arg459Leu); two patients harbored variants responsible for Fabry disease, with one patient with a GLA NM_000169.3:c.886 A > G (p.Met296Val) and one with a GLA NM_000169.3:1067G > A (p.Arg356Gln); and one patient harbored a CYBB NM_000397.4:c.1284 C > A (p.Cys428Ter), responsible for XL-chronic granulomatous disease. The demographic and genotypic characteristics are shown in Tables 1 and 2, respectively. The most prevalent diseases were G6PD deficiency (0.17%, 5/3001), autosomal recessive deafness 1A (0.13%, 4/3001), and Fabry disease (0.07%, 2/3001), followed by Krabbe disease (0.03%, 1/3001) and XL-chronic granulomatous disease (0.03%, 1/3001). Notably, the predominant variant for autosomal recessive deafness 1A was GJB2 c.109 G > A (p.V37I).

Evaluation and Counseling

At the time of evaluation, the majority of the potentially affected individuals were asymptomatic (85%, 11/13). Only two patients (15%, 2/13) exhibited mild clinical phenotypes, indicating Fabry disease and XL-chronic granulomatous disease. Surveillance for all potentially affected individuals was recommended because of the possibility of delayed-onset manifestations, and prompt treatment can contribute to effective disease control.
GJB2 Variants for Autosomal Recessive Deafness 1A

GJB2-related AR nonsyndromic hearing loss is the most common type of congenital sensorineural hearing loss. None of the four individuals carrying the pathogenic genotype complained of any hearing problems. Pure-tone threshold and immittance audiometry were performed, which yielded consistently negative outcomes. The otolaryngologist recommended hearing protection by avoiding repeated overexposure to loud noises and regular monitoring of hearing function to ensure timely implementation of treatment.
GALC Variants for Krabbe Disease

Krabbe disease is an AR lysosomal disorder that affects the white matter of both the central and peripheral nervous systems. While infantile-onset Krabbe disease manifests as severe motor and mental deterioration, leading to decerebration and death by age 2 years, patients with late-onset Krabbe disease can be clinically normal until weakness, vision loss and intellectual regression manifest, and those with adult-onset Krabbe disease may have spastic paraparesis as the only symptom. The woman with the homozygous GALC c.1901T > C denied experiencing any visual, motor, cognitive, or mental impairments. She possessed a college degree and held a formal occupation. At the last follow-up, she was in her puerperium after delivering a healthy boy. As recommended, she intended to undergo testing for GALC enzyme activity.

passages.text: G6PD Deficiency

XL G6PD deficiency is the most common genetic cause of chronic and drug-, food-, or infection-induced hemolytic anemia. Five women with heterozygous G6PD pathogenic variants did not exhibit any manifestations associated with hemolytic anemia, such as fatigue, back pain, anemia, or jaundice. Pregnancy is generally considered safe for these patients, but drugs and chemicals that may trigger the disease should be avoided.
GLA Variants for Fabry Disease

Fabry disease is a rare XL genetic lysosomal storage disorder. This systemic disease can present as progressive renal failure, cardiac disease, cerebrovascular disease, small-fiber peripheral neuropathy, skin lesions, and other abnormalities. The woman with the heterozygous GLA c.886 A > G denied experiencing any discomfort. Comprehensive clinical evaluation revealed corneal opacity and reduced activity (10.2%) of the lysosomal enzyme alpha-galactosidase A, which fell below the normal range (29%-64.4%), indicating a diagnosis of late-onset Fabry disease. Subsequent genetic testing revealed that the variant was inherited from her father, who presented with ventricular septal hypertrophy, impaired renal function, and multiple brain ischemic lesions, accompanied by significantly deficient enzyme activity of 1.1%, confirming the diagnosis of Fabry disease. Notably, this was the first time that he was told that he had Fabry disease. Consequently, enzyme replacement therapy and symptomatic treatment were initiated.
The woman with a heterozygous GLA 1067G > A inherited the variant from her mother, and neither exhibited any manifestations. Further evaluation was recommended.
CYBB Variants for XL-Chronic Granulomatous Disease

XL-chronic granulomatous disease is a rare primary immunodeficiency syndrome characterized by recurrent infection and inflammation with an onset of symptoms in the first months or years of life. Although heterozygous females do not exhibit substantial symptoms, increasing evidence has shown that the risk of infection is increased, and half of carriers have immune-related manifestations. The woman who was heterozygous for CYBB 1284C > A exhibited recurrent aphthous ulcers. Her twin boy and girl, at age 3, remained asymptomatic. It was presumed that the boy inherited the unaffected X chromosome, while the girl either inherited the unaffected X chromosome or was a heterozygote, similar to her mother.
Discussion

In addition to detecting 28 (1.9%) ARCs, 13 potentially affected individuals (0.43%) were identified in the ECS cohort during pregnancy and preconception. Most of the potentially affected individuals were asymptomatic at the time of assessment, with only two displaying mild clinical symptoms. Recommendations for medical evaluation and surveillance were provided to all 13 individuals.

The reporting of incidental findings not related to the indication has been the subject of considerable debate. This controversy is further intensified in the context of ECS, as ECS integrates the ethical challenges of both clinical service and population screening. At the clinical service level, disclosing incidental findings presents an inherent ethical dilemma, balancing the opportunity to manage health risks against the potential imposition of psychological burdens associated with diseases that have yet to manifest. To address this challenge, a three-pronged approach is essential to maximize benefits while minimizing harm: (1) disclosing medically actionable findings with utility, (2) obtaining informed consent during pre-test counseling, and (3) providing comprehensive counseling with multidisciplinary support upon disclosure. Correspondingly, in our study, this framework was operationalized as follows: (1) all incidental findings were deemed medically actionable through treatment or surveillance, (2) the possibility of being identified as potentially affected individuals was explained prior to testing, and (3) for all identified cases, a detailed counseling accompanied by referral, if indicated, was provided. Future corresponding improvements should include (1) establishing a clinical review panel to validate the utility of the findings, (2) implementing opt-out mechanisms for receiving incidental findings, and (3) conducting impact surveys while providing tailored psychological support.

At the population screening level, scaling ECS raises justice and equity concerns for two key reasons. First, widespread implementation creates flow-on effects, such as the allocation of medical resources (e.g., variant interpretation, post-test support, etc.). Second, differential access may foster genomic privilege, where only those who can afford testing gain access to consequential genetic information. While professional guidelines address disclosure protocols for actionable incidental findings in genomic sequencing, these equity considerations must be central when deploying ECS at the population scale.

Few studies have focused on detecting potentially affected individuals during ECS. Reiner et al. reported 0.10% of individuals potentially affected for severe ARDs and 0.45% for XLDs in a pan-ethnic cohort. Li et al. reported that among 2926 Chinese individuals, ECS revealed one GJB2 c.109 G > A homozygote, one GJB2 compound heterozygote (c.235del/c.109 G > A), and three women with FMR1 premutations. Moreover, a sperm donor screening identified 0.80% as homozygotes/compound heterozygotes for ARDs. Collectively, published prevalence rates are similar to ours, though variability exists due to three factors. First, population differences exist: pan-ethnic versus single/oligo-ethnic cohorts. While our cohort balanced sexes, one study involved only male sperm donors. Notably, GJB2 was predominant in incidental findings within another Chinese cohort, aligning with our data. Second, variability in gene panel selection stems from differing priorities, including carrier prevalence, severe phenotype criteria, and cost-effectiveness. For example, while included in other studies, MEFV was excluded from our panel due to its low prevalence in East Asian populations; additionally. Third, definitions of "potentially affected individuals" vary. Reiner et al. included disorders with mild presentations, hemizygous males, and cancer-risk heterozygotes, which were excluded from our analysis. Table S1 summarizes published findings and recalculates prevalence using our definition. However, prior reports emphasize incidental finding risks without addressing post-test counseling. In contrast, our study details relevant phenotypes and provides specific recommendations for medical evaluation and surveillance. Notably, cascade management performed in relatives of a female carrying a heterozygous GLA variant demonstrates that disclosing incidental findings extends benefits beyond participants to their families.

Based on our observations, two points should be conveyed during genetic counseling. First, despite the presence of pathogenic variants, the conditions may exhibit varying degrees of symptoms and onset ages yet remain medically actionable. For example, among the ARDs in our study, most potentially affected individuals carried homozygous or compound heterozygous GJB2 c.109 G > A. Despite its high prevalence (8% of the East Asian population) and low penetrance (17% in the Chinese Han population), it was included in our screening panel due to its clinical implications. Homozygous or compound heterozygous genotypes are linked to severe to profound hearing loss (with frequencies of 1.63% and 9.9%, respectively), and individuals with these genotypes may exhibit progressive hearing decline at an approximate rate of 1 dB per year. After being identified as potentially affected individuals, they can benefit from hearing protection measures and the timely use of hearing aids in response to auditory loss during surveillance. Another example is the GALC c.1901T > C, associated with Krabbe disease, which preferentially exists in Asian populations, especially in Japan and China. The age of disease onset ranges from 14 to 70 years. For late-onset Krabbe disease, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation has been reported to be effective for stopping progression.

Second, while heterozygous carriers of AR diseases are typically asymptomatic, heterozygous female "carriers" of XLDs may exhibit symptoms due to skewed X-inactivation, where the normal X chromosome is preferentially silenced. This complicates clinical counseling, as carriers are often perceived as clinically unaffected. Our findings align with the ACMG recommendations to report heterozygotes of XLDs in secondary findings, given their potential for health risks at a reasonable frequency and eligibility for preventive or therapeutic interventions. For example, female heterozygotes for G6PD deficiency may exhibit induced hemolytic anemia, covering the full range from very mild to a severe, similar to that observed in hemizygous males. The G6PD variant observed in our study results in either class 2 (< 10% of normal activity without chronic non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia) or class 3 (10%-60% of normal activity) disease, but the classification is based on the level of enzyme deficiency and the severity of hemolysis in hemizygous males. Enzyme testing can distinguish females with variable deficiency from those with normal activity. Another example is that females with Fabry disease often have a milder phenotype, later symptom onset, and slower disease progression than males, causing delayed diagnosis and undertreatment. The GLA c.886 A > G variant has been well documented as being associated with the cardiac variant of Fabry disease or nephropathy, which is consistent with the conditions observed in our study. ECS not only played a key role in diagnosing late-onset Fabry disease in the female participant who only exhibited clinically measurable indicators without any associated discomfort but also provided further evidence confirming her father as a typical Fabry disease patient.

While the genes in the ECS panel are associated with diseases exhibiting significant phenotypes that influence clinical decisions, some P/LP variants may cause only mild manifestations. This creates counseling challenges when reporting all detected variants. For example, despite GLA 1076G > A being reported in several Fabry disease screening studies, current evidence suggests that the variant may not be associated with a severe phenotype, even in hemizygous males. Selective reporting of variants associated with clinically meaningful presentations could alleviate this dilemma; however, comprehensive variant stratification proves impractical due to laboratory resource constraints. Consequently, implementing variant-specific counseling adapted to individual clinical contexts emerges as the most feasible resolution.

There were several limitations to our study. First, the sample size of our ECS cohort was relatively small. The frequency of alleles in our cohort differed slightly from that reported in gnomAD, possibly due to variations in the ethnic composition and the limited sample size of our cohort. Second, targeted laboratory evaluations were not performed for all identified cases. Specifically, four cases with GJB2 variants received auditory assessments, and one case with GLA variant underwent enzyme activity testing. The remaining cases did not undergo these specialized investigations; consequently, the presence of clinical biomarker abnormalities could not be determined. Nevertheless, detailed clinical interviews administered during post-test counseling confirmed that all non-investigated participants either maintained apparently asymptomatic status or exhibited only mild phenotypic features.
Conclusion

People who intend to undergo ECS during pregnancy or preconception should be informed that they themselves may be identified as potentially affected individuals. Although most potentially affected individuals exhibit mild manifestations or are even asymptomatic, clinical evaluation and surveillance are recommended. However, the ethical concerns surrounding the disclosure of such findings must be carefully considered when scaling ECS to large populations.
Ethics Statement

This study was carried out following the Helsinki Declaration's ethical guidelines. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, and the study was approved by the ethics review committee of Peking Union Medical College (I-22PJ217).
Conflicts of Interest
The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
Supporting information
Data Availability Statement

The datasets generated and/or analyzed during the current study are not publicly available in order to comply with hospital and IRB policy. According to the consent form, sequencing data cannot be accessed without the patient's permission. But they are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.

passages.text: The role of fat-soluble vitamins on bone metabolism and osteoporosis: a literature review
Abstract
Purpose

The purpose of this review is to discuss the role of fat-soluble vitamins in bone metabolism and explore whether there is a relationship between each fat-soluble vitamins in the occurrence and development of osteoporosis.
Methods

We selected several databases, including PubMed, PubMed Central (PMC), Embase, and Web of Science, as the primary sources for the search. Keywords closely related to the subject of this study, such as 'osteoporosis', 'vitamin A', 'vitamin D', 'vitamin E', 'Vitamin K', 'ferroptosis', 'osteoblast' and 'osteoclast', were used in the search. The search deadline is April 20, 2025. All included clinical studies were graded for critical analysis GRADE.
Results

Among 573 reviewed articles, 182 were included (52 met GRADE criteria: A=10, B=26, C=11, D=5; 130 N/A). Vitamins D and K enhance osteoblast differentiation via RUNX2/ALP upregulation. Vitamin A's bone effects remain debated, potentially interacting with vitamin D. Vitamins E and K may jointly regulate bone metabolism as ferroptosis inhibitors.
Conclusion

i Fat-soluble vitamins (D, K, E) may positively impact bone mineral density (BMD), while vitamin A's effects remain controversial, potentially harming BMD at high doses. Current single-vitamin studies have limitations; future research should explore combined vitamin interactions to advance osteoporosis diagnosis and treatment.
Introduction

Osteoporosis is a chronic bone disease characterized by decreased bone strength and bone mineral density. This common systemic skeletal disorder leads to bone fragility and an increased risk of fractures. A diagnosis of osteoporosis is typically made when the T score falls below -2.5 on the bone mineral density (BMD) of the lumbar spine or hip. Studies have shown that 10% of men and 10%-30% of women over the age of 40 suffer from osteoporosis in Asia. The disease burden caused by osteoporosis and its related bones is still inadequately managed and treated in China. Fractures, especially hip and vertebral compression fractures, pose the greatest risk associated with osteoporosis and occur most frequently. A 2021 epidemiological study in the United States showed that about 40% of postmenopausal women will have bone loss, and about half of these will have fragility fractures. Therefore, the treatment of osteoporosis is crucial for human health.

passages.text: Healthy bones are comprised of a dense matrix of osteoblasts, with minerals formed from calcium and phosphate shaping the skeleton, thereby preserving the bone's rigidity and hardness. Osteoblasts secrete the bone matrix, while osteoclasts are responsible for breaking down and absorbing bone tissue. In normal physiological conditions, there exists a dynamic balance between bone absorption and bone formation, ensuring the maintenance of bone health. When the body is in a pathological state, such as endocrine disorders and insufficient nutrition, this balance will be destroyed, resulting in bone loss. As an important micronutrient in the human body, vitamins participate in many biochemical reactions in the body and prevent a variety of diseases. Several studies have shown that vitamins also play an important role in regulating bone metabolism. Studies have indicated that metabolic disorders involving vitamins may occur in the elderly population, which could be related to osteoporosis.

Despite their small size, vitamins are essential for maintaining good health. Vitamins are categorized into water-soluble vitamins and fat-soluble vitamins based on their solubility. Fat-soluble vitamins, mainly soluble in fat or non-polar organic solvents, include vitamin A, vitamin D, vitamin E, and vitamin K. Except for vitamin D, which can be synthesized through exposure to ultraviolet light on the skin, the remaining vitamins must be obtained through dietary sources. Traditionally, vitamin deficiency has been directly linked to specific diseases, such as vitamin A deficiency leading to night blindness, vitamin D deficiency causing rickets, vitamin E deficiency resulting in oxidative stress, and vitamin K deficiency contributing to blood clotting disorders. Furthermore, postmenopausal osteoporosis patients frequently exhibit deficiencies in various fat-soluble vitamins. Supplementation with fat-soluble vitamins has been shown to enhance bone mass. Currently, an increasing body of research evidence indicates a growing correlation between fat-soluble vitamins and bone health. However, no studies have reviewed the effects of all fat-soluble vitamins on bone metabolism, and no studies have reviewed the interactions between fat-soluble vitamins in bone metabolism. Therefore, this review focuses on the effects of fat-soluble vitamins on bone metabolism and their relationship with osteoporosis, and tries to find the interactions of fat-soluble vitamins in bone metabolism.
Methods
Search methods

In order to ensure the comprehensiveness and accuracy of this review, we adopted a systematic literature search strategy, which was performed by H.L. and Y.Z. First, we selected several authoritative databases, including PubMed, PubMed Central (PMC), Embase, and Web of Science as the primary sources for searches, which were selected because past systematic reviews, literature reviews, meta-analyses and other studies related to osteoporosis have used these representative databases. We used the TI = (vitamin A, vitamin D, vitamin K, vitamin E, osteoporosis, osteoblast, osteoclast, ferroptosis) AND Language = English search strategy on the Web of Science to collect all the original articles and reviews on osteoporosis research. Medical Subject Words (MeSH) terms are a standard vocabulary from the National Library of Medicine (NLM) National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI). We also conducted a similar online search in PubMed based on the screening criteria of 'vitamin A, vitamin D, vitamin K, vitamin E, osteoporosis, osteoblast, osteoclast, ferroptosis' [MeSH]. All the downloading processes were completed within one day, on April 20, 2025. Through this series of strict screening and search, we ensured the comprehensiveness and research quality of the review, providing a solid literature foundation for this study.
Study selection

To further ensure the quality of the above screening literature, W.C. and L.T. screened the search results and decided on paper eligibility. Briefly, the evaluator will read the title, abstract, keywords, and literature type of the article to determine whether it is relevant to the subject headings. Irrelevant articles are excluded, while relevant articles are further read in full text to decide whether to be included. Therefore, the included articles are divided into basic and clinical studies on fat-soluble vitamins and osteoporosis.
Critical appraisal and GRADE classification for literatures on clinical studies

Two reviewers completing this process independently for robustness. The critical appraisal skills programme (CASP) was used to assess the quality of the literatures on clinical studies (results are shown in Table 1). Furthermore, the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology was used to grade the quality of evidence of eligible clinical studies. So that we can determine to what extent we can trust the evidence. The grading criteria are shown in Table 2. The results of GRADE classification are shown in Table 3. At the same time, for the clinical research, we further critically evaluate. Basic research is not appropriate for Critical appraisal and GRADE classification.

Results
Literature screening and GRADE classification

A total of 573 literatures were screened by the above strategy, and 182 literatures were screened out related to the target topic. A total of 52 clinical studies applicable to GRADE criteria were included (A: 10; B: 26; C: 11; D: 5). A total of 130 literatures, including basic research and literature reviews, were not applicable to GRADE classification (N/A). Detailed results are displayed in Table 2.
Vitamin D
Relationship between vitamin D and bone metabolism

There were 50 literatures related to vitamin D included (GRADE A: 4; B: 5;  C: 4 D: 1 N/A: 26. Table 4). Vitamin D exists in two forms and several metabolites. These forms are vitamin D2 and vitamin D3. The body primarily produces vitamin D through exposure to ultraviolet light on the skin, but it can also be obtained from certain foods such as liver or egg yolk. Upon entering the bloodstream, vitamin D undergoes hydroxylation in the liver to form 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25 (OH) D], and subsequently in the kidneys to form 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, which is the active component of vitamin D [1,25 (OH)2D]. Vitamin D primarily functions through binding to the vitamin D receptor (VDR) in the small intestine. This process enhances calcium absorption by activating intestinal epithelial calcium channels and calcium-binding proteins. These processes are essential for bone mineralization. Indeed, the vitamin D receptor (VDR) is not only located in the gut but also in various other organs, including bones, kidneys, brain, breast, and prostate. Since its discovery in 1922, vitamin D has been recognized as a vitamin associated with calcium deposition. As a result, it plays a role in bone mineralization by enhancing the formation of osteoblast calcium matrix in vivo. A variety of factors regulate vitamin D levels and function. Due to its production primarily through exposure to ultraviolet light on the skin, vitamin D deficiency is more likely to occur in winter when the skin receives less sunlight compared to other seasons. This deficiency can lead to bone loss. Additionally, various hormone levels impact the function of vitamin D. In postmenopausal women, the most common change is a decrease in estrogen levels, which can affect the bone-promoting effects of vitamin D. The exact mechanism is unclear but could be attributed to reduced interaction between estrogen and vitamin D-binding protein (VDBP). Parathyroid hormone (PTH) also plays a significant role in the physiological effects of vitamin D. Hyperparathyroidism (excessive secretion of PTH) can disrupt the body's calcium absorption, leading to bone loss, decreased bone density, and an increased risk of fractures. In addition, fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), a vitamin D-regulating protein secreted by osteoblasts, regulates vitamin D metabolism and function by inhibiting the transcription of the enzyme 1alpha-hydroxylase. PTH regulates the secretion of FGF23, and the PTH-FGF23-vitamin D axis is crucial in regulating calcium and phosphorus metabolism. Vitamin D promotes the synthesis of FGF23 by osteoblasts, and FGF23, in turn, enhances the absorption of calcium by cells. It reduces blood calcium concentration, and causes hypocalcemia, which will inhibit bone mineralization. An in vivo longitudinal study in Caucasian subjects showed a marked decrease in PTH levels when serum 1,25 (OH) 2D levels were reduced to 150 pmol/L, which resulted in an increase in FGF23 levels. A positive correlation between 1,25 (OH) 2D levels and PTH and FGF23 levels was also found in a Chinese cohort study. These results suggest that the balance of the PTH-FGF23-vitamin D axis plays an important role in the regulation of bone metabolism.

Effects of vitamin D supplementation on bone mass

Vitamin D deficiency is defined as a serum vitamin D concentration of less than 50 nM. It has been associated with osteoporosis. Studies have demonstrated that vitamin D deficiency can elevate the risk of osteoporosis and result in fragility fractures. Previous large clinical cohort studies have shown that vitamin D and calcium supplementation can prevent osteoporosis, decrease bone loss, and reduce the risk of fractures. Clinical trials have indicated that vitamin D deficiency can negatively impact bone mass in adolescents. In a Finnish randomized, controlled trial involving 228 adolescent girls (mean age, 11.4 +- 0.4 years), 10 mug of vitamin D daily increased mineral deposits in the femur by 17.2% compared with placebo for 1 year. In everyday life, a daily intake of vitamin D less than 400 IU, along with calcium supplementation, is believed to enhance femoral bone mineral density (BMD). However, when the daily intake exceeds 400 IU, it is generally considered to have no significant effect on BMD. Furthermore, a double-blind trial involving 249 healthy postmenopausal women revealed that administering 500 IU/d of vitamin D prevented bone loss in these women during winter, compared to a control group receiving 100 IU/d. This increase in vitamin D intake proved effective in preventing winter-related bone loss in postmenopausal women. Daily supplementation of vitamin D has been shown to improve bone loss. However, a randomized controlled trial in New Zealand involving 4000 participants found no significant effect of vitamin D intake above 1200 mg daily on whole-body bone mineral density. This means that excessive vitamin D supplementation is not advisable. The reason for this could be that an increase in the serum level of 1,25(OH)2D enhances intestinal calcium absorption. However, the rise in calcium levels also stimulates the secretion of PTH, which leads to a decrease in 1,25(OH)2D levels. This complex interplay between vitamin D, calcium, and PTH regulation may explain the lack of significant effect on bone mass with excessive vitamin D intake. High levels of 1,25 (OH)2D(greater than 5 mug/kg*d) in animals can increase osteoclast activity and induce bone loss.

Additionally, vitamin D, when combined with other drugs like alendronate, is used to treat osteoporosis. Alendronate primarily inhibits bone resorption by decreasing osteoclast activity. A daily intake of 10 mg can significantly reduce the incidence of vertebral, wrist, and hip fractures, playing a preventive role in osteoporosis. Hence, the efficacy of vitamin D alone is limited, and it needs to be combined with other drugs, such as alendronate and calcium supplements, to significantly improve bone mass. While vitamin D plays a clear role in preventing osteoporosis, numerous studies have concluded that it does not serve as a direct treatment for osteoporosis.
Molecular mechanism of vitamin D affecting bone metabolism

The enzyme 25-hydroxyvitamin D31-alpha hydroxylase (CYP27B1) converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to its active form, 1,25(OH)2D. In the degradation process of 1alpha, 25-OHD3, the first step involves hydroxylation at the C-1 position by 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1). Following this hydroxylation, 1alpha, 25-OH exhibits a strong ability to bind to the vitamin D receptor (VDR). After binding, 1,25(OH)2D is involved in intracellular calcium and phosphorus metabolism, as well as the regulation of intracellular genes. In a study involving 139 osteoporosis patients, 54 osteopenia subjects, and 73 healthy Italian individuals, transcriptome sequencing revealed that mutations in the VDR gene play a crucial role in the development of osteoporosis. In the past, this physiological process was believed to take place in the kidneys and exert intracellular regulatory functions through binding with VDR. However, recent studies have revealed that osteoblasts can regulate their own activity and that of neighboring osteoblasts. They achieve this by regulating the activity of alkaline phosphatase (ALP), promoting the expression of osteocalcin (OC), and facilitating the mineralization of the surrounding calcium matrix. These processes occur through paracrine and autocrine mechanisms. Vitamin D may not only up-regulate the level of FGF23 in osteoblasts by binding with VDR but also promote the absorption of calcium ions in osteoblasts, additionally, it can also increase the proportion of RANKL/OPG expression, stimulating the proliferation and maturation of osteoblasts. Fluoride poisoning is also a cause of bone destruction and osteoporosis, Fluoride can induce oxidative stress in osteoblasts, promote osteoblast apoptosis, and contribute to osteoporosis. A recent study has demonstrated that vitamin D has a protective effect against fluoride-induced cytotoxicity by alleviating oxidative stress and endoplasmic reticulum stress. Insulin-like growth factor binding protein (IGFBP) functions in conjunction with insulin-like growth factor (IGF). Together, they interact with molecules both inside and outside the cell, influencing various biological processes, such as regulating osteoblast proliferation and the growth cycle of tumor cells. An in vitro experiment suggested that IGFBP-3 may interact with VDR and inhibit the effect of vitamin D on promoting osteoblast differentiation and inducing osteocalcin and ALP expression. IGFBP -6, also a member of the IGFBP family, has also been shown to inhibit the effect of vitamin D on osteogenic differentiation by binding to VDR. In an in vitro experiment, a calcium carbonate scaffold was engineered to gradually release vitamin D. Scanning electron microscope observations demonstrated that this approach promotes osteoblast proliferation and maturation, inhibits osteoclast activity, and aids in the treatment of bone defects.
