passages.text: Furthermore, studies have indicated that vitamin D can enhance bone mass by regulating osteoclast activity. Vitamin D reduces osteoclast precursor cells, inhibits osteoclast activity, and weakens bone resorption. In an in vitro experiment, vitamin D treatment of osteoclasts was found to significantly decrease the expression of transient receptor potential cation channel V member subfamily 5 (TRPV5), a calcium channel protein involved in osteoclast differentiation. This demonstrated that vitamin D inhibited osteoclast differentiation. Vitamin D may promote FGF23 synthesis, and a study involving 70 white peoples found that vitamin D supplementation resulted in an increase in intracellular 1,25 (OH) 2D concentration, thereby increasing FGF23 synthesis and secretion. An in vitro study to investigate the effects of vitamin D and FGF23 on osteoclasts found that both vitamin D and FGF23 significantly inhibited the production of early osteoclasts. The difference was that vitamin D had no effect on the bone resorption activity of osteoclasts, while FGF23 could promote osteoclast activity. This suggests that the regulation of FGF23 on osteoclasts may be bidirectional, Whether vitamin D regulates osteoclast activity may be controversial, further experiments are needed to prove this point because of the paucity of relevant studies. Therefore, vitamin D can promote osteoblast activity and differentiation, inhibit osteoclast production, and perhaps inhibit osteoclast activity.
Vitamin A

There were 26 literatures related to vitamin A included (GRADE A: 1; B: 6;  C: 3 D: 0 N/A: 16. Table 4). Vitamin A comprises a series of retinol derivatives, including retinol, retinene, retinoic acid, and others. It primarily binds to long-chain fatty acids like palmitic acid. The liver is the most abundant food source of vitamin A, where retinol is absorbed, transported by chylomicrons after absorption, and carried in a free form to the blood by binding to retinol-binding proteins. After being transported to target cells, vitamin A is converted into active all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA). ATRA then binds to the retinol receptor (RAR) and retinoid X receptor (RXR) within the cell. In addition to the important role of vitamin A in immune function, vision, growth and development, previous studies have shown that vitamin A is also closely related to the occurrence and development of bone metabolism related diseases such as osteoporosis, periodontal disease, osteoarthritis and so on. In this part, we focus on the effects of vitamin A on bone metabolism and osteoporosis.

There is a significant contradiction and controversy regarding the effect of vitamin A on bone health. In a cross-sectional study involving 232 postmenopausal women with vitamin D deficiency, higher levels of vitamin A were identified as an independent factor contributing to an increased risk of osteoporosis. A cross-sectional study conducted in 2018, involving untreated osteoporotic postmenopausal women aged over 65 years, demonstrated that higher serum retinol levels were associated with lower bone mineral density (BMD) in the spine and hip. Nevertheless, a cross-sectional study conducted in 2015 with 3,154 older Chinese adults revealed a positive correlation between levels of retinol and beta-carotene and bone mineral density (BMD). Vitamin A is essential for good health. During childhood, supplementing dietary vitamin A and maintaining an appropriate retinol concentration in the body (not less than 1.24 mumol/L) has a positive effect on bone growth and development. According to current research evidence, both animal studies, human trials, and in vitro experiments indicate that excessive vitamin A stimulates bone resorption and inhibits bone formation. In an animal experiment, rats were administered vitamin A to elevate their serum vitamin A levels to twice the normal value. The study revealed that their bone formation rate and mineral deposition rate were significantly lower than those in the control group. A 2014 research suggested that high intake of vitamin A or retinol increased the risk of hip fracture. A 2020 meta-analysis of 13 prospective cohort studies involving a total of 384,464 participants indicated that increasing vitamin A intake had no significant effect on the risk of osteoporosis. Among the included clinical studies on vitamin A and osteoporosis, the results were that vitamin A improved bone mineral density in 2 studies, GRADE A and B respectively. Four studies showed no or negative effect of vitamin A on bone mineral density, 2 of which were GRADE B and the other 2 were C. The results of these studies suggest that the effect of vitamin A on bone mineral density is still controversial. However, we found that there was A U-shaped relationship between vitamin A intake and BMD, and both excessive and too little vitamin A intake may affect BMD. We also noted that the intake of vitamin A was generally high in European countries (1804 +- 1023 mug/d), owing to differences in dietary habits. In China, the average intake of vitamin A was 463-765mug/d. The recommended dietary intake of vitamin A is 600-840mug/day. This may lead to conflicting results when studying the effect of vitamin A level on bone mineral density in different regions.

Currently, the impact of vitamin A on bone mass remains controversial. However, a substantial body of research has demonstrated that vitamin A can inhibit the activity of osteoblasts and promote osteoclasts, thereby negatively affecting bone metabolism. Experiments have indicated that all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) at a concentration of 1 muM can counteract the stimulatory effect of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) on osteoblasts and inhibit the differentiation of mouse osteoblasts. According to the results of in vitro experiments, vitamin A promotes bone concentrations within the range of 1 to 100 nM, however, high concentrations of vitamin A (100 nM, 1 muM, 100 muM) inhibited the formation of calcium nodules, potentially through the NF-kappaB signal transduction pathway. Vitamin A inhibits the generation of osteogenic mineralization by suppressing ALP, COL, and other genes. It may also hinder osteoblast differentiation and compromise bone structure stability by down-regulating the expression of transcription factors Sp7 and Axin2 through the Wnt signaling pathway. The intake of high doses of vitamin A may activate RAR signaling, leading to the inhibition of osteoblast-related protein expression and bone formation. Additionally, vitamin A can down-regulate the expression of the FGF23 gene through the RAR receptor, reducing the formation of calcitriol (the active form of vitamin D), consequently inhibiting bone formation.

However, there are also studies indicating that vitamin A can enhance osteoblast activity. Early findings demonstrated that at a concentration of 200 muM, vitamin A promoted the activity of alkaline phosphatase in osteoblast precursor cells. Moreover, this effect was observed to synergize with vitamin D. Subsequent studies revealed that treating mouse mesenchymal stem cells with 3 muM ATRA similarly enhanced alkaline phosphatase activity, stimulated Runx2 mRNA expression, and promoted mineralization in bone nodules. Recent studies have demonstrated that the combination of ATRA (10 muM) with human salivary peptide statin 1 (Hst1) significantly enhances osteoblast activity. When compared to ATRA alone, this combination promotes osteoblast migration and diffusion. Zhenjun Weng and colleagues constructed a rat bone defect model and demonstrated that after 5 weeks of treatment with all-trans retinoic acid, the ratio of bone volume (BV) to tissue volume (TV) in rats significantly increased compared to the control group. Ashley A. Vu designed a 3D printed calcium carbonate scaffold incorporated with vitamin A, enabling the controlled release of vitamin A within 7 days. Osteoblasts were cultured in the scaffold, and the results demonstrated that vitamin A played a significant role in promoting osteoblast proliferation. Although the specific molecular mechanism of the effect of vitamins on osteoblasts has not been elucidated, we seem to find from the above contradictory results that high concentrations of vitamin A (greater than 100 nM) alone have a negative effect on osteoblasts. However, Vitamin A combined with other compounds (vitamin D, Hst1) or using a drug delayed-release scaffold could promote osteoblast differentiation at the same concentration as above. The effects of vitamin A on bone may be complex and require further investigation.

Maintaining adequate vitamin A intake through diet or supplements is essential for supporting bone health. According to the results of in vitro experiments, moderate levels of all-trans retinoic acid may promote bone growth. However, it's crucial to note that these findings are currently limited to in vitro experiments, and more robust studies are required to confirm the role of vitamin A in bone growth. What is certain is that excessive vitamin A can inhibit osteoblast mineralization and may counteract the bone-protective effects of vitamin D, leading to decreased bone density and an increased risk of fractures. Therefore, further research should concentrate on understanding the optimal vitamin A concentration for bone health within the human body. Additionally, additional experiments are necessary to elucidate the interaction mechanisms between vitamin A and vitamin D, which would help establish the connection between vitamin A and bone metabolism (Figure 1).
The Metabolism of vitamin a and vitamin D and their effects on osteoblasts.

Vitamin D is produced in the skin through UV radiation, binds with VDBP in the liver for transportation in the blood, and transforms into its active form 1,25 (OH)2D within cells. It exerts its effects by binding with VDR, upregulating the expression of osteoblastic genes such as OC, ALP, RANKL/OPG, and promoting FGF23 expression. FGF23, regulated by PTH, forms a negative feedback loop with vitamin D. FGF23 also inhibits the expression of the CYP27B1 gene, reducing the activity of 1-alpha hydroxylase. Vitamin A is primarily obtained from animal liver and transforms into its active form ATRA within the body. When bound to RAR/RXR, it reduces FGF23 expression and binds to Wnt proteins on cell membranes, downregulating the expression of osteoblastic genes like ALP, COL1, SP7, and inhibiting osteoblast activity. FGF23: fibroblast growth factor 23; VDBP: vitamin D-binding protein; VDR: vitamin D receptor; RAR: retinol receptor; RXR: retinoid X receptor.
Vitamin K

There were 44 literatures related to vitamin K included (GRADE A: 1; B: 5 C: 1 D: 1 N/A: 36. Table 4). Vitamin K as a clotting factor has been demonstrated in past studies. Vitamin K is a collective term for 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone derivatives. It is primarily found in dark green vegetables such as kale and spinach. There are different forms of vitamin K in nature: vitamin K1 (also known as phylloquinone), is mainly derived from vegetables, such as cabbage, cucumber, Chinese cabbage, spinach and so on. Vitamin K1 is mainly involved in the clotting process, such as coagulation factors II, X, VII and IX, and proteins C, S and Z all depend on the action of vitamin K1. Vitamin K2 (mainly synthesized by gut bacteria), its main dietary sources are fermented foods (such as natto and cheese) and animal livers. It is mainly associated with bone metabolism, such as the carboxylation of osteocalcin, matrix Gla protein (MGP), which promotes bone formation. Vitamin K3, which is a synthetic form, however, it has also been found that in the gut, vitamin K3 can act as an intermediate for the conversion of vitamin K1 to vitamin K2. The vitamin K2 (MKn) form possesses a plant-side chain, which is characterized by a variable number of connected isoprene units (MKn), For instance, MK-4 and MK-7 are specific forms of vitamin K. Vitamin K is absorbed in the gut and transported in the blood by lipoproteins. Vitamin K absorption occurs at different locations in the intestine, vitamin K1 is absorbed in the jejunum and vitamin K2 is absorbed in the colon. Compared to vitamin K2, vitamin K1 has a shorter half-life. To make better use of vitamin K, they enter the cells in the form of vitamin K circulation, allowing the body to reuse it effectively.

Vitamin K enters the cell in the endoplasmic reticulum where it serves as a cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase (GGCX). GGCX carboxylates glutamate residues on specific proteins, converting vitamin K to hydroquinone. Under the action of vitamin K reductase, the oxidized form of vitamin K is then converted back to hydroquinone for further utilization. The biochemical action of vitamin K involves making specific post-translational modifications to certain glutamate (Glu) residues in target proteins, converting them to gamma-carboxyglutamate (Gla) residues. Consequently, Therefore, vitamin K-dependent proteins for this modification are also called vitamin K-dependent proteins (VKDPs) or Gla proteins. Gla protein is composed of intrahepatic protein and extrahepatic protein, and intrahepatic protein is mainly related to blood coagulation. Extrahepatic Gla proteins perform different functions in different tissues, and the common property of their function is the affinity of their Gla residues to calcium ions. Recent studies have revealed that vitamin K can impact bone metabolism by binding to VKDPs(Gla proteins). A Chinese randomized controlled trial involving 60 participants found that serum levels of Gla protein were significantly lower in osteoporosis patients compared with controls, and Gla protein levels were positively correlated with bone mineral density. Osteocalcin (OC) is one such Gla protein synthesized and secreted by bone cells. Vitamin K reduces the concentration of serum uncarboxylated OC (ucOC) and increases the concentration of carboxylated OC (cOC). Carboxylated OC (cOC) can bind to calcium salts, promoting bone density. A cross-sectional study in the UK involving 374 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis found an inverse association between lumbar BMD and serum ucOC protein levels. This suggests that vitamin K can improve bone mass through Gla protein.

People with osteoporosis often have abnormal levels of vitamin K, As early as 1995, Japanese scholars measured the levels of vitamin K in the serum of postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and women with normal bone mass. They discovered that the level of vitamin K in women with osteoporosis (3.29 +- 3.63 ng/ml) was significantly lower than that in women with normal bone mass (6.26 +- 5.62 ng/ml). These findings suggest that vitamin K deficiency may be one of the factors influencing postmenopausal osteoporosis. Furthermore, clinical studies have indicated that serum vitamin K levels can be utilized alongside other biochemical indicators to assess osteoporosis. Presently, an increasing number of studies demonstrate that vitamin K supplementation may have a protective effect on bone health. In a study involving 1,662 Japanese men over the age of 65, conducted by Y. Fujita, it was found that men who consumed natto daily (a food rich in vitamin K) had significantly higher hip and femoral neck bone mineral density (BMD) compared to the group that did not consume natto. In a cross-sectional study involving 374 postmenopausal women, it was observed that those who took vitamin K1 supplements long-term (with a serum concentration of 0.65 mug/L) had a 25% lower risk of hip fracture compared to women in the normal group (with a serum vitamin K1 concentration of 0.53 mug/L). These findings suggest that vitamin K may indeed play a significant role in bone metabolism. Furthermore, animal studies have demonstrated that the administration of teriparatide, zoledronic acid, and combined vitamin K in postmenopausal rats significantly increased femur strength and enhanced fracture healing. This notion is supported by Amelia E. Moore's randomized controlled trial, which involved 105 postmenopausal women divided into three groups: vitamin K1 (1 mg/day), MK-4 (45 mg/day), and placebo. All three groups received vitamin D, bisphosphonates, and calcium supplements for 18 months. The results revealed that both vitamin K1 and MK-4, in conjunction with bisphosphonates, contributed to the improvement of femur bone mineral density.

Vitamin K plays a crucial role in the carboxylation of Gla proteins, facilitating bone matrix formation. It acts as a cofactor in the carboxylation process of Gla proteins. After carboxylation, Gla proteins require subsequent phosphorylation to activate their ability to bind to calcium salts. Even this phosphorylation process necessitates the involvement of vitamin K. The main Gla protein in this process is MGP. Studies have shown that MGP can promote the osteogenesis of mouse osteoblasts and delay the aging of osteoblasts through the PI3K-AKT signaling pathway. MGP can also activate the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway, resulting in increased Runx2 expression, promoting osteoblast proliferation and differentiation, and thus promoting bone matrix formation. In addition, vitamin K can enhance bone mass by influencing the balance between osteoblasts and osteoclasts. It promotes the proliferation and differentiation of osteoblasts and activates alkaline phosphatase activity within osteoblasts. This activation facilitates the deposition of bone matrix and calcium salts, ultimately promoting the formation of calcium nodules. In vitro experiments demonstrated that the addition of vitamin K2 (at concentrations ranging from 10-7 to 10-5M) to mouse osteoblast culture medium resulted in the promotion of osteoblast differentiation. Moreover, the promotion effect was more pronounced at higher concentrations of vitamin K. Vitamin K also promotes osteoblast activity by up-regulating genes such as OCN and RUNX2 in osteoblasts, thereby exerting a bone-protective function. Vitamin K can act on the nuclear receptor steroid and xenobiotic receptor (SXR) and up-regulate SXR target genes. SXR is a nuclear receptor and an essential transcription factor that regulates bone cell homeostasis. Decreased autophagy in osteoblasts may lead to an increase in intracellular oxidative stress. Research indicates that vitamin K can enhance autophagy by activating kinases like LC3-II, beclin 1, and unc-51 in osteoblasts. This activation stimulates autophagy and reduces the production of oxidative stress. In osteoclasts, studies have demonstrated that both MK-4 and MK-7 can inhibit their activity. Experimental results reveal that vitamin K2 can suppress the mRNA expression of specific osteoclast differentiation markers like c-Fos, NFATc1, OSCAR, and TRAP, indicating its anti-osteoporotic properties.

Recent studies have shown that vitamin K is an inhibitor of ferroptosis. Ferroptosis, a recently discovered form of cell death characterized by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, has gained significant attention in recent years and is known to play a pivotal role in various diseases. During ferroptosis, the reduction in the activity of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) results in the accumulation of glutathione (GSH), leading to an imbalance of iron ions inside and outside the cell. This imbalance manifests as the swelling and rupture of intracellular mitochondria and an increase in intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS). In a study conducted in 2022 by Eikan Mishima and colleagues, it was discovered that vitamin K, specifically in its reduced form VKH, exhibits strong anti-ferroptosis properties. This finding opens up new avenues for exploring the impact of vitamin K on bone metabolism. Ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1) is a regulatory molecule involved in ferroptosis within cells. The vitamin K cycle can interact with FSP1 through the FSP1-Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10)-NAD(P)H axis. This presents a novel pathway for inhibiting ferroptosis, independent of the traditional GSH-GPX4 axis. Recent studies have revealed that vitamin K plays a role in regulating ferroptosis in osteoblasts. Specifically, it has been discovered that vitamin K can inhibit ferroptosis in type 2 diabetic osteoporosis through the AMPK/SIRT1 pathway. This finding highlights the intricate involvement of vitamin K in cellular processes related to bone health and metabolism. After adding vitamin K, the level of glutathione in mouse osteoblasts decreased, and the cell ferroptosis was inhibited.

Vitamin K plays a significant role in improving bone health by participating in the carboxylation of Gla proteins, promoting osteoblast proliferation and differentiation, and inhibiting osteoclast activity. Its multifaceted impact on bone metabolism positions it as a potential treatment for osteoporosis. Despite the current lack of drugs specifically targeting vitamin K, there is potential for designing targeted medications focused on vitamin K metabolism. Exploring these avenues could pave the way for innovative osteoporosis treatments. Moreover, emerging research indicates that vitamin K might serve as a potential inhibitor of ferroptosis. Further studies delving into the relationship between vitamin K and ferroptosis could unveil novel mechanisms underlying osteoporosis, opening up new avenues for research and potential therapeutic interventions.
Vitamin E

There were 50 literatures related to vitamin D included (GRADE A: 1; B: 3 C: 0; D: 0; N/A: 24. Table 4). Vitamin E is a collective term for eight compounds, including tocopherols (alpha, beta, gamma, delta) and tocotrienols (alpha, beta, gamma, delta). Tocopherol is found in corn oil and nuts, while tocopherol is mainly found in barley and palm oil. Both tocopherols and tocotrienols share the same basic structure, the chromanol ring. According to the position of the methyl group on the chromanol ring, it can be divided into alpha, beta, gamma and delta subtypes. Unlike tocopherol, the side chain of tocotrienol has three unsaturated bonds, which makes it more antioxidant. alpha-tocopherol is the main form of vitamin E in humans, and its bioavailability is higher than that of other forms of vitamin E, and is the most commonly found form of vitamin E in food. Vitamin E functions as a free radical scavenger, safeguarding cell membranes from lipid peroxidation. The anti-inflammatory effects of alpha-tocopherol are primarily associated with inhibiting NFkappaB, reducing COX activity, and suppressing the production of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), which is an inflammatory mediator. In addition to its classic function as an antioxidant, vitamin E plays a role in various physiological responses, including inflammatory reactions, cell proliferation, programmed cell death, and lipid homeostasis. Osteoporosis has been shown to be a systemic chronic condition characterized by oxidative stress and inflammation, and vitamin E, as an antioxidant, may also inhibit osteoporosis by inhibiting oxidative stress.

The relationship between vitamin E and osteoporosis is indeed complex and multifaceted. While vitamin E deficiency can lead to osteoporosis, there is also evidence suggesting that high serum levels of vitamin E might be associated with a lower risk of osteoporosis. This indicates the importance of maintaining an adequate but balanced level of vitamin E in the body to support bone health. However, it's crucial to note that individual responses to vitamin E can vary, and consulting with a healthcare professional is always advisable to determine the appropriate supplementation or dietary changes for specific health needs. However, a study conducted on elderly individuals in the United States revealed a negative correlation between high levels of alpha-tocopherol in the serum and bone mineral density (BMD) in the femoral neck. Different subtypes of vitamin E supplementation may exert varying effects on bone density. As early as 2010, an animal experiment conducted on rats explored the impact of alpha-tocopherol (alpha-TF) and gamma-tocopherol (gamma-TT) on bone mass. The results demonstrated a significant increase in bone trabecular volume and cortical thickness in both the alpha-TF and gamma-TT groups compared to the control group. Moreover, the effect was more pronounced in the alpha-TT group than in the gamma-TF group. A Canadian study has demonstrated that supplementing with alpha-tocopherol increases the levels of the bone formation marker BAP (bone-specific alkaline phosphatase) in the body. This finding suggests a potential association with the process of bone formation. alpha-tocopherol was administered to postmenopausal rats to enhance the bone healing fraction and load intensity following femoral fracture, thereby promoting the healing of fractures in postmenopausal conditions. In a 12-week clinical trial, researchers hypothesized that vitamin E inhibits bone loss in postmenopausal women by targeting the OPG/RANK/RANKL pathway, but this conjecture has yet to be confirmed.

A previous US study showed that statins can be inhibited 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A(HMG-CoA)through the mevalonate pathway, thereby stimulating the expression of BMP-2 to promote osteoblast activity. But a Malaysian animal study showed that statins alone (11 mg/kg) did not improve bone strength in mice. Vitamin E also acts as an inhibitor of the mevalonate pathway. Studies have shown that vitamin E alone and in combination with low-dose statins can alleviate bone loss in osteoporotic mice, and the combination of the two drugs can produce a synergistic effect on the generation of bone protection. This combined approach may offer significant benefits in promoting bone health and density. Additionally, this combination can up-regulate the expression of RUNX-2 and osteocalcin, further promoting bone formation. Upregulation of these genes may be associated with inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase in the mevalonate pathway. These findings suggest a potential synergistic effect in enhancing bone health through the combined action on multiple pathways related to bone formation.

The impact of vitamin E on osteoblasts has been studied extensively. Different subtypes appear to exert distinct effects on bone metabolism. Tocotrienol, in particular, offers superior bone protection compared to tocopherol. Research findings indicate that alpha-tocopherol inhibits osteoblast differentiation and decreases the expression of ALP (alkaline phosphatase) and OCN (osteocalcin) in the early stages. However, these effects normalize in the later stages of differentiation. Weili Xu discovered that gamma-tocotrienol regulates the cell cycle of MC3T3-E1 cells by stimulating the Wnt/beta-catenin signaling pathway, thereby promoting cell differentiation and proliferation. Anureet Kaur Shah found that delta-tocotrienol induced differentiation of MC3T3-E1 cells and increased the generation of mineralized nodules by alizarine red staining, and the effect was concentration-dependent (0-25 mumol/L). Vitamin E can reduce oxidative damage to osteoblasts by scavenging free radicals in cells, it can reduce intracellular inflammation by reducing the production of PGE2, TNF-alpha and IL-6. For osteoclasts, alpha-tocopherol supplementation promoted osteoclast fusion through p38alpha, Mitf and DC-STAMP, and accelerated bone resorption and bone loss. alpha-tocotrienol alpha-tocotrienol inhibits NF-kappaB ligand (RANKL) receptor activator expression in osteoblasts, inhibits osteoclast activity and differentiation, and reduces bone resorption.

As mentioned above, cellular ferroptosis is a type of cell death characterized by oxidative stress, and vitamin E, as an antioxidant, may also play a role in inhibiting cellular ferroptosis. Studies have shown that vitamin E can work with GPX4 to reduce lipid peroxidation in hematopoietic stem cells to protect the cells from ferroptosis. Other studies have shown that vitamin E can act as a coenzyme Q-dependent free radical reductase to inhibit ferroptosis. While research has not yet confirmed whether vitamin E has the same inhibitory effect on ferroptosis in osteoblasts or osteoclasts, its antioxidant properties suggest a potential anti-ferroptosis mechanism that could enhance osteoblast activity. However, this hypothesis requires further investigation for validation. In summary, vitamin E's antioxidative properties can improve osteoblast activity. Nevertheless, because different vitamin E subtypes have varied therapeutic effects on bone metabolism, future studies should focus on identifying which subtypes are more effective in treating osteoporosis and develop corresponding drugs. Additionally, further research is necessary to explore the relationship between vitamin E and ferroptosis in bone metabolism.
Discussion

Our study suggests a strong association between fat-soluble vitamins and osteoporosis. Vitamin D, vitamin K, and vitamin E may have A positive effect on bone mineral density. The effect of vitamin A on bone mineral density is still controversial, and excessive intake of vitamin A may have a negative effect on bone mineral density.

Fat-soluble vitamins are associated with bone metabolism. Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin that was first found to promote bone formation. Daily supplementation of vitamin D for the treatment of osteoporosis and the promotion of bone formation has been confirmed by sufficient evidence. Vitamin K, owing to its distinctive protein carboxylation, facilitates osteoblast differentiation. Daily supplementation with vitamin K has been shown to enhance bone density as well. As an antioxidant, vitamin E can alleviate chronic inflammation in the body and reduce oxidative stress. In vivo, vitamin E may enhance osteoblast activity and stimulate bone formation by mitigating oxidative stress in osteoblasts. Furthermore, both vitamins E and K might contribute to inhibiting ferroptosis in osteoblasts. However, the impact of vitamin A on bone health remains controversial. This ambiguity could stem from the narrow concentration range within which vitamin A exerts its normal physiological effects; deviations from this range, either too high or too low, can lead to adverse effects. Additionally, it has been observed that fat-soluble vitamins often do not function in isolation; rather, multiple vitamins may interact synergistically within the body. This complex interplay might explain the conflicting findings regarding the effects of fat-soluble vitamins on bone mass.

As previously discussed, the contentious impact of vitamin A on bone mineral density could be attributed to its interference with the bone-enhancing properties of vitamin D. Low vitamin A concentrations might encourage osteoblast differentiation, but elevated serum levels of vitamin A can diminish the effectiveness of vitamin D and exacerbate the detrimental effects of vitamin D deficiency on bone health. Studies have shown that higher serum levels of retinol are a risk factor for vitamin D deficiency. The mechanism leading to this result is still unclear. The current research evidence may be due to the fact that vitamin A inhibits the expression of FGF23 by binding to the RAR receptor, destroys the vitamin D-PTH-FGF23 axis, and weakens the bone-promoting effect of vitamin D. It also stimulated the activity of osteoclasts and increased bone resorption. We hypothesized that both vitamin A and vitamin D, as fat-soluble vitamins, enter the cell through the cell membrane and bind to the nuclear receptor (VDR and RAR), upon binding, there could be intricate mechanisms between these two vitamins that influence their effects on the regulation of cellular gene expression. Consequently, evaluating the impact of a single vitamin supplement on bone mass might have limitations. It becomes crucial to monitor vitamin D levels in the body during vitamin A supplementation to better understand their complex interplay and optimize the outcomes.

The role of ferroptosis in bone metabolism has been paid more and more attention by scholars. Saving the ferroptosis of osteoblasts has become one of the possible methods to treat osteoporosis. Both vitamin E and vitamin K, as antioxidants, have been shown to inhibit ferroptosis in cells (especially vitamin K). Vitamin E inhibits ferroptosis through the coenzyme Q pathway, and FSP1 can also participate in the vitamin K cycle to inhibit ferroptosis through the same pathway. This suggests that vitamin E might possess an anti-ferroptosis effect similar to FSP1 and could potentially be involved in vitamin K metabolism. There is a possibility that the combination of these two vitamins may have a synergistic anti-ferroptosis effect, but further research is necessary to confirm this hypothesis. Moreover, there are limited studies on the effects of vitamin E and vitamin K in preventing ferroptosis in osteoblasts and improving osteoporosis (Figure 2).
The metabolism of vitamin E and vitamin K and their effects on osteoblasts.

Vitamin K is primarily obtained from leafy green vegetables and exerts its effects through the vitamin K cycle metabolism within the body. In this process, KH2 acts as a cofactor for GGCX, participating in the carboxylation of Gla proteins. Carboxylated Gla proteins promote calcium deposition, influencing osteoblast differentiation. Vitamin K can enter osteoblasts and promote osteoblast differentiation by upregulating RUNX2 and ALP through the SXR/PXR pathway. Additionally, it can bind to cell membrane Wnt proteins, activating downstream pathways to enhance osteogenic gene expression. Humans can supplement vitamin E through fats and grains, and it is transported in the blood via VLDL. Once inside osteoblasts, vitamin E promotes the expression of ALP and BMP-2. Furthermore, as an anti-inflammatory factor, vitamin E can alleviate intracellular inflammation by inhibiting inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-alpha. Vitamin E also regulates the cell cycle by binding to Wnt proteins. Both vitamin E and vitamin K can promote the expression of GPX4 to inhibit ferroptosis in cells. GGCX: gamma-glutamyl carboxylase; SXR: steroid and xenobiotic receptor; PXR: pregnane X receptor; GPX4: glutathione peroxidase 4.

In summary, this paper outlined the significant role of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) in regulating bone metabolism and maintaining bone homeostasis. While these vitamins are crucial micronutrients for the human body, it was demonstrated in this review that fat-soluble vitamins interact with each other during metabolism in the body. Furthermore, determining specific doses for dietary supplementation of fat-soluble vitamins in individuals with deficiencies necessitates additional clinical data. When osteoporosis patients consider vitamin supplementation, it is essential to assess the levels of other vitamins in the body concurrently. Relying solely on one fat-soluble vitamin might have limitations. Therefore, evaluating the impact on bone mass requires assessing all fat-soluble vitamins simultaneously. Future research should delve into the intricate relationships between multiple fat-soluble vitamins, particularly vitamins A and D, E and K. Understanding the specific mechanisms of their interactions can advance the diagnosis and treatment of osteoporosis. However, more studies are needed to further the relationship between fat-soluble vitamins and bone health in vivo.

passages.text: Conclusion

In this review, which describes the mechanisms of the effects of fat-soluble vitamins on bone metabolism, in this review, we included 52 clinical studies (grade A: 10; B: 26; C: 11; D: 5), and 130 basic studies and reviews were included. we found that vitamin D and vitamin K may ameliorate osteoporosis by promoting osteoblast activity. The effects of vitamin A and vitamin E on bone are unclear, and vitamin A may influence the bone-promoting effects of vitamin D via FGF23. Vitamin E and vitamin K may simultaneously inhibit the ferroptosis of osteoblasts through anti-ferroptosis, which needs to be further studied. We believe that in patients with osteoporosis, there may be limitations in evaluating the effects of a single fat-soluble vitamin, and it is necessary to jointly evaluate the levels of other fat-soluble vitamins to be more comprehensive.
Limitation

In this review, we systematically summarized the relationship between fat-soluble vitamins and bone health, indicating that the combined consideration of fat-soluble vitamins is very important for the diagnosis and treatment of bone metabolic diseases such as osteoporosis. However, this review is not a systematic review, but a literature review, which relies on the judgment of the authors artificially to evaluate the quality of the literature. It might ignore issues such as the eligibility of the study, confounding factors in the analysis, and the variability of the study population. Furthermore, although all the included studies were graded by GRADE, there were still many basic studies included in this review. Therefore, the conclusions are more theoretical, which requires the verification of more high-quality clinical studies in the future.

passages.text: Genetic insights into hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: pathogenesis, diagnosis, and therapeutic implications

We conducted a comprehensive literature review of sarcomeric gene studies, registry analyses, and recent cohort investigations, focusing on genetic testing outcomes and clinical prognostication. Sarcomeric mutations account for approximately 60% of familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) cases and exhibit variable penetrance and expressivity. Additionally, mitochondrial DNA variants and nonsarcomeric genetic modifiers contribute to the phenotypic heterogeneity observed in HCM. Genetic testing facilitates diagnosis in atypical cases, guides cascade testing in families, and supports reproductive decision-making. Long-term follow-up data from registries indicate that sarcomere-positive patients are diagnosed approximately 13 years earlier and experience nearly double the 50-year incidence of adverse cardiovascular events compared to sarcomere-negative individuals. In Korean cohorts, the mutation detection rate is reported at 43.5%, with genotype-positive status independently associated with worse outcomes. However, for certain prognostic outcomes:particularly sudden cardiac death:more robust data are needed. Emerging therapies, including myosin inhibitors and gene-editing approaches, show promise in targeting the underlying molecular mechanisms of HCM. Therefore, integrating comprehensive genetic screening:including sarcomeric, mitochondrial, and modifier genes:is essential for precise risk stratification and personalized management of HCM. Future efforts should focus on refining variant interpretation and advancing genotype-guided therapeutic strategies.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s44348-025-00055-4.
Background

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a prototypical genetic cardiomyopathy. Understanding its genetic background can enhance our insight into its pathogenesis and potential therapeutic targets. While the clinical presentation is variable:from asymptomatic to sudden cardiac death (SCD):advances in molecular genetics have revolutionized our understanding of HCM pathogenesis. In this review, we aim to synthesize current evidence on the genetic architecture of HCM, including sarcomeric and nonsarcomeric variants, inheritance patterns, genotype-phenotype correlations, and their implications for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment.
Role of genetic testing and variant interpretation

Genetic testing is recommended for index HCM cases and at-risk relatives to enable early detection and surveillance. High-throughput panels and whole-genome sequencing enhance detection rates by identifying structural and deep intronic variants, improving diagnostic yield by up to 12% compared to conventional panels. Interpreting variants of uncertain significance (VUS) remains a challenge; standardized workflows incorporating the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guidelines, ClinGen expert curation, and computational tools (e.g., CardioClassifier, CardioVAI) help optimize classification accuracy and clinical utility.
Genetic architecture of HCM
Sarcomeric gene mutations

Pathogenic variants in sarcomere protein genes account for 60% to 70% of familial HCM cases. Mutations in MYBPC3 and MYH7 constitute approximately 80% of identified sarcomeric defects, with TNNT2, TNNI3, TPM1, ACTC1, MYL2, and MYL3 comprising the remainder. These autosomal dominant mutations exhibit variable penetrance, with MYH7 carriers often displaying earlier onset and more severe hypertrophy compared to MYBPC3 carriers. A recent reappraisal by the ClinGen Gene Curation Expert Panel reaffirmed the pathogenic relevance of these core sarcomeric genes and newly included TNNC1 among the curated gene set.
Nonsarcomeric variants

Recent US-based studies have further advanced the genetic understanding and therapeutic landscape of HCM. The ClinGen Hereditary Cardiovascular Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel recently reevaluated 31 genes, resulting in the reclassification of 17. Notably, TNNC1 was upgraded to a definitive HCM gene, while TRIM63 and ALPK3 were recognized for their dual inheritance patterns. Additionally, FHOD3 was newly classified as definitively associated with HCM. This reclassification enhances the precision of genetic testing and variant interpretation in HCM management. The panel reported that sarcomere-associated genes with moderate, strong, or definitive evidence include FHOD3, KLHL24, ALPK3, TRIM63, CSRP3, PLN, ACTN2, JPH2, and MT-TI. In addition, they identified phenocopy gene variants:such as GLA, TTR, DES, LAMP2, and PRKAG2:which are associated with syndromic diseases (e.g., Fabry disease or hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis) that can present with myocardial thickening (Figs. 1, 2).
Mitochondrial genetics

A subset of HCM patients lacks sarcomeric mutations but harbors pathogenic mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) variants or deep intronic/structural alterations in sarcomeric loci. Privately inherited mtDNA haplogroups and transfer RNA (tRNA) mutations further modulate disease susceptibility. Recent Korean studies have identified mitochondrial variants, including MT-RNR2, associated with apical HCM. Emerging evidence highlights the role of mitochondrial dysfunction and mtDNA variants in the pathogenesis of genotype-negative HCM. One study demonstrated that mitochondrial dysfunction correlates with septal hypertrophy in genotype-negative cases, suggesting the potential utility of mitochondria-targeted therapies and advocating for the inclusion of mitochondrial genome sequencing in HCM genetic evaluation. Investigations into mitochondrial respiratory function in HCM have shown that genotype-negative patients exhibit impaired oxidative phosphorylation and specific deficiencies in complexes I and IV, implicating mitochondrial dysfunction as a potential primary driver in these cases. Early reports of HCM attributable to mtDNA mutations described point mutations that led to cardiomyopathy confirmed by pathology and sequencing, establishing the concept that mtDNA variants can directly cause HCM. Population studies have also identified private mtDNA variants as susceptibility factors for HCM, with certain haplogroups showing increased risk:underscoring the importance of considering mtDNA in genetic risk assessments. Furthermore, pathogenic variants in mitochondrial tRNA genes (e.g., MTTK, MTTL1) have been associated with hypertrophic phenotypes in mitochondrial cardiomyopathies, reinforcing the need to screen for tRNA mutations in comprehensive HCM evaluations.

passages.text: Rare and common variant contributions to HCM risk

A cohort study integrating exome sequencing and the Genome-Wide Association Study data from the UK Biobank and the Mass General Brigham Biobank demonstrated that pathogenic rare variants in 14 core ACMG-designated genes conferred up to a 55-fold increased risk of HCM (e.g., MYH7 odds ratio [OR], 61; MYBPC3 OR, 72). In parallel, a polygenic risk score derived from 27 common variants independently improved risk prediction (OR per standard deviation, 1.6), jointly increasing the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.71 to 0.82 when combined with clinical factors. Bagnall et al. demonstrated that incorporating whole-genome sequencing in HCM diagnostic workflows increased variant detection rates by 12% over standard panels, uncovering deep intronic and structural variants in MYBPC3 and TNNT2 which were previously missed, and influenced clinical management in 8% of cases. Lopes et al. used high-throughput sequencing of 41 genes in a UK cohort (n = 150) and identified novel genotype-phenotype associations, showing that additional nonsarcomeric variants modulate disease severity in sarcomere mutation carriers, and that compound heterozygosity was linked to earlier onset and more severe hypertrophy. A recent large-scale genome-wide association and multitrait analysis including 5,900 HCM cases and over 68,000 controls identified 70 loci, of which 50 were novel, associated with HCM risk and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging traits. These findings underscore the polygenic architecture of HCM in European populations and support integrating polygenic risk scores alongside monogenic testing for risk stratification.

ECG, electrocardiography; TTE, transthoracic echocardiogram; VUS, variants of uncertain significance

Genetic testing facilitates diagnosis in atypical cases, guides cascade testing in families, and supports reproductive decision-making. It can help differentiate thickened myocardium, such as in phenocopy diseases (e.g., cardiac amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, Fabry disease or syndromic cardiomyopathies) (Figs. 1 and 2), hypertensive heart disease, and athlete's heart. Most importantly, it guides family surveillance by cascade testing (Table 1). For pregnancy planning, during genetic counseling, it should be clearly communicated to the proband and their partner about the inheritance rate and the potential for phenotypic development. Identifying a pathogenic variant allows for preimplantation genetic testing. In this process, embryos are created via in vitro fertilization, and those not carrying the pathogenic variant are selected for implantation. However, due to ethical concerns, this technique is not widely performed.
Genotype-phenotype correlations

Certain mutations correlate with distinct phenotypes. MYH7 mutations tend to produce earlier and more severe hypertrophy. MYBPC3 mutations are associated with late-onset disease and may exhibit incomplete penetrance. Mutations in TNNT2 are often linked to a high risk of SCD despite minimal hypertrophy.
Genetic contributions to HCM phenotypes in Korean data

Chung et al. conducted a comprehensive genetic analysis involving 212 HCM patients, examining 82 nuclear DNA (sarcomere associated genes, phenocopy genes and mitochondria related genes) and 37 mtDNA variants. Their study revealed that pathogenic variants in sarcomere-associated genes were more prevalent in nonapical HCM (41.4%) compared to apical HCM (20.8%). Interestingly, apical HCM exhibited a higher frequency of TNNI3 variants (35%) and a lower frequency of MYH7 variants (9%). Additionally, mitochondrial gene MT-RNR2 was positively associated with apical HCM, suggesting a distinct genetic profile for this subtype. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of HCM and underscore the importance of considering both sarcomere and mitochondrial gene variants in understanding its phenotypic diversity.
Impact of sarcomere mutations on myocardial fibrosis and mechanics

Several studies confirmed that sarcomere-associated mutations were significantly related to increase in myocardial fibrosis. In addition, Kim et al. investigated the effects of sarcomere mutations on myocardial mechanics and fibrosis patterns using cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and echocardiography. Their study demonstrated that patients with sarcomere mutations had lower left ventricular circumferential strain and higher basal rotation, along with a higher prevalence of mid-wall fibrosis. These alterations in myocardial mechanics and fibrosis patterns were independent of the extent of hypertrophy, indicating a direct impact of genetic mutations on myocardial function. In asymptomatic carriers without left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) at baseline, those who developed LVH over an 8-year period had reduced peak global strain rate during the isovolumic relaxation period and lower global longitudinal strain (GLS) compared to those who did not develop LVH. In a recent study, myocardial work indices were significantly worse in sarcomere mutation carriers compared to controls, suggesting that myocardial work indices is more sensitive to early changes than GLS and could play an important role in the evaluation and follow-up of carriers. Therefore, left ventricular GLS and myocardial work index may serve as sensitive indicators for detecting early myocardial changes in mutation carriers without overt LVH. This group of family members should be monitored more closely. Regarding diffuse early interstitial fibrosis in carriers without hypertrophy, some studies have shown elevated extracellular volume and abnormal T1 values, suggesting diffuse fibrosis in mutation carriers. These findings support the hypothesis that fibrosis may be a primary phenotype in HCM prior to the development of overt hypertrophy. However, since both studies were conducted by the same research group, further confirmation is needed.
Impact of sarcomere mutations on left atrial function

In another study, Chung et al. explored the relationship between sarcomere gene mutations and left atrial function in HCM patients. They found that patients with pathogenic sarcomere mutations exhibited larger left atrial volumes and reduced left atrial emptying fractions, independent of left ventricular filling pressures. This suggests that sarcomere mutations may contribute to atrial myopathy in HCM, potentially influencing the risk of atrial fibrillation and other complications
Genetic evidence related to clinical course or prognostication

Currently, the evidence supporting the use of genetic testing for prognostication in HCM remains limited. This may be partly due to the uncertainty surrounding disease duration, as many HCM patients remain asymptomatic for extended periods. Additionally, for certain prognostic outcomes:particularly SCD:more robust data are needed. The 2024 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines classify the utility of genetic testing for SCD risk stratification as uncertain (class IIb). Nevertheless, emerging genetic-based studies provide valuable insights that may inform future risk assessment and clinical decision-making.
Insights from the US and global registry

The Sarcomeric Human Cardiomyopathy Registry analyzed over 4,500 patients and found that sarcomere mutation carriers were diagnosed younger and experienced more adverse outcomes than noncarriers. By age 50 years, 29% of sarcomere mutation carriers experienced major adverse events, compared to 14% of noncarriers. Early diagnosis (before age 40 years) was associated with a significantly greater lifetime burden of disease such as cumulative incidence of major adverse events:comprising heart failure, atrial fibrillation, ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death:reached 77% by age 60 years. In contrast, patients diagnosed after age 60 years had a 32% cumulative incidence of such events by age 70 years. Notably, heart failure and atrial fibrillation were the most prevalent complications, often emerging in later decades of life. These findings highlight the importance of genetic testing in HCM for risk stratification and management. Identifying pathogenic sarcomere mutations can inform prognosis and guide surveillance strategies. Furthermore, the data suggest that early intervention and continuous monitoring are crucial, especially for patients diagnosed at a younger age, to mitigate the progression to heart failure and atrial fibrillation. Patients with VUS exhibited an intermediate risk profile, suggesting that some VUS may have pathogenic potential .
Insights from European studies

Mazzarotto et al. critically reviewed three decades of genetic testing in HCM, highlighting that while pathogenic sarcomeric variants facilitate family screening, ambiguous gene associations and VUS complicate interpretation. They proposed a tiered genetic testing approach focused on a validated panel of sarcomeric genes to enhance diagnostic yield and variant classification accuracy, leveraging standardized ACMG guidelines and resources like ClinGen, CardioClassifier, and CardioVAI. Furthermore, they emphasized that genotype-negative patients often represent non-Mendelian HCM with a comparatively benign prognosis, underscoring the importance of differentiated clinical counseling and management strategies. Although several studies showed that patients with MYH7 variants had worse outcomes regarding development of atrial fibrillation and progression to advanced heart failure compared to MYBPC3 mutation carriers, an Austrian registry found that patients with MYBPC3 mutations were significantly older, predominantly male and more likely to have implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) compared to those with MYH7 mutations. It suggests that the association between specific genotype and prognosis is affected by several factors such as type of variants, clinical risk factors and racial difference.
Findings from Korean studies

Gwak et al. investigated prognosis in 492 Korean patients with suspected HCM who underwent genetic testing. Disease-causing sarcomere mutations were detected in 43.5% of patients, with 40.7% classified as genotype-positive HCM. Genotype-positive patients experienced higher rates of composite adverse outcomes, including death, resuscitated arrest, heart failure admission, appropriate ICD shocks, and stroke (28.0% vs. 13.2%, P < 0.001), and sarcomere gene positivity remained an independent predictor of poor prognosis (hazard ratio, 1.70; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.04-2.78; P = 0.034) in multivariable analysis. Kim et al. evaluated the genotype-phenotype relationship and its prognostic implications in 89 Korean HCM patients, finding pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in sarcomere genes (MYBPC3, TNNI3, MYH7, MYL7) in 27 patients, and overall genetic variants in 55 of 89 subjects (61.8%). Variant-positive patients exhibited higher rates of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia (30.0% vs. 12.5%; P = 0.030) and increased myocardial fibrosis on cardiac magnetic resonance (P = 0.029). Event-free survival was significantly lower in variant-positive patients (log-rank P = 0.006), demonstrating that genetic status provides independent prognostic information beyond clinical and imaging parameters.
Oligogenic mutation and rare variant contribution

Girolami et al. analyzed 488 unrelated HCM index patients screened across 8 sarcomeric genes and identified 4 individuals (0.8%) harboring rare triple sarcomere mutations (e.g., MYH7-R869H, MYBPC3-E258K, TNNI3-A86fs). Triple mutation carriers exhibited an aggressive clinical course, with most progressing to end-stage HCM by the fourth decade, necessitating transplantation or advanced pacing, and presenting higher rates of ventricular arrhythmias requiring ICD intervention. This work underscores the prognostic significance of multiple sarcomeric defects and supports comprehensive genetic panels for risk stratification in HCM.
Inheritance patterns and genotype-phenotype correlations

HCM exhibits predominantly autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity. However, recently some variants have been shown to be related to autosomal recessive (ALPK3) or X-lined (FHL1) inheritance. Lastly, data from the Mass General Brigham Biobank indicate that many genotype-positive but phenotype-negative individuals may remain clinically unaffected over extended follow-up, emphasizing the complex interplay of genetic and environmental factors in HCM penetrance.
Modifier genes, epigenetics, and environmental interactions

While sarcomeric gene mutations serve as the primary drivers of HCM, they do not fully explain the disease's phenotypic heterogeneity. Modifier genes are those that do not directly cause HCM but influence the severity, age of onset, and associated complications are increasingly recognized for their role in modulating clinical expression. For example, variants in angiotensin-converting enzyme, transforming growth factor beta, and ion channel genes have been implicated in myocardial remodeling and arrhythmogenesis. Epigenetic mechanisms such as DNA methylation, histone acetylation, and noncoding RNAs may regulate gene expression in cardiomyocytes without altering the underlying DNA sequence. These changes can be driven by aging, comorbidities, or inflammation, and may interact with inherited mutations to shape disease progression. Penarroya et al. presented a unique pair-matched model, based on three monozygotic twin pairs carrying the same founder pathogenic variant and different phenotypes. This study provides further evidence of the pivotal role of epigenetics in HCM for variable expressivity. Environmental factors, including hypertension, physical exertion, and metabolic stress, also contribute significantly to disease variability. In genotype-positive/phenotype-negative individuals, high-intensity athletic training or chronic pressure overload may precipitate hypertrophy or arrhythmic events. In the Korean National Health Insurance Registry data, a significant association was found between body mass index (BMI) and the incidence of clinical HCM after multivariate adjustment. The hazard ratio per 1 kg/m2 increase in BMI was 1.063 (95% CI, 1.051-1.075). Metabolically unhealthy participants had a higher incidence of HCM than metabolically healthy participants, regardless of obesity status. The effect of BMI was more pronounced in several subgroups, including participants without hypertension, those under 65 years of age, and men. Therefore, the authors suggested that efforts to manage obesity and metabolic abnormalities could modify the clinical expression of HCM. These results were consistent with a previous European study. These gene-environment interactions underscore the need for tailored surveillance strategies.
Role of genetic testing
Diagnostic utility
Genetic testing is recommended for individuals with a clinical diagnosis of HCM, first-degree relatives of affected individuals, and asymptomatic at-risk family members.
Genetic counseling
Genetic counseling is crucial for interpreting test results, understanding inheritance risks, and guiding surveillance strategies.
Variants of uncertain significance
A challenge in clinical genetics is the interpretation of VUS, which requires integration of family history, phenotype, and emerging functional data.
Family screening recommendations
Genetic testing and counseling
Offer genetic testing to patients with HCM
Genetic testing should be offered to individuals diagnosed with HCM to identify pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants. This facilitates cascade testing in at-risk family members.
Counseling before and after genetic testing
Individuals undergoing genetic testing should receive genetic counseling before and after testing to understand the implications of test results.
Cascade genetic testing in families
First-degree relatives
If a pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant is identified in a proband, cascade genetic testing should be offered to first-degree relatives (parents, siblings, and children).
Variants of uncertain significance
In cases where a VUS is identified, serial reevaluation of the variant's clinical significance is recommended, as reclassification may impact family screening strategies.
Clinical screening for relatives
Initial evaluation
First-degree relatives should undergo a comprehensive clinical evaluation, including a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) and a two-dimensional transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE).
Ongoing surveillance

For asymptomatic children and adolescents who are genotype-positive but phenotype-negative, clinical screening (ECG and TTE) is recommended every 1 to 2 years. For asymptomatic adults who are genotype-positive but phenotype-negative, clinical screening is recommended every 3 to 5 years. If a relative tests negative for the familial pathogenic variant, additional clinical screening is not recommended (Table 1).
Special considerations
Early-onset disease in family
In families with early-onset HCM or a history of SCD, earlier and more frequent screening may be warranted.
Athletes
Individuals involved in competitive sports should undergo thorough evaluation, as HCM is a leading cause of SCD in young athletes, although there are some controversies.
Implications for management and therapy
Risk stratification

Genetic data can inform risk assessment for SCD, particularly in the presence of malignant mutations or family history of SCD. Ho et al., a US-based team, have demonstrated genotype-associated outcomes and guided early-stage clinical trials for gene-targeted therapies.
Genotype-guided therapy
Although current treatment remains largely phenotype-based (e.g., beta-blockers, ICD placement), emerging therapies aim to target specific molecular pathways.

Mavacamten or aficamten, a myosin ATPase inhibitor, has shown promise in reducing hypercontractility in sarcomeric HCM. In sarcomere geno-positive patients, mavacamten achieved the primary composite endpoint with an OR of 4.43 (95% CI, 1.56-12.58), compared to an OR of 2.52 (95% CI, 0.99-6.42) in sarcomere geno-negative patients in the EXPLORER-HCM study. A stronger and more sustained response has been observed in patients with pathogenic or likely pathogenic sarcomere variants. Therefore, genetic testing may be a useful tool for predicting therapeutic response and guiding personalized management strategies, including decisions regarding septal reduction therapies.

In a groundbreaking effort, the Cleveland Clinic initiated the first human gene therapy trial for HCM in 2023, targeting MYBPC3 with an adeno-associated virus vector (TN-201). Preclinical data support reversal of disease manifestations through restoration of sarcomeric protein expression.
Gene-editing technologies (e.g., CRISPR/Cas9) and RNA-based therapies are being explored for mutation correction or silencing.
Cost-effectiveness of genetic test

One of the key hurdles in performing genetic testing is cost-effectiveness. Although the cost of genetic testing has decreased due to advances in next-generation sequencing technologies, the overall cost:including interpretation:remains relatively high. Additionally, insurance coverage (whether governmental or private) varies significantly across countries. However, considering current guidelines on cascade screening and regular clinical follow-up, several studies have shown that genetic testing is cost-effective. This is because genetic testing allows for the identification of genotype-negative individuals among family members. According to current guidelines, regular ECG and echocardiographic follow-up are not recommended for these genotype-negative family members. In contrast, without genetic information, all first-degree relatives:starting from childhood:would require regular clinical surveillance, leading to unnecessary healthcare costs for asymptomatic individuals. Moreover, genetic testing can help identify high-risk patients earlier, potentially reducing the cost and burden associated with managing advanced disease stages.
Future directions

The field is moving toward precision medicine in HCM, integrating genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics to personalize care. Longitudinal studies and registries are essential to validate genotype-phenotype associations and assess the long-term impact of genetic interventions.

passages.text: Genetics, cardiac phenotype and cardiovascular outcomes in Fabry disease patients in Finland
Abstract
Aims
To investigate the genetics, cardiac phenotype and cardiovascular outcomes of Finnish Fabry patients.
Methods and results

Among the 109 patients with Fabry disease (FD) diagnosed in Finland by 2018, 97 (89%; 32 males and 65 females, mean ages 42 and 52 years) were followed for a mean of 12 years. Data on genetics, phenotypes, cardiac imaging and cardiovascular outcomes were collected from the Fabry Registry and medical records. The 26 families with FD harboured 22 different hemi-/heterozygous GLA variants, most commonly p.R227X, p.A143T or p.P409A. The Fabry phenotype in males was classic in 19 (59%), late-onset in 10 (31%) and intermediate in 3 (9%) patients. Among the females, 62 (95%) were symptomatic. Fabry cardiomyopathy (FC, maximal left ventricular wall thickness >=13 mm, or an increased cardiac mass and decreased T1 time, or typical late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) in CMR) was present in 21 (66%) males manifesting since their 20s, and in 32 (49%) females since their 40s. LGE in CMR was detected in most subjects with cardiomyopathy, particularly in females. Among the 53 patients with FC, 16 (30%) developed atrial fibrillation, 17 (32%) stroke, 14 (26%) heart failure (HF) and 3 (6%) end-stage renal disease. Nine patients died during the follow-up at mean ages of 48 (males) and 75 years (females), three of whom died from HF and three from stroke. Eight of those who died had cardiomyopathy.
Conclusions

In Finland, FD is caused by multiple GLA variants. Classic phenotype is more common. Contrasting previous studies, most women are symptomatic. Cardiomyopathy is very common also in women since their 40s and associates with atrial fibrillation, HF, stroke and death, emphasizing the malignant natural course of FC. Our findings highlight the need for even more diligent monitoring of cardiac manifestations also in females with FD by regular cardiac imaging with CMR.
Introduction

Fabry disease (FD) OMIM: #301500) is a rare and underdiagnosed lysosomal storage disease with an estimated prevalence of 0.01% in the general population. FD is caused by a low or absent level of alpha-galactosidase A enzyme (alpha-Gal A) due to genetic defects in the alpha-galactosidase A gene (GLA) on the X chromosome (Xq22.1). Enzyme deficiency leads to the accumulation of sphingolipids, mainly globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) and lysoglobotriaosylceramide (lyso-Gb3), in the lysosomes of cells in multiple organs. FD is a progressive disease that, if untreated, significantly reduces quality of life and leads to premature death. FD can be treated with specific enzyme replacement therapy (ERT), or in some cases, chaperone therapy migalastat. However, for the treatment to be effective, it should be started before sphingolipid accumulation has caused extensive fibrosis in the organs.

More than 1000 different variants in the GLA gene have been reported. Most of them are identified in a single family. In addition phenotype of FD is often nonspesific, which makes interpretation of the pathogenicity and phenotype of genetic variants challenging. Due to X-linked dominant inheritance pattern, hemizygous males always develop some degree of FD, whereas the phenotype of heterozygous females can range from as severe as that of males to asymptomatic.

The classic form of FD is caused by pathogenic GLA variants that induce the absence or near absence alpha-Gal A activity in hemizygous males. Classic FD patients suffer from severe intermittent limb pain, a lack of sweating, gastrointestinal problems, and fatigue beginning in early childhood. Angiokeratomas and cornea verticillata may be present during childhood. If left untreated, affected males in their 30s and females in their 40s usually develop multiorgan disease, including kidney failure, stroke and Fabry cardiomyopathy (FC). The more common late-onset form of FD is caused by GLA variants which allow for over 5% residual alpha-Gal A activity in males. Both sexes can be affected, and often, the most prominent and only manifestation is cardiomyopathy in the middle age. In addition to the effects of the GLA variant, sex, age and yet unknown factors contribute to the phenotype of FD, which can vary even between males in the same family. The plasma levels of alpha-Gal A and lyso-Gb3 predict, at least to some extent, the severity of the disease in a GLA variant carrier.

To our knowledge, there is only one previous comprehensive nationwide study from Iceland on the genotype and cardiac phenotype of FD. The Finnish population differs from others in terms of its unique genetic architecture and its own set of hereditary diseases. Nearly all Finnish patients diagnosed with FD have been included in the national Fabry Registry, which is filled comprehensively by a nationwide network of Fabry experts, who actively follow the national and international guidelines of FD. Therefore, we conducted the present study to investigate the genetics, phenotypes, cardiac imaging findings and cardiovascular outcomes of Finnish Fabry Registry patients. As cardiac causes are the leading cause of death in Fabry patients, our focus was particularly on FC and its natural course. Finally, as FC is the most common manifestation of late-onset FD, the aim of this study was to improve cardiologists' knowledge of FC.
Methods
Setting

The Fabry Disease Centre of Excellence was established at Turku University Hospital in 2002. The Centre maintains the Fabry Registry in Finland. The Fabry Registry (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier NCT00196742) is a multicentre, international, longitudinal, patient-centred, observational study open to all patients with a confirmed diagnosis of FD.

Currently, the treatment and follow-up of Fabry patients in Finland are centralized in five university hospitals and a few central hospitals, with FD expertise. Among all 109 Finnish patients diagnosed with FD and/or pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in GLA from 1972 to 2018, a total of 97 (89%) patients from 26 families were included in the Fabry Registry and the present study (see Figure  1  and Data S1). When the index patient was diagnosed with FD, systematic cascade screening of the disease-causing variant was carried out in family members. Many late-onset FD cases were found when patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy were investigated by cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) and genetic testing by comprehensive cardiomyopathy gene panels, including the GLA gene, as suggested by the current 2023 ESC cardiomyopathy guidelines.
The Finnish Fabry disease expert network and study patient numbers.
Data sources

The data for this study were collected from both the Fabry Registry and the patients' hospital medical records by cardiologists with FD expertise until 17 October 2018. In addition, major cardiovascular and renal events, and cardiac imaging data were recorded from the Fabry Registry until the end of 2019.
Genetic data

The genetic analyses of the GLA were performed in a clinical setting either in the Finnish Functional Genomics Centre in Turku, Genome Center of Eastern Finland in Kuopio, Blueprint Genetics Laboratory in Espoo, Finland, ARCHIMEDlife Laboratories in Vienna, Austria, or the laboratory of Academic Medical Centre of University of Amsterdam, the Netherlands. The genetic data were available for all the study subjects. In this study, the pathogenicity of the variants was reassessed. Variants were annotated by AlaMut batch software V.1.8 (Interactive Biosoftware, France) and by the transcript NM 000169.2 Pathogenicity was assessed according to guidelines for the interpretation of single nucleotide variants by the American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) and guidelines for the interpretation of copy number variants by the ACMG and Clinical Genome Resources (ClinGen).
Fabry disease phenotype classification

In this study, the FD phenotype in male patients was classified as classic, intermediate or late-onset by cardiologists and internists participating in the present study on the basis of characteristic symptoms, age at onset, long-term disease manifestations, enzyme activity and the type of disease-causing genetic variant as suggested by European FD experts (see Data S1). The phenotype was not definable if only females were affected. Females were classified as either symptomatic or asymptomatic.
Alpha-galactosidase A enzyme activity and lyso-Gb3 level
See Data S1.
Cardiac imaging
See Data S1.
FC diagnosis

According to current ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiomyopathies, the diagnostic criterion for FC is maximal left ventricular wall thickness of 13 mm or greater on cardiac imaging measured at the end-diastole in a patient with FD and no other reason for left ventricular hypertrophy, which we used as the FC criterion in our study. In a family with the GLA p.A143T variant and cardiomyopathy, FC was confirmed by histological and immunohistochemical analyses of endomyocardial biopsies. In addition, for one female with GLA p.T410A, and another with p.R227X variant, an increased cardiac mass and decreased T1 time or typical LGE on CMR, respectively, were considered sufficient criteria for FC, as suggested by recent literature, although LV maximal wall thickness was under 13 mm.
Cardiovascular outcomes and mortality

Cardiovascular events and deaths of patients were carefully reviewed on a case-by-case basis from medical records, laboratory test results, ECGs, X-ray reports and pathology reports by cardiologists with FD expertise.
Statistical analyses

Continuous variables are presented as the means with standard deviations. Categorical variables are shown as frequencies with percentages. Continuous variables were statistically compared by independent samples t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests when appropriate. Categorical variables were statistically compared by chi-square test or Fisher's exact test. P values <0.05 were considered statistically significant. The data were analysed by IBM SPSS software (IBM Corp. Released 2019. IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 27.0. Armonk, NY: IBM Corp) by a cardiologist familiar with FD and a statistician.
Ethics approval
The protocol of the present study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the Northern Savo Hospital District and was performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Results
Study subjects and clinical characteristics

Until 2018, 109 patients were diagnosed with FD in Finland, resulting in a prevalence of approximately 1:50000. Among the 97 Finnish patients with FD included in this study, 32 (33%) were males and 65 (67%) were females. The clinical characteristics and symptoms are presented in Table 1.

The patients were diagnosed at a mean age of 37 years (range 3-80). Males were diagnosed significantly earlier than females, with mean ages at diagnosis being 29 and 41 years (P < 0.001), respectively. The mean age at the end of this follow-up study was 49 years (SD 19; 10-86, 42 years for males and 52 years for females), and the mean follow-up time was 12 years. Six individuals were aged less than 18 years (3 males aged 10-17 years, 3 females aged 10-15 years). Symptoms and findings of classic FD were common.
Nephropathy

The creatinine levels were normal in most patients. Severe proteinuria was diagnosed in 13% of FD males and 8% of FD females (Table 1). Three (9%) males but none of the females developed end-stage kidney disease. Three males received a kidney transplant, one with the GLA deletion encompassing exons 4-7 in his 20s, another with the p.R227Q variant in his 40s, and one with the p.P409A variant in his 40s.
Medical treatment
ERT was started for 88% of FD males at the mean age of 35 years, and for 57% of FD females at the mean age of 52 years. Migalastat was used in few patients only.

Genetics

In total, 22 different GLA variants were identified in the 26 families with FD (Table  2 ). Five (23%) of these variants were nonsense variants, and 13 (57%) were missense variants. Initially, 20 of 22 variants were classified as disease-causing, and reassessment led to the downgrading of p.L311F as a VUS. We previously reported that the p.A143T variant with controversial interpretation was the cause of late-onset FC in the Finnish family included in this study.

The three most common variants (p.R227X, p.A143T and p.P409A) were identified in more than one family, p.143T in three families and the other two in two families. All other variants were found in single families.
Fabry disease phenotypes

With a comprehensive assessment of FD phenotypes in males (n = 32, Tables  1  and  2 ), we classified 19 (59%) with the classic FD phenotype, 10 (31%) with the late-onset phenotype, and three (9%) males with GLA p.T410A as the intermediate FD phenotype. Among the 65 female patients, all but three (two teenage girls and one female in her 70s, all with p.A143T) were diagnosed with symptomatic FD.
CMR findings and cardiac biomarkers in FC

FC was diagnosed in approximately half of all patients (21 (66%) males and 32 (49%) females), manifesting on average over 10 years earlier in males (mean age at 41 years, vs. females 55 years, P < 0.001). Cardiomyopathy was diagnosed in males since their twenties and in females since their 40s, earlier in subjects carrying deletions or nonsense variants (data not shown). However, in a female carrying the missense p.T410A, an increased cardiac mass and decreased T1 time indicated that FC had been present since her 30s. In females, lyso-Gb3 values were nominally greater in subjects with FC than in those without FC, but the difference was not statistically significant (data not shown).

Table  3  shows the latest CMR findings and cardiac biomarkers in patients with FC. NT-proBNP and TnT were highly variable from normal to very high values. On CMR, most FC patients presented moderate to severe left ventricular hypertrophy (mean maximal LV wall thickness 15 mm, range up to 26 mm) with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction, normal LV dimensions and LVMI. Late gadolinium enhancement was detected in most patients with FC and was particularly prevalent (85%) and severe in females.

Cardiovascular manifestations

The cardiovascular manifestations of all FD patients are shown in Table  4  and Figure  2 . In contrast to cardiomyopathy, the prevalence of hypertension, coronary artery disease, and the need for a pacemaker or ICD was low. Atrial fibrillation (AF), HF and stroke developed in 15-22% of patients. Among FC patients with symptomatic heart failure (HF), most males (67%) had HF with reduced ejection fraction (< 50%), whereas the majority of the females (83%), had HF with preserved left ejection fraction.
