passages.text: Orthodontic treatment improves gingival morphological symmetry parameters: a retrospective study
Background

The pursuit of an aesthetically pleasing smile is closely tied to the symmetry of teeth and gingival morphology, yet the impact of orthodontic treatment on gingival contour symmetry remains underexplored. This study aims to investigate the effects of orthodontic treatment on gingival morphology symmetry.
Methods

This retrospective study includes 50 eligible patients as the experimental group and 50 healthy individuals as the control group. Digital intraoral scans were performed for malocclusion patients both before and after clear aligner treatment, as well as for individuals in the control group. Geomagic Control X software was used to assess quantitative indices affecting gingival morphology and contour symmetry. Specifically, mean deviation distance (MDD) was used to measure the average deviation of gingival points relative to the contralateral gingival contour, root mean square (RMS) to reflect the overall level of deviation across all gingival points, and the percentage within tolerance to indicate the proportion of points falling within the tolerance range. Statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS 24 software, with significance set at P < 0.05. The reproducibility of measurements was assessed by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC).
Results

Significant statistical differences in gingival contour symmetry measurements were observed within the study group before and after orthodontic treatment. (P < 0.001). Comparisons between the postorthodontic group and the control group revealed no significant differences in most gingival contour symmetry parameters. Additionally, there were no statistically significant differences in the mean changes of MDD and RMS across different tooth positions before and after orthodontic treatment. However, a statistically significant difference was observed in the changes of percentage within tolerance (p = 0.019) across tooth positions before and after orthodontic treatment.
Conclusion

Orthodontic treatment significantly enhances gingival contour symmetry in patients with mild anterior crowding and skeletal Class I malocclusion. A comparison of the gingival morphology symmetry in the anterior teeth between postorthodontic patients and healthy individuals revealed no statistically significant differences.
Trial registration
This study was approved by the Biomedical Research Ethics Committee of Stomatology Hospital of Fujian Medical University (approval no. 2024-14).
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12903-025-06452-x.
Background

A smile is a reflection of coordinated facial movements, and achieving an aesthetically pleasing smile primarily requires consideration of facial aesthetics, which enables dental professionals to develop a treatment approach from the aesthetic perspective. Psychological and anthropological studies have shown that symmetrical faces are generally perceived as attractive and healthy. Although facial symmetry enhances attractiveness, smile symmetry plays a more critical role in aesthetic perception. Studies have shown that a symmetrical smile enhances aesthetic resonance by reducing visual tension, while slight facial asymmetry adds charm through its personalized characteristics. Therefore, smile symmetry contributes more to overall aesthetic appeal and pleasure than facial symmetry.

A beautiful and symmetrical smile results from the harmonious integration of facial aesthetic factors and oral aesthetic factors, with oral symmetry playing a decisive role in the visual appeal of a smile. Darby's study demonstrated that oral symmetry can significantly enhance the beauty and pleasantness of a smile, even when there are slight asymmetries in other facial areas. Similarly, well-aligned teeth and symmetric gingival morphology are considered key factors in enhancing the harmony of a smile. In oral aesthetics research, Pham and Nguyen further confirmed that symmetry in gingival morphology significantly impacts the visual attractiveness of a smile. Zhang indicated that the dynamic symmetry of the gingival contour during smiling greatly influences the perception of gingival aesthetic parameters. Collectively, these studies highlight the crucial role of gingival symmetry in improving the aesthetic appeal of a smile, which complements overall smile symmetry.

In orthodontic treatment, the alignment of teeth and aesthetic improvement in patients with malocclusion are often the primary concerns of both clinicians and patients. However, the critical factor of gingival symmetry changes is frequently overlooked. Maxillary anterior crowding (MxAC) is a common issue in orthodontic treatment, characterized by labial or buccal displacement of the canines and palatal displacement of the lateral incisors. This type of malocclusion is mainly caused by a mismatch between tooth size and arch length, not only leading to functional problems but also significantly impacting the patient's aesthetic appeal. Orthodontic treatment can typically improve the symmetry of tooth alignment and enhances overall aesthetics. However, existing studies indicate that in some orthodontic patients, after teeth are properly aligned, the visual aesthetic balance may be compromised due to asymmetry of the gingival margin in either the vertical or horizontal planes. This asymmetry can reduce the aesthetic outcome of orthodontic treatment and negatively affect patient satisfaction. At the same time, we understand that laser therapy has potential in reshaping gingival contours and enhancing gingival symmetry. Currently, most research on smile aesthetics in malocclusion patients focuses on the impact of orthodontic treatment on tooth symmetry, while the symmetry and changes in gingival morphology before and after orthodontic treatment have not received sufficient attention.

With advancements in digital oral scanning technology, obtaining high-precision and reproducible 3D models of the oral cavity now provides comprehensive three-dimensional data on tooth and gingival morphology. Through reverse engineering techniques and 3D surface matching algorithms, deviation analyses can be conducted to derive three-dimensional symmetry assessments. A review of the current literature indicates that there are limited methods or studies available that objectively assess gingival morphological symmetry within the dental arches of orthodontic patients before and after treatment. This study aims to assess changes in gingival morphological symmetry before and after orthodontic treatment in patients with mild anterior crowding and skeletal Class I malocclusion using digital models, to explore the impact of orthodontic treatment on gingival symmetry. The null hypotheses of this study are: (1) There is no significant difference in gingival contour symmetry in patients with mild anterior crowding and skeletal Class I malocclusion before and after orthodontic treatment; and (2) After orthodontic treatment, gingival symmetry in patients with mild anterior crowding is not significantly different from that of individuals with normal occlusion.
Materials and methods
Ethical approval
The current retrospective study was ethically reviewed and approved by the Biomedical Research Ethics Committee of Stomatology Hospital of Fujian Medical University, China (approval no.2024-14).

The data used in this retrospective study were obtained from the Zhengya Dental Company(Shanghai Smartee Denti-Technology Co.,Ltd.) and the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at the Affiliated Stomatological Hospital of Fujian Medical University, posing no risk to human subjects.
Informed consent was not required considering the retrospective nature of the study.

This study utilized a retrospective design with analysis conducted at the individual level. Based on previous studies and preliminary trial results, the minimum sample size was determined using PASS software (PASS 2020, Kaysville, USA). The sample size derived from the power analysis indicates that data from 50 participants would achieve a 95% confidence level and a beta error level of 20%, making it sufficient to detect statistically significant differences.

Following the study design, a retrospective collection was conducted by the Zhengya Dental Company, with the study group (SG) comprising 50 patients (20 males, 30 females) who had completed clear aligner treatment between June 2020 and June 2023. The age of the patients ranged from 18 to 33 years, with a mean age of 23.3 +- 5.3 years. The average active treatment time was 2.3 years. To achieve optimal treatment outcomes, this study adopted individualized auxiliary methods for each patient, such as selectively performing molar distalization or arch expansion.
Inclusion criteria for the SG:

(1) Patients with dental and skeletal Class I relationship (1 < ANB<3 on lateral cephalograms)and an average vertical skeletal pattern (MP-FH: 31.1 +- 5.6 ) before and after orthodontic treatment; (2) Before orthodontic treatment, the degree of anterior crowding met the criteria for mild crowding, as defined by Little's Irregularity Index, with an irregularity index value of 1-3 mm and no available space within the dental arch; (3) Clear aligners were used for orthodontic treatment, and standard orthodontic and periodontal maintenance plans were received during the orthodontic treatment, which achieved normal individual occlusions after orthodontic treatment, with upper and lower incisors upright in the basal bone; (4) After orthodontic treatment, the maxillary anterior teeth are free from crowding, spacing, rotation, or missing teeth, with normal overbite and overjet; (5) The anatomical morphology of the maxillary anterior teeth was normal before and after orthodontic treatment, excluding conditions such as microdontia, malformed teeth, defects, caries, and restorations; (6) No gingivitis or periodontitis or gingival recession were observed when digital models were obtained before and after orthodontic treatment; (7) No congenital syndromes or abnormalities in tooth number were observed; (8) No surgical correction was performed; (9) Complete diagnostic and treatment records from pre- and post-treatments were available; (10) Age between 18 and 35 years when completing orthodontic treatment.
Exclusion criteria for the SG:

(1) Presence of gingivitis or periodontitis when the models were obtained from pre- or post-orthodontic treatment; (2) Presence of cleft lip, palate deformities, facial deformities, history of tumors or trauma, history of maxillofacial surgery or cosmetic procedures, or previous orthognathic surgery; (3) History of periodontal surgery in the maxillary anterior region; (4) Use of any medication affecting bone or soft tissue metabolism; (5) History of previous orthodontic treatment; (6) Presence of other diseases that may affect the assessment, including but not limited to epilepsy, hypertension, and diabetes.

The control group (CG) was randomly selected from volunteers recruited from the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at the Affiliated Stomatological Hospital of Fujian Medical University between November 2022 and June 2023. A total of 50 digital three-dimensional maxillary models were included, comprising 25 male and 25 female volunteers. The average age of the volunteers was 21.8 +- 2.2 years.
Inclusion and exclusion criteria for the CG:

Aside from the absence of malocclusion and no history of orthodontic treatment, the inclusion and exclusion criteria were the same as those for the study group. To minimize the influence of gender on the parameters, the gender distribution in the control group was kept parallel to that of the study group. Demographic characteristics of both groups are shown in Table 1. All subjects in both the SG and the CG were of Han ethnicity. All records were anonymized before assessment to comply with ethical requirements.
Experimental design
Data collection

Prior to collecting intraoral scan data, each participant received oral hygiene maintenance instructions. Based on the recommended scanning protocol from previous studies, the TRIOS 3 intraoral scanner (3Shape, Copenhagen, Denmark) was used. Before scanning, the dental surfaces and soft tissues of each participant were carefully dried. All intraoral scan models were saved in StereoLithography (STL) format (Fig. 1).

(A) Digital maxillary intraoral scan model of an orthodontic patient before treatment; (B) Digital maxillary intraoral scan model of an orthodontic patient after treatment; (C) Digital maxillary intraoral scan model of a healthy individual in the control group
Procedure
The workflow for three-dimensional deviation analysis consists of the following five steps:

Segmentation: Using the "Crop" function in Geomagic Control X software (Geomagic Control X, version 2022; 3D Systems, Rock Hill, SC), the crowns of the anterior teeth were segmented at the gingival margin, resulting in a three-dimensional digital model of each crown in the anterior region (Fig. 2A).

Extraction of Gingival Contour and Gingival Curve: Using the "Curve" function in Geomagic Control X software, the gingival contour of each individual tooth and the gingival curve of the bilateral anterior region were extracted from the surface boundary for enhanced precision (Fig. 2B and C).

Mirroring: The software's internal algorithm was then used to automatically generate a mirroring plane (Fig. 2D-F). To ensure consistency and facilitate analysis, the right-side teeth were selected as the reference shape, while the corresponding left-side teeth were used as the comparison shape. The gingival contour and gingival curve of the left-side teeth were mirrored relative to the mirroring plane (Fig. 3A-D).

(A) Segmented digital model of the maxillary anterior region; (B) Extracted bilateral gingival curves from the model, with the yellow curve representing the gingival contour of teeth 11-13 and the red curve that of teeth 21-23.; (C) Extracted gingival contours of homologous teeth on both sides of the model, with the yellow curve representing the gingival contour of the canines, the green that of the lateral incisors, and the red that of the central incisors; (D, E and F) Software-generated mirror plane views at left 45 , frontal, and right 45  angles, respectively

Final Alignment: The "best fit" option in Geomagic software was used for the final alignment. To ensure the reference data and test data were pre-aligned before analysis, initial alignment was performed using landmarks such as the mesial contact point, distal contact point, and gingival apex. These landmarks were used to align the mirrored right-side model with the left-side model (Fig. 3E-H). Once this process was completed, fine matching was conducted using the best fit method, and surface deviations were calculated.

Three-dimension (3D) Deviation Analysis: A 3D curve deviation analysis was performed after the mirrored gingival curve was prepared. Geomagic software automatically calculated the maximum, minimum and mean deviation distance, and RMS distances between the two curves (Fig. 3I-L), and displayed these values on a color analysis map. The map visually represented deviations with different colors: green for values within tolerance, yellow for minimal deviations, and purple for maximum deviation distances. The maximum deviation was set to 2 mm, and the tolerance range in this study was +- 0.25 mm. Deviation values were expressed as absolute values to avoid any potential confusion.

(A, B, C and D) The red curves represent the gingival contours of the right central incisor, lateral incisor, and canine, as well as the mirrored gingival curve of the anterior region, projected onto the opposite side to generate the mirror model; (E, F, G and H) Fitting of the gingival contours and curves between homologous teeth on both sides at specific positions; (I, J, K and L) Results of the deviation analysis for the gingival contours of the bilateral central incisors, lateral incisors, canines, and the gingival curve of the anterior region

After the deviation analysis, the percentage of deviation values within the tolerance range (from 0.25 mm to -0.25 mm) was calculated. These values indicate the percentage of matching between the gingival contours of corresponding teeth. Additionally, the minimum and maximum matching percentage values for each group were also calculated (as shown in Table 2).
The deviation analysis of gingival curves for preorthodontic models, postorthodontic models, and control group models of normal individuals was performed following the same procedure (Fig. 4A-C).

(A) Deviation analysis of the bilateral gingival curves in orthodontic patients before treatment; (B) Deviation analysis of the bilateral gingival curves in orthodontic patients after treatment; (C) Deviation analysis of the bilateral gingival curves in the control group of healthy individuals
Method error

To minimize random and systematic errors, all measurements and analyses of the digital models in this study were performed by the same experienced software operator. This study strictly adhered to a blinded design. During the two-month study period, the same operator measured all models three times, and the mean values were used for statistical analysis. In addition, to assess the operator's repeatability, 10 digital maxillary models were randomly selected from the preorthodontic group, postorthodontic group, and control group, respectively. These models were remeasured and analyzed by the same operator after a 4-week interval. Data reliability was evaluated using a 95% confidence interval (CI), and operator consistency was analyzed using the intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC). ICC values higher than 80% indicate excellent reproducibility.
Data analysis

All measurements were recorded in a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet (Microsoft, Redmond, Wash) and analyzed using SPSS version 24 statistical software (IBM Corp, Armonk, NY). The Shapiro-Wilk test was used to assess the normality of all continuous variables. Descriptive statistics are presented as mean +- standard deviation (X+-S) or median and interquartile range. Since the experimental data in this study do not fully follow a normal distribution, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used for paired sample comparisons between the preorthodontic group and postorthodontic group. For unpaired comparisons between the post-orthodontic and control groups, the Mann-Whitney U test was applied. The Friedman test was used to compare multiple paired non-parametric samples. Differences in gender distribution were analyzed using the chi-square test, while age differences were assessed using the independent samples t-test. All statistical analyses were two-sided, with a significance level set at 0.05.
Results
The reliability of the measurements was evaluated using the ICC, which yielded a value of 0.952. This result, being above 0.9, indicates excellent reliability in the operator's measurement analysis.
The demographic data of each group are presented in Table 1, where no significant differences were observed in age and gender distribution among the groups.

Table 5 indicates that in the preorthodontic group, there were no significant differences in MDD or RMS across different tooth positions, but there were statistically significant differences in the percentage of values within tolerance (P < 0.01), with the central incisors having the highest percentage and the lateral incisors the lowest. In the postorthodontic group, significant differences were found across different tooth positions in terms of MDD, RMS, and percentage of values within tolerance (P < 0.001). The central incisors had the smallest MDD and RMS, while the canines had the largest, and the trend was reversed for the percentage within tolerance, with the central incisors showing the highest values and the canines the lowest. In the control group, significant differences were also observed across tooth positions in terms of MDD, RMS, and percentage within tolerance (P < 0.001). Similarly, the central incisors showed the smallest MDD and RMS, and the highest percentage within tolerance, while the canines exhibited the opposite trend. Overall, all three groups demonstrated that the central incisors had the highest percentage of values within tolerance and the lowest RMS and MDD.
Discussion

Symmetry is a key factor in smile aesthetics, and orthodontists must thoroughly understand all components of oral aesthetics, especially the symmetry of tooth alignment and gingival morphology when restoring a patient's smile. This study aimed to assess the impact of orthodontic treatment on gingival morphology symmetry in patients with mild anterior crowding and skeletal Class I malocclusion by analyzing digital maxillary models before and after orthodontic treatment. The results demonstrated a significant improvement in gingival morphology symmetry after orthodontic treatment, particularly in the central and lateral incisor regions (see Table 2). Therefore, we rejected the first null hypothesis. This improvement may be attributed to tooth movement and alveolar bone remodeling during orthodontics, which affects the reconstruction of periodontal soft tissues. As teeth become aligned symmetrically within the dental arch, gingival contour and gingival curve symmetry also improve. Moreover, as most parameters between the postorthodontic and control groups showed no statistically significant differences, we did not fully reject the second null hypothesis. This may be attributed to the role of clear aligners in promoting good oral hygiene and periodontal health during orthodontic treatment, which, in turn, supports gingival soft tissue remodeling. This study not only confirms the effectiveness of clear aligners in treating anterior tooth crowding but also shows that patients using clear aligners achieve satisfactory clinical outcomes in gingival remodeling and symmetry adjustment. These results support the use of clear aligners as an alternative option in orthodontic treatment, particularly for adult patients.

The results show that the central incisors have the best gingival contour symmetry post-treatment, while the canines exhibite the poorest symmetry (see Table 5). This phenomenon may be related to the gingival phenotype of different tooth positions. Rasperini reports that the gingival phenotype varies by tooth position. The width of keratinized gingiva and gingival thickness increases with greater dental crowding in central and lateral incisors but decreases in canines. Evidence suggests that patients with a thin gingival biotype are more susceptible to periodontal attachment loss and gingival recession during orthodontic treatment. This suggests that the gingival phenotype of the canines in patients with anterior crowding may lean towards a thin biotype, making them more susceptible to gingival recession and asymmetry during orthodontic treatment. This indicates that gingival phenotype modification procedures, such as soft or hard tissue grafting, could be considered before orthodontics to improve post-treatment gingival symmetry. In the control group, significant differences were also found in gingival contour symmetry among different tooth positions, with the central incisors being the most symmetrical, followed by the lateral incisors, and the canines having the least symmetry (see Table 5). This suggests that teeth closer to the midline have higher gingival morphology symmetry, while teeth further from the midline tend to have lower symmetry, consistent with the findings of Betrine et al..

Patients with anterior crowding often present with misaligned teeth that are difficult to clean, leading to a higher susceptibility to gingivitis and periodontal disease. If sufficient space can be accurately predicted during the mixed dentition phase and an effective treatment plan is established to align the teeth, adverse effects on periodontal tissues can be prevented. However, during the permanent dentition phase, ectopically erupting lateral incisors and canines in patients with anterior crowding will require more tooth movement and periodontal tissue remodeling during orthodontic treatment to achieve normal alignment. This would result in more significant changes in gingival contour symmetry parameters for these teeth compared to central incisors. However, the results of this study contradict this assumption. The study indicates that despite the presence of severe individual tooth malposition, the changes in most parameters measuring gingival contour symmetry before and after orthodontic treatment do not show statistically significant differences (see Table 4). This suggests that, although the degree of tooth movement varies across tooth positions in patients with anterior crowding, gingival soft tissue remodeling remains relatively consistent across all positions. The findings of this study suggest that gingival remodeling and periodontal tissue reconstruction in orthodontic treatment do not always align with expectations. Therefore, prior to the initiation of treatment, clinicians should engage in thorough communication with patients to adjust their expectations regarding treatment outcomes, thereby avoiding potential discrepancies between actual results and anticipated outcomes.

Current research on gingival symmetry primarily focuses on quantifying the vertical positional differences in the gingival zeniths of contralateral teeth. Correa et al. found that orthodontists' perception threshold for asymmetry in maxillary canine gingival margins is approximately 0.5 mm, while non-experts had a significantly higher threshold. Pinho S et al. demonstrated that when the asymmetry of the maxillary central incisor gingival margin reaches or exceeds 0.5 mm, orthodontists and restorative dentists rate smile attractiveness lowest. However, the position of the gingival zenith of a single tooth cannot fully reflect the overall morphology of the gingival contour, and the perception thresholds of professionals and laypersons are significantly influenced by factors such as gender and race. Recent studies have moved toward quantifying gingival morphology to assess the symmetry of gingival contour and gingival curve, comparing parameters such as the gingival angle (GA) between contralateral teeth, the gingival line angle (GLA), and the distance between the gingival zenith of the lateral incisor and the gingival line (LID) across anterior teeth. However, these methods provide less accurate indirect measurements, as a single quantified parameter cannot capture the overall morphology of the gingival contour and gingival curve. In contrast, the three-dimensional analysis method used in this study directly measures and comprehensively assesses the overall symmetry of gingival contours in the anterior region, providing precise data and reliable results, which can guide higher-level aesthetic restorations. Furthermore, the use of color-coded heat maps to visually demonstrate changes in gingival symmetry before and after treatment helps clinicians make more precise adjustments during the treatment process.

A symmetrical gingival curve enhances the overall harmony of the smile. Orthodontists should not only focus on the gingival contour symmetry of contralateral teeth but also consider the overall curve formed by the gingival margins of the maxillary anterior teeth. This view is supported by Pham TAV et al.. Therefore, this study served to expand the scope of gingival symmetry research from individual tooth gingival contours to the gingival curve of the anterior region. Additionally, the study found that the impact of gingival morphology symmetry varies by tooth position within the aesthetic anterior region. The gingival morphology of the central incisors is critical for anterior aesthetics. Even if there is slight asymmetry in the bilateral gingival curves, as long as the gingival morphology of the central incisors remains symmetrical and harmonious, the anterior aesthetic outcome can still be acceptable. However, any asymmetry in the gingival morphology of the central incisors significantly diminishes anterior aesthetics. This viewpoint is supported by Marcio Costa Sobral, who further emphasized the dominant role of the central incisors in anterior aesthetics. Additionally, Panchali et al. found that laypeople are more sensitive to changes in the morphology of the central incisors than to changes in the lateral incisors or canines, particularly in cases of unilateral variations. In summary, while the overall symmetry of the gingival curve is important, the morphology of the central incisors has the most significant impact on aesthetic perception. This insight is particularly valuable for managing cases with existing gingival asymmetry. Clinicians can prioritize the correction of asymmetry in the central incisors, as this may yield more pronounced aesthetic effects compared to addressing the asymmetry of lateral incisors or canines, thereby enhancing patient satisfaction and treatment outcomes.

passages.text: Despite the significant findings of this study in evaluating gingival contour symmetry, there are still some limitations. First, the small sample size and the study's focus on a specific type of malocclusion:patients with mild anterior crowding and skeletal Class I malocclusion:limit its generalizability. Future studies should include larger sample sizes and encompass various types and severities of malocclusions to enhance the reliability and applicability of the findings. Second, further exploration is needed into other factors that affect gingival contour symmetry, such as tooth shape and papilla height, to provide more comprehensive guidance for orthodontic treatment. Lastly, this study did not fully consider individual patient differences, such as gingival phenotype and the impact of race on gingival contour symmetry, which should be addressed in future research.
Conclusion
Within the limited framework of this cross-sectional study, the conclusions were drawn as follows:
Orthodontic treatment significantly enhances gingival contour symmetry in patients with mild anterior crowding and skeletal Class I malocclusion.
A comparison of the gingival morphology symmetry in the anterior teeth between postorthodontic patients and healthy individuals reveals no statistically significant differences.

The cytotoxicity of compound A14 on Caco-2 cells was found to be lower than that of amphotericin B.

passages.text: Over the past decades, the incidence and modality of invasive fungal infections have been significantly underestimated. And the limited availability of clinically effective antifungals further underscores the need for novel therapeutic agents. In this study, a series of novel 8-hydroxyquinolin-5-ylidene thiosemicarbazone derivatives (A5-A32) were designed and synthesized via a condensation reaction between 5-formyl-8-hydroxyquinoline and substituted hydrazinecarbothioamides. The in vitro antifungal activity of all synthesized compounds was evaluated against a panel of clinically relevant fungal pathogens using the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) broth microdilution method, with minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) ranging from 4 to <= 0.0313 mug/mL. Notably, compound A14 was the most active, demonstrating the lowest MICs among the compounds against each of the tested seven fungal pathogens. Specifically, A14 exhibited remarkable potency against Cryptococcus gattii, C. neoformans, C. glabrata, and C. auris, with MICs ranging from <= 0.0313 to 2 mug/mL. This potency is significantly higher than that of the lead compound 5r (MICs: 0.25- >16 mug/mL) and fluconazole (MICs: 2->16 mug/mL). Furthermore, A14 inhibited hyphal formation in C. albicans SC5314 at 8 mug/mL, and remarkably inhibited biofilm formation in both C. albicans SC5314 and C. neoformans H99, achieving >90 % suppression at 32 mug/mL. The cytotoxic effects of compound A14 on the viability of HUVECs and Caco-2 cells were evaluated using the CCK-8 assay, demonstrating acceptable safety profiles. As an innovative antifungal agent, 8-hydroxyquinolin-5-ylidene thiosemicarbazone A14 warrants further investigation.

passages.text: Graphical abstract
Introduction

Invasive fungal diseases (IFDs) pose a significant global health burden, characterized by high mortality and morbidity rates, particularly among patients with compromised immune systems, including those with AIDS, organ transplants, undergoing cancer chemotherapy, suffering from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), or experiencing viral respiratory tract infections. Recent estimates indicate that over 6.55 million individuals worldwide are afflicted by life-threatening fungal infections annually, resulting in approximately 2.55 million attributable deaths. These infections are predominantly caused by 19 invasive fungal pathogens, prioritized and categorized into critical, high, and medium-risk groups by the World Health Organization (WHO) in its first-ever Fungal Priority Pathogens List in 2022. The critical group comprises Cryptococcus neoformans, Candida auris, Aspergillus fumigatus, and Candida albicans, while the high-priority group includes Candida glabrata, Candida tropicalis, and Candida parapsilosis, among others.

The clinical therapy for IFDs is severely constrained by the limited availability of effective antifungal agents. The four major classes of antifungals currently in use:azoles, echinocandins, pyrimidines, and polyenes:often fall short of providing optimal treatment outcomes. Furthermore, the clinical application of these drugs is frequently hampered by their narrow antifungal spectra, associated hepatotoxicity or nephrotoxicity, drug-drug interactions, oral formulation only, and the emergence of drug resistance.

The escalating issue of drug resistance in fungi presents a formidable challenge. Cases of pan-drug resistance in A. fumigatus, multi-drug resistance in C. auris, azole cross-resistance, and intrinsic resistance in certain fungal species are increasingly reported, threatening to exhaust therapeutic options. Azoles, widely employed as fungicides in agriculture and antifungals in clinics, are particularly susceptible to the development of cross-resistance. For example, novel azole agents previously synthesized in our group demonstrated high activity against the drug-sensitive C. albicans SC5314 (MICs < 0.125 mug/mL) but exhibited significantly reduced activity against drug-resistant isolates (MICs ranging from 16 to >64 mug/mL). Such cross-resistance greatly complicates the development of new drugs via the optimization of existing agents. As emphasized in the WHO report, despite posing a growing threat to human health, fungal infections receive very little attention and resources globally. Thus, the research on new antifungal drugs with novel structures, new targets and mechanisms is urgently needed to human health.
The structural optimization of the thiosemicarbazone compounds.
Fig 1

Our group previously reported the discovery of novel antifungal compounds bearing a thiosemicarbazone scaffold, represented by compound 5r (Fig. 1). Compound 5r demonstrated promising in vitro antifungal activity against C. auris, C. glabrata, and C. krusei, and moderate activity against C. albicans and C. neoformans. In the present study, we report the further optimization of lead compound 5r by replacing the phenol ring with an 8-hydroxyquinoline moiety, a privileged structure known to be present in broad-spectrum antimicrobial agents such as clioquinol and nitroxoline, which exhibit antifungal, antibacterial, antiviral, and antiparasitic activities. To date, there are no reports on the antifungal research of 8-hydroxyquinolin-5-ylidene thiosemicarbazone derivatives. We have designed and synthesized compounds A5-A32 by introducing diverse aliphatic and aromatic groups at the amino side (R1 and R2) of the thiosemicarbazone. Compared to clioquinol (CQ), fluconazole (Diflucan), amphotericin B (AmB), and lead compound 5r, the synthesized compounds A5-A32 exhibited broader antifungal spectra and more potent activity against C. neoformans, C. parapsilosis, C. glabrata, C. krusei, and C. auris.
Results and discussion
Chemistry
Reagents and conditions: (a) 1,1'-Thiocarbonyldiimidazole, THF, 0  C, 1 h; (b) NH2NH2 H2O, THF, r.t., 1 h; (c) EtOH, 80  C.
Scheme 1

The synthetic route for the preparation of target compounds A5-A32 is outlined in Scheme 1. The secondary amines 1 reacted with 1,1'-thiocarbonyldiimidazole in THF at 0  C gave intermediate 2, which then reacted in situ with hydrazine hydrate to give compound 3 without further purification. Compounds A5-A32 were obtained via the coupling reaction of the substituted hydrazinecarbothioamides 3 with 8-hydroxyquinoline-5-carbaldehyde 4.
In vitro antifungal activity

passages.text: Abbreviations: MIC, minimum inhibitory concentration; C. alb, Candida albicans; C. neo, Cryptococcus neoformans; C. par, Candida parapsilosis; C. kru, Candida krusei; C. tro, Candida tropicalis; C. gla, Candida glabrata; C. aur, Candida auris; FLC: fluconazole; AmB, amphotericin B; CQ, Clioquinol.

All target compounds A5-A32 were submitted to preliminary screening for in vitro antifungal activity by determining the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) against seven common human pathogenic fungi including C. albicans SC5314, C. neoformans H99, C. parapsilosis 22,019, C. krusei 4946, C. tropicalis 2718, C. glabrata 537, C. auris 922, as shown in Table 1. FLC, AmB and CQ were used as reference drugs. MICs were determined using the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CISI, M27-A3 and M60) standard micro broth dilution method with minor modification. The MICs were defined as the minimum concentration of drug to inhibit 50 % growth of fungal cells compared to that of a drug-free control.
All target compounds A5-A20 showed in vitro antifungal activity against the tested seven fungal pathogens with MICs ranging from 4 to <= 0.0313 mug/mL as shown in Table 1.

Compound A5, which is originally designed by replacing the 2-hydroxyphenyl group of lead 5r with 8-hydroxyquinolin-5-yl group, showed moderate antifungal activity against the seven tested fungal pathogens with MIC values range of 0.25-4 mug/mL. This encouraged us to fix the 8-hydroxyquinolin-5-ylidene thiosemicarbazone scaffold, then to optimize the 3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenyl amino group of A5 with a series of secondary amino groups (-NR1R2). The replacement of R1 and R2 with methyl and substituted aryl methylene groups yielded compounds A6-A20, most of which exhibited good antifungal activity with MICs of <= 0.0313 mug/mL against C. glabrata 537, C. auris 922, C. parapsilosis 22,019 and C. neoformans H99. The MICs of A6-A20 are 0.25-0.5 mug/mL against C. krusei 4946, 1-2 mug/mL against C. tropicalis 2718, and 0.25-2 mug/mL against C. albicans SC5314. Compounds A6-A20 showed more potent antifungal activity than the reference drugs FLC (0.125-16 mug/mL), AmB (1-8 mug/mL), and CQ (0.25-0.5 mug/mL). This indicated the introduction of 8-hydroxyquinolin-5-ylidene group, aryl methylene groups and methyl group to the thiosemicarbazone promotes their antifungal activity.

Among the compounds with aryl methylene groups bearing phenyl, pyridyl, and naphthalenyl ring, the pyridyl derivatives (A17, A18, A19) showed lower activity against C. neoformans H99 with higher MICs of 0.0625, 0.125, 0.0625 mug/mL, respectively, than that of the phenyl and naphthalenyl derivatives (A11, A14, amd A20) with MICs of <= 0.0313 mug/mL. Moreover, the MICs of compound A17, A18, and A19 against C. parapsilosis 22,019 are 0.125, 0.25, and 0.25 mug/mL, respectively, which are higher than the phenyl and naphthalenyl derivatives (A11, A14, and A20) with MICs of 0.0625 mug/ml. This finding indicates that the presence of an electron-deficient pyridyl ring negatively impacts their antifungal activity.

Compounds A6, A8, A9, A11, A14, and A15, bearing phenyl, 3-fluorophenyl, 4-fluorophenyl, 4-chlorophenyl, 4-trifluoromethylphenyl, and 4-methoxyphenyl groups, respectively, showed the same lowest MIC of <= 0.0313 mug/mL against C. glabrata 537, C. auris 922, and C. neoformans H99, which is more active than the other phenyl compounds among A6-A19.

Compounds A22-A32, designed and prepared by replacing groups R1 and R2 of A6-A20 with aliphatic rings including piperidine, pyrrolidine, or azetidine rings, showed decreased antifungal activity, which suggested that aliphatic rings are not favorable to their antifungal activity. Many of compounds A22-A32 also showed higher activity with MICs of 0.0625-0.125 mug/mL than FLC, AmB and CQ, thus indicated the 8-hydroxyquinolin-5-ylidene thiosemicarbazone scaffold plays an important role for their antifungal activity.

Notably, compound A14 is the most active compound with lowest MICs against the tested seven fungal pathogens, as shown in Table 1, including C. krusei 4946 (0.25 mug/mL) C. tropicalis 2718 (1 mug/mL), C. glabrata 537 (<= 0.0313 mug/mL), C. auris 922 (<= 0.0313 mug/mL), C. albicans SC5314 (0.25 mug/mL), C. parasilosis 22,019 (0.0625 mug/mL), C. neoformans H99 (<= 0.0313 mug/mL), respectively. Then, compound A14 was subjected to the second-round antifungal activity screening against the isolates shown in Table 2.

Compound A14 showed more potent activity against the isolates of Cryptococcus gattii (2 and E56672H), C. neoformans (D2-12 and D2-13), C. glabrata (259, 260 and 261), and C. auris (787, 788 and 799) with MICs ranging <= 0.0313-2 mug/mL, which is lower than that of lead 5r (0.25->16 mug/mL) and FLC (2->16 mug/mL). C. neoformans and C. auris are two of the four pathogens listed in the Critical Group by WHO in 2022, and C. glabrata is the first pathogen listed in the High Group, which means the current antifungal therapy cannot meet the clinic need and innovative antifungal agents are urgently need. Compound A14 demonstrated stronger antifungal activity than FLC, the standard therapeutic agent against both Candida glabrata and C. neoformans, and therefore deserves further investigation for its antifungal effect against the above-mentioned fungi.
Inhibitory effects of A14 against C. albicans hyphal formation

Filamentation microscopy in C. albicans SC5314 with or without the treatment of different concentrations of compound A14. Exponentially growing C. albicans SC5314 cells were transferred to RPMI-1640 liquid medium. The cellular morphology was photographed by using the inverted imaging microscope after incubation at 37  C for 3 h. The hyphal length was measured using ImageJ. ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.005, **** p < 0.0001. Scale bar = 100 mum.
Fig 2

Due to the high potency of compound A14, it was selected to further investigate the antifungal activity on hyphal formation in C. albicans SC5314. As shown in Fig. 2, when cultured in RPMI 1640 medium for 3 h, untreated control group exhibited extensive hyphal development in C. albicans SC5314. In contrast, treatment with 8 mug/mL (**** p < 0.0001,), 4 mug/mL (*** p < 0.005), and 2 mug/mL (** p < 0.01) of compound A14 resulted in a significant reduction in hyphal length compared to the control group, respectively.
Compound A14 inhibits the biofilm formation of pathogenic fungi

Anti-biofilm activity of compound A14. Effects of A14 on biofilm formation of C. albicans SC5314 (A) and C. neoformans H99 (B). C. albicans, Candida albicans; C. neoformans, Cryptococcus neoformans; ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.005, **** p < 0.0001, ns, not significant.
Fig 3

We further investigated the inhibitory effects of compound A14 on biofilm formation in C. albicans SC5314 and C. neoformans H99 strains. As demonstrated in Fig. 3, compound A14 exhibited a dose-dependent inhibitory activity against biofilm formation in both fungal pathogens. Specifically, treatment with 4 mug/mL of compound A14 achieved approximately 90 % inhibition of biofilm formation in C. albicans SC5314 and 70 % inhibition in C. neoformans H99. The anti-biofilm efficacy progressively increased with higher compound concentrations, reaching >90 % inhibition for both strains at 32 mug/mL. These results indicate that compound A14 demonstrates potent concentration-dependent suppression of fungal biofilm development, with complete biofilm inhibition observed at the highest tested concentration.

passages.text: Fig 4

To determine the safety of the optimal compound A14, we evaluated its cytotoxicity on HUVEC and Caco-2 cells. As shown in Fig. 4A, compound A14 exhibited slight toxicity toward HUVECs, with an IC50 value of approximately 2 mug/mL, which is more toxic than FLC (>64 mug/mL), AMB(8-16 mug/mL), 5r (16-32 mug/mL)[12] and CQ (9.177 mug/mL)[17]. In contrast, no significant toxicity was observed in Caco-2 cells at lower concentrations (Fig. 4B), with an IC50 value of approximately 32-64 mug/mL. However, at concentrations exceeding 16 mug/mL, A14 displayed higher toxicity than FLC (>64 mug/mL) but remained less toxic than AmB (16-32 mug/mL), and CQ (19.29 mug/mL). Collectively, these results indicate that A14 has acceptable cytotoxicity within the tested range.

(A)The BOILED-Egg model prediction of A14, 5r and FLC; (B) Bioavailability radar for A14; (C) Bioavailability radar for 5r; (D) Bioavailability radar for FLC; FLC: fluconazole.
Fig 5

In silico ADMET prediction of compounds A14, 5r and FLC was performed using SwissADME online free tool. The polarity and lipophilicity of small molecules were calculated by Brain Or IntestinaL EstimateD permeation (BOILED-Egg) method. According to Fig. 5A, compound A14 and FLC are both located in the white circle, representing that both compounds are highly absorbed through the gastrointestinal tract. The red-spotted compound A14, on the other hand, is not a substrate for P-glycoproteins, which might help to overcome the resistance mechanism mediated by the pathogenic fungus through the efflux pump. Furthermore, as shown in the bioavailability radar (Figs. 5B, 5C and 5D), compounds A14 and 5r are comparatively similar in terms of physicochemical properties, lipophilicity, solubility, pharmacokinetics and drug-likeness, unlike FLC where all the parameters are in the pink zone, suggesting that further optimization of compound A14 is required in the future.
Conclusion

In summary, this study successfully synthesized a series of novel 8-hydroxyquinolin-5-ylidene thiosemicarbazone derivatives that demonstrated promising in vitro antifungal activity against the seven fungal pathogens tested. Notably, compounds A6-A20 exhibited exceptional antifungal efficacy, with minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of <= 0.0313 mug/mL against C. auris, C. glabrata, C. neoformans, and C. parapsilosis, all of which are classified as critical or high-priority pathogens by the World Health Organization. Given that AmB and FLC are primary treatments for infections caused by C. neoformans, C. parapsilosis, and C. glabrata, our novel compounds, which displayed superior activity to both, warrant further optimization as innovative antifungal agents. In particular, compound A14 stood out as the most active, achieving the lowest MICs against each of the seven tested fungal pathogens and exhibiting remarkable potency against C. gattii, C. neoformans, C. glabrata, and C. auris, with significantly lower MICs than those of the lead compound 5r and FLC. Furthermore, A14 inhibited hyphal formation in C. albicans SC5314 at 8 mug/mL, and remarkably inhibited biofilm formation in both C. albicans SC5314 and C. neoformans H99, achieving >90 % suppression at 32 mug/mL. Additionally, the cytotoxicity of compound A14 on Caco-2 cells was found to be lower than that of AmB. Overall, compound A14 exhibits a combination of high-potency antifungal activity, a broad spectrum of efficacy, and low cytotoxicity. Although the current study is limited to in vitro evaluations and lacks in vivo efficacy or resistant strain profiling, these gaps are being actively addressed in ongoing research. Further studies are currently underway to optimize the structure of compound A14 and elucidate its target and mechanism of action.

passages.text: Experiment section
Strains and agents

C. albicans SC5314, C. glabrata strains (537, 259, 260, and 261), C. krusei 4946, C. parapsilosis ATCC 22019, C. tropicalis 2718, C. neoformans strains (H99, D2-12, and D2-13), C. gattii strains (2 and E56672H), C. auris (787, 788, 790, and 922), were from the fungi collection of our laboratory. Frozen stocks of isolates stored at -80  C in yeast extract-peptone-dextrose (YPD) medium (1 % yeast extract, 2 % peptone, 2 % dextrose) supplemented with 40 % (v/v) glycerol were cultured twice on YPD plates at 30  C before use. For the chemical part, all the solvents and agents (including reference drugs: AmB, CQ and FLC) were purchased from Adamas-beta, and used directly or dried prior to use if necessary.
Chemistry
Procedure for the synthesis of hydrazinecarbothioamides (3)

Amine (1, 10 mmol) was dissolved in THF (20 mL), and 1,1'-Thiocarbonyldiimidazole (10 mmol) was added into the mixture portion wise at 0  C, the resulting mixture was stirred at this temperature for 1 h. After the reaction was completed, hydrazine monohydride (100 mmol) was added dropwise, then the resulting mixture was stirred at this temperature for 2 h. After the reaction was completed, water (50 mL) was added and then the solid precipitated out. The solid is obtained by filtration and then vacuum dried at 50  C. The product was used directly in the next step without further purification.
Procedure for the synthesis of 8-Hydroxyquinolin-5-ylidene thiosemicarbazone derivatives (A5-A33)

8-hydroxyquinoline-5-carbaldehyde (4, 1 mmol) and the substituted hydrazinecarbothioamides (3, 1.1 mmol) was dissolved in 95 % Ethanol (10 mL), and the resulting mixture was stirred at 80  C for 2 h. After the reaction was completed, water (5 mL) was added and then the product precipitated out. The solid is obtained by filtration and washed with 95 % ethanol, then vacuum dried at 50  C.
In vitro antifungal activities assay

The MIC values of the target compounds were tested according to the broth microdilution protocol of the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI, M27-A3, M60) with minor modification, all compounds were screened in duplicate, and detailed procedures are provided in the supplementary material.
Filament inhibition assay
The Filament inhibition assay was performed as described previously. This experiment was repeated twice, and detailed procedures are provided in the supplementary material.
Biofilm formation assay
The in vitro biofilm formation assay was performed as described previously. This experiment was performed in triplicate, and detailed procedures are provided in the supplementary material.
Cell viability assay

The cytotoxic effect of compounds on HUVECs and Caco-2 viability was assessed by the cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8, Target Molecule Corp. USA) assay, This experiment performed in triplicate, and detailed procedures are provided in the supplementary material.
ADME/T prediction
The Swiss ADME software (www.swissadme.ch) was used to estimate individual ADME properties of compounds, the specific experimental operation details can be found in the supplementary material.

passages.text: Calcium binding by gamma-carboxyglutamic acid: it takes two to tether
Background

The small family of vitamin K-dependent proteins are characterized by posttranslational modification of specific glutamic acid residues to yield gamma-carboxyglutamic acid (Gla). Gla residues give these proteins calcium ion-binding properties, which are essential for a number of coagulation factors and mineralization processes. Biophysical characteristics of Gla are, however, incomplete, hindering molecular dynamics simulations and protein structure predictions.
Objectives

This study aimed to elucidate the general biophysical characteristics (pKa and KD) of calcium binding to gamma-carboxyglutamic acid in a protein environment and determine how positioning of gamma-carboxyglutamic acid influences cooperative calcium binding and protein structure.
Methods

Residue-based pKa of Gla carboxyl groups in model peptides was individually determined by measuring 1H and 13C nuclear magnetic resonance chemical shift changes as a function of pH. In addition, residue-based KD values of Ca2+ binding were determined using Ca2+ nuclear magnetic resonance titrations. Secondary structure of peptides and proteins was assessed using circular dichroism and nuclear magnetic resonance.
Results

Carboxylic acid groups present on Gla residues have 2 different pKa values of 2.62 +- 0.07 and 5.02 +- 0.05. In presence of calcium ions, pKa values drop to 2.54 +- 0.02 and 4.55 +- 0.04. Affinity of a single Gla residue for calcium is low (~15 mM); 2 Gla residues show cooperativity, resulting in a 25-fold increased affinity for calcium ions (0.6 mM). Finally, cooperative calcium ion binding led to increased alpha-helical content in model proteins.
Conclusion

Vitamin K-dependent proteins present Gla residues in a different manner but benefit from cooperative calcium ion binding. Experimentally determined pKa and KD values can be used for interpretation of binding interactions or for molecular dynamics simulations of Gla domains with unknown structure.
Essentials
gamma-Carboxyglutamic acid (Gla) is an essential amino acid for coagulation and mineralization.
Biophysical characteristics of Gla are not completely known.
Gla has 2 different pKa values that decrease in presence of calcium.
Two Gla residues are required for optimal calcium binding.
Introduction

Posttranslational carboxylation of glutamic acid (Glu) yields gamma-carboxyglutamic acid (Gla), an amino acid with a dicarboxylic acid and Ca2+-binding capabilities. Glu is converted to Gla via vitamin K-dependent carboxylation.

Proteins containing Gla amino acids are referred to as vitamin K-dependent (VKD) proteins. The most well-known are coagulation factors such as prothrombin and factor (F)VII, FIX, and FX and anticoagulants such as protein S, protein C, and protein Z. However, VKD proteins also include proteins associated with mineralization such as matrix Gla protein, osteocalcin, and Gla-rich protein (GRP). Gla residues are vital for the function of VKD proteins through their Ca2+-binding capabilities. However, mechanisms by which individual Gla residues bind calcium ions or how secondary structure influences Ca2+ binding are not well understood. In addition, acid dissociation constants (pKa) for Gla in a protein environment have not been experimentally determined. These biophysical characteristics are of great importance to molecular modeling approaches as they may be used to predict protein structure and function.

Molecular structures of (A) gamma-Carboxyglutamic acid (Gla)-domain of prothrombin (Protein Data Bank (PDB): 2PF2), (B) osteocalcin (PDB: 1Q8H) and (C) conantokin T (1ONT). Gla residues are shown as sticks in orange and calcium ions as gray balls, and N-terminus and C-terminus are denoted.

Multiple sequence alignment (MSA) of gamma-carboxyglutamic acid (Gla) domains of coagulation factors, Gas6, transmembrane Gla proteins, and mineralization proteins (all of human origin). Results shown are the result of 2 separate MSAs using Clustal Omega. Highlighted glutamic acid residues are posttranslationally modified to Gla. aFor clarity, the first 28 residues from matrix Gla protein (MGP) were omitted, position 2 in MGP contains an additional Gla residue.

VKD proteins involved in blood coagulation have highly homologous N-terminal Gla domains containing 9-13 Gla residues optimally spaced (i, i + 1 and i, I + 2) to ensure Ca2+ binding in a compact globular fold (Figures 1A and 2). Upon Ca2+ binding, a structural change is induced, leading to the exposure of phospholipid membrane-binding (exo)sites. The location of Ca2+ binding is highly conserved among the Gla domains of coagulation factors. In contrast to coagulation factors, bone mineralization VKD proteins such as osteocalcin and matrix Gla protein have very different Gla domain sequences. In this case, Gla residues are spaced in (i, i + 3 or i, i + 4) motifs that present Gla residues on 1 side of an alpha-helix (Figures 1B and 2). Specific Gla spacing may make binding to a calcium phosphate crystal lattice more favorable for the bone mineralization group of VKD proteins whereas the spacing in the coagulation group of proteins may be better suited for binding calcium ions.

passages.text: Crystal or nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) structures available for osteocalcin, FIX, FX and prothrombin show multiple Gla residues are involved in binding a single Ca2+ ion with an apparent ratio of 2 Gla residues per calcium ion. This may suggest cooperativity in Ca2+ binding. Previous studies have shown Gla residues in protein C have different affinities for calcium, with high and low affinity-binding sites. Moreover, binding affinities of some coagulation factor Gla domains for phospholipid membranes are known.

Previous studies have shown that side-chain carboxylic acids in Gla residues may have 2 different pKa values, similar to other dicarboxylic or tetracarboxylic acids such as methylmalonic acid or EDTA. In addition, the protonation state of Gla may be influenced by the surrounding protein structure as well as calcium binding. An early study has looked at pKa values of isolated D,L-Gla residues but detailed studies of Gla in a protein environment, including effects of neighboring Gla residues or calcium ions, are lacking.

We hypothesize that Ca2+ binding by Gla residues is cooperative and influenced by protein secondary structure. We therefore synthesized multiple model peptides incorporating Gla in random coil or defined secondary structure. Residue-based pKa of each Gla carboxyl group was individually determined by measuring 1H and 13C chemical shift changes as a function of pH. In addition, dissociation constants (KD) of Ca2+ binding were determined using a Ca2+ titration using NMR 13C spectroscopy. Secondary structure was determined using a combination of circular dichroism (CD) and NMR spectroscopy.
Materials and Methods
Fmoc synthesis of peptides

Rink amide resin (0.05 mmol) was swelled in dimethylformamide (DMF) (5 mL, 1 hour) and subsequently in dichloromethane (DCM) (5 mL, 1 hour). Initial Fmoc group was deprotected using 20% piperidine in DMF (2 mL) in a mechanical shaker (2 x 5 mins). Next, resin was washed with DMF (5 x 2 mL) and DCM (5 x 2 mL). Amino acids were subsequently iteratively coupled using the following steps: in short, the resin was washed with DMF (5 x 2 mL) and DCM (5 x 2 mL), and the Fmoc group of resin-bound amino acid was removed with 20% piperidine in DMF (2 x 2 mL x 5 minutess) with mechanical shaking, followed by resin washing with DMF (5 x 2 mL) and DCM (5 x 2 mL). Amino acids (0.2 mmol) were preactivated with OxymaPure (0.4 mmol), diisopropylcarbodiimide (DIC) (0.2 mmol) and DMF (1 mL), and added to the resin. Coupling time was 60 minutes for the first amino acid, and 40 minutes for all remaining amino acids at room temperature. After completion of the peptide chain and Fmoc deprotection, the resin was washed with DMF (5 x 2 mL) and DCM (5 x 2 mL), and the N-terminus was acetylated using 50/50 v/v pyridine and acetic anhydride (2 x 5 mins). After acetylation, the peptides were washed with DMF (5 x 2 mL) and DCM (5 x 2 mL). The peptides were cleaved from resin using a mixture of trifluoroacetic acid (TFA)/triisopropylsilane/H2O (90/5/5, 2 mL) at room temperature (2 hours). Following cleavage, TFA was evaporated with a stream of nitrogen gas, and subsequently the peptide was precipitated in diethyl ether (30 mL) and centrifuged (4500 rpm, 5 minutes). After centrifugation, diethyl ether was decanted, and the peptide was dissolved in 50% v/v MeCN in H2O (5 mL) and lyophilized. Impurities were removed using high-performance liquid chromatography at a gradient of 1% B/min. The final products were lyophilized and stored at -20  C. Gla residues were incorporated using Fmoc-Gla(OtBu)2-OH using a modified coupling protocol; Fmoc-Gla(OtBu)2-OH (2 equivalents) was preactivated in situ with DIC (2 equivalents) and OxymaPure (4 equivalents) in 2 mL DMF for 1 minute, added to the growing peptide chain and coupled for 60 minutes at room temperature with continuous N2 bubbling.
Boc synthesis of peptides

4-Methylbenzhydrylamine resin (0.1 mmol) was swelled in DMF (60 minutes) in an solid phase peptide synthesis reactor. Amino acids were manually coupled using the following steps: in short, the resin was washed with DMF (2 x 5 mL), followed by addition of neat TFA for Boc deprotection (2 x 1 min). Amino acids (0.2 mmol) were simultaneously preactivated with O-(1H-6-chlorobenzotriazole-1-yl)-1,1,3,3-tetramethyluronium in DMF (0.5 M, 1 mL) and i-Pr2NEt (0.2 mL). Resin was washed with DMF (4 x 3 mL) and the preactivated amino acid was added to the resin and reacted for 20 minutes at room temperature with continuous nitrogen bubbling. Following peptide chain assembly, the final Boc group was removed, and the resin was washed with DMF (2 x 5 mL). Optionally, peptides were acetylated with acetic anhydride in pyridine (1:1). After acetylation, the peptide was washed again with DMF and DCM, and dried. p-Cresol (4% v/v) was added to the dry sample, and the sample was cleaved from solid support with anhydrous HF (1 hour, 0  C). Gla residues were incorporated using Boc-Gla(OcHx)2-OH using a modified coupling protocol; resin was neutralized after TFA treatment using 5% i-Pr2Net in DMF (2 x 1 minute). Boc-Gla(OcHx)2-OH (2 equivalents) was preactivated in situ with DIC (2 equivalents) and OxymaPure (4 equivalents) in 2 mL DMF for 1 minute, added to the growing peptide chain and coupled for 60 minutes at room temperature with continuous N2 bubbling. After cleavage, the peptide was precipitated in diethyl ether and filtered. The peptides were redissolved in 50% v/v MeCN in H2O (25 mL). Impurities were removed using high-performance liquid chromatography at a gradient of 1% B/min. The final products were lyophilized and stored at -20  C.
NMR titrations

NMR measurements were performed on a Bruker AVANCE III HD 700 MHz NMR spectrometer equipped with a TCI (13C, 15N, 1H) cryoprobe. All samples were measured at a temperature of 286 K. Peptide samples (10 mM or 2 mM for conantokin T) were prepared in 5-mm NMR tubes containing 600 muL MilliQ water with 2% (v/v) D2O for lock, DSS-d6 (3.2 mM) and EDTA (0.13 mM). DSS-d6 was used as the chemical shift reference (0 ppm), and a small excess EDTA (0.13 mM) was used to remove potential divalent metal impurities present in the peptide sample or solvent.

To measure the NMR pH titration curves, pH values per titration point were adjusted using small additions of milliliter aliquots of NaOH and HCl stock solutions (0.1 N, 0.2 N, and 1 N). pH values were measured before and after every NMR experiment with a Thermo Scientific Orion 3-star Benchtop pH meter (Fisher Scientific) at 21  C, connected to a Thermo Scientific pH microelectrode (3 mm diameter). The pH meter was calibrated daily using standard calibration buffers (pH 4.01, 7.00, 10.01). To measure the Ca2+ titration curves, small aliquots of CaCl2 stock solution (100 mM and 1 M) were added stepwise to the prepared peptide samples at a constant pH (7.6). To assign all peptide resonances, several 2-dimensional (D) spectra were run at low pH and at regular intermediate pH intervals. The set of 2D spectra include Decoupling In the Presence of Scalar Interactions (DIPSI) (80 millseconds mixing time), Nuclear Overhauser Effect Spectroscopy (350-500 milliseconds mixing time), 13C-1H Heteronuclear Single Quantum Coherence (HSQC), 13C-HSQC-DIPSI (70 milliseconds mixing time), 13C-1H Constant Time-Heteronuclear Multiple Bond Correlation (CT-sHMBC) (using a 5- to 7.5-Hz transfer step optimized for detection of long-range proton to carbonyl connectivity's of Glu and Gla residues and water presaturation during the relaxation delay).

One-dimensional 1H and 13C spectra were averaged >32 and 256 scans, respectively. HSQC spectra were run at standard for 8 scans for 512 increments each, the DIPSI was run at standard for 4 scans and 256 increments each, and the selective 13C-1H CT-sHMBC was run for 16 scans and 256 to 292 increments each, covering a spectral range of 18 ppm in the carbonyl region. Optimal delay times for magnetization transfer in the sHMBC experiment were based on the experimental determined 3J(CD-HB1/2) and 2J(CD-HG) coupling constants (4.05 and 6.6 Hz, respectively) extracted from the proton-coupled 13C spectrum of fully deprotonated ethylmalonate. For all spectra, the 90  pulse length for maximum sensitivity was calibrated at each individual pH point, and this value varied between 10 and 20 microseconds (depending on the varying salt concentration after pH adjustments). For most 1D and 2D spectra, a cosine-squared apodization function was used before zero filling. 1H spectra were recorded with 32 or 64 scans, and water suppressing was achieved using excitation sculpting with gradients. Specific pulse sequence schemes that were used Supplementary Table S4.

For all peptides at all pH points, chemical shift profiles of most Gla (Glu) 13C and 1H resonances could be reconstructed as a function of pH and Ca2+ concentration, derived from high resolution 1H and 13C (proton-decoupled) spectra with support of data assigned by 2D NMR spectra.

The acquisition software used was Topspin 3.6.5 (Bruker GmbH). Xcrvfit 5.0.3 was used fit single and dual pKa profiles for the Gla chemical shift pH titration curves, and GraphPad Prism 10.4.1. (Dotmatics) was used to fit all single sigmoid Ca2+-binding curves and to generate the graph plots.

Data were fitted using the following formula to determine the binding affinity for peptides 1 to 6:where P represents the peptide concentration, [Ca2+] represents the Ca2+ concentration, Deltadeltaobs represents the observed change in chemical shift, Deltadeltamax represents the maximum change in chemical shift, and KD represents the binding affinity.

To account for cooperativity in the case of conantokin T, data were fitted using the following formula:where P represents the peptide concentration, [Ca2+] represents the Ca2+ concentration, Deltadeltaobs represents the observed change in chemical shift, Deltadeltamax represents the maximum change in chemical shift, n represents the Hill coefficient, and KD represents the binding affinity.
CD spectroscopy of osteocalcin P15-N26 and conantokin T

CD spectra were recorded on a Chirascan v100 (Applied Photophysics) spectrometer operating at wavelengths between 190 and 260 nm, wavelength intervals of 0.5 nm, and half-bandwidths of 1 nm using a 1-mm quartz cuvette. The sample cell temperature was set to 20  C. Before each sample measurement, a background measurement was performed without cuvette, followed by a blank measurement with experiment buffer.

Osteocalcin P15-N26 stock solutions (1 mg/mL in H2O with 100 muM EDTA) were diluted to 0.1 mg/mL in borate buffer (25 mM) with EDTA (100 muM) at pH 7.4 and mixed with 0%, 10%, 20%, or 30% trifluoroethanol (TFE). All samples were measured with and without CaCl2 (10 mM).

Conantokin T stock solutions (1 mg/mL in H2O with 100 muM EDTA) were diluted to 0.1 mg/mL in H2O and EDTA (100 muM). Conantokin T was measured at pH 2, 5, and 7.5 at 20  C. At 20  C and pH 7.5, 37.2 muM CaCl2, 186 muM CaCl2, and 372 muM CaCl2 were added to the conantokin T sample solution. Finally, at pH 7.5, a temperature titration was recorded from 20  C to 80  C at 5  C increments.
Conversion to mean residue ellipticity was performed using the following formula:

To determine the percentage alpha-helicity, the following formula was used:where  represents the observed ellipticity at 222 nm, and n represents the peptide chain length. Data were thereafter analyzed using GraphPad Prism version 10.4.1.

Gla residues are denoted as gamma. pKa values were determined based on delta-carbon and gamma-carbon chemical shift differences, average values are reported. Peptide concentration was 10 mM in all experiments.

Calcium ion-binding properties of gamma-carboxyglutamic acid likely depend on the protonation state of the amino acid. For this reason, we started with the determination of side-chain pKa values of Gla within a peptide chain. In order to rule out effects of charged or bulky neighboring amino acids, model peptides were synthesized with Gla residues flanked by glycine residues and N-terminus and C-terminus were acetylated and amidated, respectively. We synthesized peptides with a single Glu residue (1), a single Gla residue (2), 2 Gla residues directly next to each other (3), or 2 Gla residues spaced by a glycine (4) (Supplementary Figure S1). The pKa was determined by fitting chemical shift differences of Gla or Glu delta and/or gamma carbons as a function of pH (Table 1 and Supplementary Tables S1, S5 and S6).

Chemical shift of gamma-carboxyglutamic acid (Gla) delta (blue) and gamma (orange) carbons as a function of pH for (A) GGEGG (B) GGgammaGG (C) GGgammagammaG and (D) GGgammaGgammaGG. Numbering of delta carbons is arbitrary. Inflection points are indicated with dotted lines. Insets in (A) and (B) show chemical structure including numbering of carbon atoms of Glu and Gla, respectively. 13C data points were averaged over 256 scans.

Glu-containing peptide 1 displayed a typical sigmoid curve (Figure 3A), with a single inflection point and an observed pKa of 4.34, which is consistent with previously reported values for glutamic acid (4.34). Similar to other dicarboxylic acids such as malonic or oxalic acid, Gla-containing peptides were expected to have 2 unique pKa values. Moreover, previous research had indicated that titration curves for gamma-carboxyglutamic acid appeared to be biphasic.

As expected, titration curves of peptides 2 to 4 showed 2 distinct inflection points and thus 2 pKa values for each of the Gla residues present (Table 1 and Figure 3B-D). While absolute chemical shift differences were larger for delta carbons than for those gamma carbons and curves may appear different, fitted pKa values were similar (Supplementary Table S1). pKa values for peptides 2 to 4 ranged from 2.47 to 2.70 for pKa1 and 4.99 to 5.08 for pKa2. We did not observe significant effects of directly adjacent Gla residues or those in spatial proximity, although pKa1 is slightly lower in peptide 2 with a single Gla residue compared with peptides 3 and 4 with 2 Gla residues. We next moved away from a model system to a more physiological peptide sequence to investigate whether the protonation state could be influenced by other amino acids, such as positively charged arginines, bulky hydrophobic amino acids such as leucine and valine, or other Gla residues. Two peptides derived from human osteocalcin (P15-N26 [PLgammaPRRgammaVSgammaLN]) with 3 gamma-carboxyglutamic acid residues in both uncarboxylated (5) and carboxylated form (6) were therefore synthesized. The native cysteine on position 23 was replaced with serine to avoid disulfide formation. Uncarboxylated glutamic acid residues in 5 showed pKa values comparable with those found in model peptide 1. Similarly to model peptides 2 to 4, peptide 6 showed 2 inflection points for each of the Gla residues present (Supplementary Figure S2). For all 3 Gla residues present, both pKa values of 6 were within range of those found in peptides 2 to 4 (Table 1). We therefore conclude that in isolated random coil peptide structures, pKa values of Gla are constant regardless of neighboring amino acids or number of Gla residues.
Calcium ion binding leads to a more stable charged state of Gla residues

Chemical shift of gamma-carboxyglutamic acid (Gla) delta carbons as a function of pH in absence (blue) and presence (green) of a 5-fold excess of calcium ions for (A) GGEGG and (B) GGgammaGG. Inflection points are indicated with vertical dotted lines. 13C data points were averaged over 256 scans.

Plasma concentrations of calcium range from 2.0 to 2.6 mM; Gla residues present in coagulation factors are thus always exposed to calcium ions. To investigate whether Ca2+ contributes to an energetically favorable environment for charge stabilization of the Gla carboxyl side chains, pH titrations were repeated in presence of a 5-fold excess of CaCl2 (10 mM peptide and 50 mM CaCl2). As expected, addition of Ca2+ had a negligible effect on the pKa values of uncarboxylated peptides 1 and 5 (Figure 4A, Table 1, and Supplementary Figure S3). Carboxylated peptides 2 to 4 and 6 showed a minor shift (average, -0.09) for the first inflection point as a result of adding Ca2+. However, the second inflection point showed a larger shift to lower pH, indicating a reduction in pKa (average, -0.47) (Figure 4B, Table 1, Supplementary Table S2 and Supplementary Figures S3 and S4). This may be explained by Ca2+ bridges being formed between Gla carboxylic acid side chains, stabilizing their charge, making the second carboxylic acid easier to deprotonate.
